### 2026-09-11 — A library that arrives after the block that needs it (`E7-T24`)

**The client ran `E7-T16`'s five-step demo in the application and reported *all good*.** That is
the evidence the suite could not give: two banners on one graph, the block running once agreed, no
banner on reopening, a rebuilt DLL asking again, and the libraries let go on *New*. The demo lives
in `artifacts/package-demo/`, which is gitignored, with its steps in a `README.txt` beside it.

**What.** `E7-T24` was found by reading the code, and its row said to withdraw it if the test was
green before any change. **It was red.** `ABlockThatFailedForAMissingLibraryRunsOnceTheLibraryArrives`
opens a graph whose block names a type from a library, evaluates it (fails), adds the library to
the catalogue exactly as *Add as a library…* and Local assemblies do, evaluates again — and the block
still failed, on the line the row predicted.

**Fixed in the catch-all rather than on each path.** `EvaluateAsync` already rebuilt the blocks when
the shared declarations moved (`E6-T36`), precisely so that no gesture had to remember to. It now
also compares the catalogue's version with the one the blocks were compiled against, and on a move
does what agreeing to a graph's packages does: a forced rebuild and a fresh cache epoch
([N146](NOTES.md)). Four paths change the catalogue, and none of them changed.
`SparkSession.ReferencesVersion()` reads the version **without** building the script factory,
because it is asked on every run and a session that never placed a code block must not load Roslyn
to answer it.

**One ordering decision that would have failed silently.** The version is recorded at the **start**
of `AdoptGraph`, not the end. A graph arrives already compiled, and `AdoptGraph` then lets go of the
previous graph's packages — a change those blocks have not seen. Recording at the end would have
marked them current against a catalogue they were not compiled against, and a block depending on the
released library would have gone on succeeding with an assembly the graph no longer has.

**What it does not do, deliberately.** A block recovers on the next **run**, not the moment its
library lands, so a Manual session shows it red until Run. Starting a run from a package gesture is
a second behaviour change and was not this step's to make.

**`E7-T25` registered.** `spark check` and `spark run` ignore a graph's package folder — seen while
preparing the demo, when `spark check` reported `Greeter` missing for a graph that runs in the
window. The row says the trust question is the work, not the wiring.

**Verified.** The reproduction test red before the fix and green after. The whole of
`Spark.UI.Tests`, **1,347**, run on its own first, because a forced rebuild moves node slots and a
test holding a slot across an evaluation would have noticed; none did. Then the three gates: build
clean with zero warnings, format clean, docs harness green, **3,055 tests over ten executables**,
zero failed, zero skipped.

and before `nodes`, omitted when empty; `PackagesFormatVersion = 5`, written only by a document that
carries a list; `CurrentFormatVersion` 4 → 5. `MinimumReaderVersion` and `Capture` learnt the new
count. **Nothing writes the section yet**, which is why this can be a commit of its own: no file any
user saves differs by a byte.

**Split because the row is two things.** The format is a promise to every future reader and is
worth getting right on its own. Using it — save records, open checks — is behaviour, and it has a
decision in it (*fail loudly* as a refusal, or as a named list) that deserves its own commit.

**The row's two open decisions, taken as it recommended.** A path is relative to the `.spark` and
kept **verbatim**: the document neither resolves nor confines it, because only the host knows where
the file lives, so confinement to the sibling folder is step B's checker. And **no hash**: trust is
decided per hash at load time by `E7-T16`'s gate, and a record that pinned bytes would make every
rebuild of a library a change to the graph.

**`E7-T7` re-proved rather than inherited**, at the document level. A file carrying the section
re-saves byte for byte; a file without it is still version 1, with no `packages` key anywhere; the
list is canonical however it was assembled — sorted, and one entry for two spellings of case,
because the file system does not tell them apart. **Checked before the constant moved**: the refusal
tests stand for *a newer build* with versions 99 and 999999. A test that had used 5 for that would
have started passing for the wrong reason the moment 5 became readable.

**Verified.** Seven new tests in `PackageRecordTests`; `Spark.Engine.Tests` at 557, green. Then the
three gates: build clean with zero warnings, format clean, docs harness green, **3,062 tests over
ten executables**, zero failed, zero skipped.

### 2026-09-11 — The file names its packages: written, and checked on open (`E7-T17`, step B)

**What.** Three functions in `GraphPackages`, beside the finder, and the view model using them on
both doors. `Entries` lists the folder as a file records it — one path per package folder and per
loose `.dll`, **listed and not hashed**, because it runs on every save and `Discover` would read
every byte of a thirty-megabyte CAD API to learn nothing a record needs. `Absent` checks a recorded
list against the folder. `ToRecord` decides what a save writes: what the file already named, plus
what is in the folder now.

**The decision the step had to take, and took: *fail loudly* means the graph opens with a named
list.** Refusing would have been a reading of the client's words, and a worse one: `E7-T6`'s
promise is that nobody's graph is damaged by opening it on a machine without a package, and a
refused graph is one nobody can open to repair. The names go in the banner that already names
absent node packages, before the gate and before any node is built, so the first thing a user sees
is *'Helpers.dll' is not there* and never *the type 'Helper' could not be found*. The banner's
**Find** button stays for node packages only — no feed search puts back a file somebody dropped in
by hand.

**Three rules, each protecting somebody else's graph.**

- **A missing entry is never dropped on save.** That is `E7-T7`, re-proved through the window:
  `AGraphNamingAMissingPackageSavesUnchanged` opens a file naming a package this machine does not
  have, saves it untouched, and compares the text.
- **The lookup ignores the folder a path was recorded under** and goes to the folder named after
  the file as it is now. That is what makes a rename in Explorer answerable: the banner names both
  folders, and renaming one to match fixes it — the ADR's *a rename outside Spark is not tracked*,
  made actionable instead of merely true.
- **A path that leaves the folder is never looked up.** Rooted, or climbing out with `..`, it is
  reported absent without touching the disk, so a file from somebody else cannot ask this machine
  whether anything outside the graph's folder exists. The test names three files that do exist and
  asserts all three are absent.

**One ordering change in the view, and why it must stay** ([N147](NOTES.md)). Save serialised the
graph and then asked where to put it. The text of a `.spark` now depends on its own name, so the
order had to flip: ask, then `TrySaveDocument(target)`. The cost is that a graph the format cannot
write is reported after the dialog rather than before it.

**Found by the design rather than by a test: `E7-T19` became urgent.** Save As records the packages
under the new name, and until the folder is copied with it, a saved-as graph reopens with every
package named absent. That is honest — the files really are not beside the copy — but it is the
first thing a user would hit, so it is *Next action*.

**Verified.** Sixteen new tests: nine for the checker in `Spark.Packages.Tests`, seven through the
window in `Spark.UI.Tests`. The byte-identity guards were run alongside them on their own before the
gates — `ExampleGraphTests`, `MissingPackageBannerTests` — because a save that suddenly wrote a
`packages` key into a graph with no folder would have broken every one. None did. Then the three
gates: build clean with zero warnings, format clean, docs harness green, **3,078 tests over ten
executables**, zero failed, zero skipped.

### 2026-09-11 — Save As carries the package folder (`E7-T19`)

**Why now.** `E7-T17` made Save As record a graph's packages under the new file's name. Until the
folder came with it, a saved-as graph reopened with every package named absent — honest, and the
first thing a user would have hit.

**What.** `GraphPackages.CopyFolder(from, to)`, and the view calling it between asking where and
producing the text: **ask, copy, serialise, write**, so the new file records what is actually
beside it. `NoteSavedTo(path)` replaces `NoteGraphPath` on the save path; it re-derives what the
file now records, re-checks the banner, and re-points the package gate when the path moved.

**Three decisions, each recorded in ADR-0024.**

- **Merge without overwriting** when the destination already has a folder. Saving over
  `tower.spark` means that folder belongs to the graph being replaced; replacing its `Helpers.dll`
  with a different build would change what that graph computes without anybody asking. Kept files
  are counted, and the status bar says so.
- **The gate moves with the file.** After Save As the graph installs into the new folder (`E7-T21`),
  and a gate still keyed to the old one would release by the wrong folder when the next graph
  opened, leaving the new installs referenced. A plain Save does not move it — re-opening would drop
  and re-add every reference and rebuild every block for no change.
- **A failed copy does not stop the save.** The file is written, the status bar carries the reason,
  and on reopening the banner names what did not arrive — something a user can act on, where a save
  that silently did not happen is not.

**Verified.** Six tests on the copy in `Spark.Packages.Tests` — including *merged, nothing
overwritten* and *a staged download is not carried* — and two through the window. The load-bearing
one saves under a new name, reopens the copy, and asserts that nothing is absent, that the original
kept its folder, and that the gate followed the file. Then the three gates: build clean with zero
warnings, format clean, docs harness green, **3,086 tests over ten executables**, zero failed, zero
skipped.

### 2026-09-11 — `--open` asks before it runs, and so does a screenshot (`E6-T40`)

**What.** The constructor builds a `--open` document without going through `TryOpenDocument`, and it
adopted it with evaluation on and never asked `ScriptTrustStore` — so a graph with code blocks ran on
`--open` where File ▸ Open held it back. It now reads the file's code blocks before anything is built,
decides `run` exactly as `TryOpenDocument` does, and adopts once with `evaluate: run`, setting the
pending count, origin and banner. The banner sentence and the *waiting for trust* diagnostic are one
constant each now, shared by both doors.

`TryOpenDocument` once the window exists — is the one the constructor's own remarks forbid: a second
adoption is a second run, and that has already produced a window showing one graph's diagnostics
under another, twice.

run, and to make sure there is one, `CaptureWhenReadyAsync` ran it itself. So `--open FILE
--screenshot` would still have executed an untrusted graph's code blocks after the constructor had
carefully not run them ([N148](NOTES.md)). The capture now skips its own run when the graph is waiting
for trust. **A screenshot is not consent**: a held-back graph is photographed unrun, with its banner,
and a trusted file runs as before.

**Verified.** `AGraphOpenedAtStartupWithACodeBlockIsNotRun` was watched red, then green; its mirror

### 2026-09-11 — The command line reads a graph's package folder (`E7-T25`)

**What.** `spark run` and `spark check` now run `GraphPackageGate` over a graph's `<name>.packages`

records is referenced; anything else refuses the graph, one line per assembly with its full SHA-256
and a line saying how to agree. `--trust-packages` references the rest for that run only, through a
new `GraphPackageGate.AgreeOnce()` that shares `Agree`'s body and skips the write. A package the file
names and the folder lacks (`E7-T17`) prints as a warning, which `check --strict` fails.

reads and a DLL is not ([N149](NOTES.md)).

them*: a block would then fail naming a type, and the cause is the folder. *Record nothing*: the
trust file is shared with the desktop application, so a scheduled job would become consent in the
window. *Only for a graph with code blocks*: nothing else compiles against the folder, and it keeps
Roslyn unloaded for everything else (`E6-T14`).

`Main` passes the console, and nothing else about the verb changed.

### 2026-09-11 — A `.spark` file's text is written as typed (`E3-T24`)

**What.** One setting in `SparkFile.Write`: `Encoder = JavaScriptEncoder.UnsafeRelaxedJsonEscaping`.
`+`, `<`, `>`, `&`, `'` and non-ASCII are now written as typed, and a quotation mark as `\"`, which
JSON requires. The client's demo files had shown `return 1 \u002B 1;`.

**The decision the row asked for: accept the one-time diff** ([D23](PRD.md#13-decision-log),
[ADR-0026](adr/0026-spark-file-text-is-written-as-typed.md)). An older file reads back to the same
document and takes the new spelling the first time it is saved; every file since re-saves byte for
byte, so `E7-T7` holds. Writing relaxed only for changed text was rejected: the reader decodes every
string, so the writer cannot know an old spelling without carrying it through `GraphDocument`, and a
file would then hold two spellings of one character for good.

**Checked before changing, because each would have made the change wrong.** `ScriptTrustStore`, the
compiled-assembly cache and a block's key all hash **decoded** script strings, never file bytes, so
trust and caches survive. `IsModified` compares against a fresh write of the document that was
opened, not the text on disk, so an older file does not open marked modified. No committed `.spark`
file holds an escaped character, so no example changes.

**Two encoder facts, in [N150](NOTES.md) because the next person will otherwise rediscover them.**
No encoder setting writes a character beyond the Basic Multilingual Plane literally — an emoji is
still an escaped surrogate pair — and `JavaScriptEncoder.Create(UnicodeRanges.All)`, which looks like
the conservative choice, still escapes `+` and the quotation mark.

**Also.** The ADR index had stopped at 0023; 0024 and 0025 were never added to it. Both are there
now, beside 0026.

**Verified.** Four tests in `ScriptTextSpellingTests`. `ScriptTextIsWrittenAsTyped` and
`NonAsciiInATitleAndANoteIsWrittenAsTyped` were **watched red** against the old encoder, then green.
The old-file test builds its fixture with System.Text.Json's default encoder and asserts the fixture
really holds `\u002B`, `\u0022` and `\u00E7` before relying on it, so it cannot quietly stop
being an old file. The emoji test pins the surrogate spelling N150 claims. Then the three gates: build
clean with zero warnings, format clean, docs harness green, **3,103 tests over ten executables**, zero
failed, zero skipped.

**A trap in the tooling, recorded because it cost two attempts.** Text handed to the file-writing
tools has `\uXXXX` sequences decoded on the way in: a doc comment written with the escape for `+`
landed as a bare `+`, and a sentence meant to say *writes `+` as the escape* said *writes `+` as `+`*.

were written through a script with a placeholder**, and anything written that way should be grepped

### 2026-09-11 — A tessellation is made at the tolerance asked for (`E12-T20`)

**The defect, found where N87 said to look.** The shim meshed what its comment called a copy of the
shape: `TopoDS_Shape meshed = shape->shape;`. A `TopoDS_Shape` is a handle, so that shares every
face, and `BRepMesh_IncrementalMesh` stores the triangulation **on the face** — so the caller's shape
kept the first mesh it ever had, and the mesher's rule of keeping a triangulation finer than the one
asked for served it to every coarser request after. It was also a race: two threads tessellating one
shape wrote into the same faces ([N151](NOTES.md)).

**The proper fix is two lines of C++ — and this machine can no longer build them.** Rebuilding the
shim failed: `C:\devcpkg` is gone, `VCPKG_ROOT` is unset, and nothing under `C:\` holds an
OpenCascade CMake config. The staged `artifacts/native/win-x64/` is intact, so everything runs and the
OCCT tests do not skip; nothing native can change. Reinstalling is about 1.3 hours at full CPU on the
client's machine and was **not started unasked**. The C++ edit was **reverted rather than committed
uncompiled**, and is written out on `E13-T21`, blocked on the toolchain.

**So the fix that ships is managed, through binaries that exist.** `OcctBrepKernel.Place`: a held
shape's first tessellation meshes the shape itself, exactly as cheap as before; every later tolerance
meshes a **fresh import** of the shape read back out, which shares nothing with it; if that import
ever fails, the shape itself is meshed, which is the old behaviour. A per-shape, per-tolerance cache
(`ConditionalWeakTable`, four meshes a shape) serves exact repeats, because the viewport tessellates
every solid on every scene rebuild and a correct answer must not also be a slow one. `ClaimInPlace`
hands the in-place mesh to exactly one caller, which ends the race as well.

**Verified.** Four tests in `TessellationToleranceTests`, every shape **asserted kernel-held** — a
managed shape is imported afresh on every call and could never show the defect, so a test built on
one passes either way. Removing the isolation reproduced N87 exactly: a coarse request after a fine
one returned **5,756 triangles where a fresh shape gives 92**, failing
`ACoarseRequestAfterAFineOneIsAsCoarseAsOnAFreshShape` and
`AShapeWithTrimmedFacesKeepsItsVolumeWhenMeshedAgain`, the second being the check that the
read-out-and-import route carries a boolean's trimmed faces faithfully. Removing the cache lookup
failed `TheSameRequestTwiceReturnsTheSameMesh`. With the fix the coarse count is exactly 92 either
way. Then the gates, **3,111 tests over ten executables**, and `--graph solids --screenshot` to see
the viewport still draw.

**Environment fact corrected**, because it would cost the next session an hour: the journal said
OpenCascade was installed at `C:\devcpkg`, and it is not.

### 2026-09-11 — A closest point no longer stops on a saddle (`E2-T62`)

**The row named two suspects, and neither was it.** It suggested `RevolutionSurface`'s analytic
derivatives, then the seam. The derivatives check out by hand (`a × offset`, `a × (a × offset)`,
`a × R p′`, `R p″`) and `Check` wraps the seam correctly.

**Then two hypotheses of my own, each measured and rejected.** First: after `ReseedOffDegeneracy`
moves to a point farther than the seed, `Descend` compared every Newton step with the *seed's*
distance and refused real progress. Plausible, fixed, and the miss did not move (8.525e-5 to
8.533e-5). Second: the Hessian is indefinite where the first fundamental form is nearly singular, so
Newton's step is a saddle step; a Gauss-Newton fallback was added, and the miss did not move
(8.56e-5). **Neither change shipped** — an unproven change is one the next refactor removes without
anybody noticing, and a proven-unneeded one is worse.

**Then a trace, which is what should have come first.** Six marked lines in `ClosestPoint` and a
single-file program (`dotnet run cp.cs`, with `#:project` pointing at `src/Spark.Geometry`) printed
the real iteration: the seed on the fold, the reseed half a cell in, **Newton's first step
overshooting below `v = 0` and clamping onto the fold**, then converging there in three steps. On
the fold both orthogonality conditions hold — the radius changes only at second order in `v` — so
it is a stationary point of the distance, and it is a **saddle** ([N152](NOTES.md)).

**The fix.** `Surface.EscapeSaddle`: at a converged point, the distance's Hessian — the very matrix
Newton solves with — has a clearly negative eigenvalue at a saddle and none at a minimum; move along
that eigenvector, both senses, with halvings, and let Newton resume. The Newton loop became
`Surface.Refine` so it can run again, up to three escapes. A minimum costs one evaluation of the
second derivatives to confirm. The threshold is relative, because a true minimum on a fold has a
singular matrix whose zero eigenvalue rounding gives a sign.

**Verified.** The query answers to 1.7e-17 of the reach (was 8.56e-5); `(0.999, 0.001)` to 1.6e-17
(was 8.57e-7). `APointBesideAFoldIsItsOwnClosestPoint` holds three points to 1e-12 and, with the
escape removed, fails on two of them (2.5e-4 and 2.5e-6). The 805 geometry tests are unchanged. Then
the gates, **3,114 tests over ten executables**.

**What it found (`E2-T63`).** Tightening the property further reached a point exactly *on* the fold,
answered 1.8e-5 of the reach away — identically before and after this change, checked by running the
committed code against the same queries. It is a genuine minimum with a singular Hessian, where the
distance is quartic and Newton creeps: slow convergence to the right point rather than fast
convergence to the wrong one, and a different row. So `SurfaceProperties` tightens from 1e-3 to
1e-4 rather than to 1e-10, which is also why the named example test exists: at 1e-4 the property
alone would not catch this defect's return.

**A scripting trap, recorded because it cost a round.** A long Python script passed to bash inline
failed to parse and ran nothing; documents with this much prose are now written to a script file in
the scratchpad and run from there.

### 2026-09-11 — A point exactly on a fold is its own closest point (`E2-T63`)

**Traced first, this time.** The marked-line pattern from `E2-T62` on the `(0.999, 0)` rim query:
the seed at `(2π, 0)` was on the right row; `ReseedOffDegeneracy` stepped *off* it, because it treats
the smaller derivative as the collapsed one and on a fold neither is; Newton's first step from there
landed 1.3e-3 from the target - enormously better than the reseed, a hair worse than the seed - and
`Descend`, comparing with the seed, refused it. `Contract`'s compass search then crept down a sheared
valley to v = 4.6e-3. **`Descend` now compares with where the iteration is and `Refine` keeps the
best apart** - the change measured and rejected for `E2-T62` because nothing reached it, proved here by
a query that does. That point answers to 2.4e-13 of the reach.

**The `(0.99, 0)` trace showed the other half: Newton going linear**, every step exactly two thirds of
the last - the signature of a quartic minimum - and running out of iterations at 1.25e-11. **A step
stretch of 1/(1 - r) once the ratio settled finished it off exactly, and was taken out**: comparing the
current code, the code without the stretch and the committed code on seven queries showed it made
`(0.01, 0.001)`, just past the seam's other end, worse by eight orders of magnitude (exact to 8.4e-7).
That was found only because the property was measured at 1e-11 and 1e-12 rather than at the bound it
asserts. **Measure one order tighter than you assert**; it is where the next defect is.

**So the bound is measured, not chosen.** At 1e-10 the property fails on a rim point in another scene at
1.32e-10 of the reach; at 1e-9 it passes everywhere. The closest-point bound goes from 1e-4 to **1e-9**,
six orders tighter than the 1e-3 it read before `E2-T62`, and it now catches either defect's return on
its own. `APointOnAFoldIsItsOwnClosestPoint` holds four rim points to 1e-10.

**Two mistakes of mine, both caught before commit.** The `sed` that measured the bound matched a second,
unrelated bound in the same file - the closed-surface gap check at line 293, `1e-9` - and left it at
`1e-4`; it is back at `1e-9`, and bounds are now edited by a script that changes only the first match.
And the first mutation meant to prove the fix - passing `best` to `Descend` again - also stopped
`Refine` recording any improvement, so it failed unrelated pole and apex tests and proved nothing. The
proof that stands is a byte-exact revert: the committed `Surface.cs` run against the new theory fails
at the 99.9% rim point.

**Found for the next step**: `E3-T10`, the impure-node declaration, is already delivered as
`[NodeSideEffect]`, with the importer, the cache key and the downstream test all in place. Its re-check
searched for `Impure`.

### 2026-09-11 — `E3-T10` closed by reconciliation: it was `[NodeSideEffect]` all along

**What.** The row said *half built*: the run epoch reached `CacheKey`, but no attribute let a node
declare itself impure, and its 2026-09-09 re-check proved it with `grep -rn Impure src/Spark.Api`.
The declaration exists — it is called **`[NodeSideEffect]`** — and so does everything the row said
would close it: `NodeImporter` reads it from a member or its declaring type into
`NodeDefinition.IsSideEffect`, `CacheKey.For` mixes the run epoch in for that node only, and
`EvaluationTests.AnImpureNodeReRunsEveryTimeAndPoisonsEverythingDownstream` asserts the downstream
value moving, zero cache hits and both nodes re-evaluated, beside a pure control.

**Read before closing, as the reconciliation rule requires**: the test asserts the key poisoning by
its consequence (no cache hits, a changed downstream value), not by checking a flag, so it would fail
if the epoch stopped reaching the key. **No code moved.**

**The lesson is about re-checks.** A re-check that searches for a *word* proves only that the word is
absent. The row, the attribute's own documentation and the cache key's comments all used *impure*;
the type used *side effect*. Search for the behaviour's call site — here `IsSideEffect` at
`CacheKey.cs` — rather than for the name the row happened to use.

### 2026-09-11 — Autosave and crash recovery (`E8-T13`)

**What.** `RecoveryStore` in `Spark.Host`: one working copy per window session, a JSON file holding
the process id, the graph's file and its `.spark` text, written by replacing a temporary file so a crash
mid-write leaves the previous copy. `MainWindowViewModel.KeepRecovery` runs from `RefreshHistory` and
`MarkSaved`, so the copy follows `IsModified` rather than the edit count. The next start offers a
leftover in a banner under the menu — triangle, **Restore**, **Discard** — and never restores silently;
a restored graph opens *modified*, still belonging to its file, and through the ordinary open, so a
graph with code blocks comes back not run.

**Three decisions, each written where the next reader looks.** *Off in the view model until the window
turns it on* ([N153](NOTES.md)): well over a thousand headless tests edit a view model, and a default
that wrote to the real folder would have had the real application offering the user a test run's graphs.
*A running process's copy is not offered, checked by id and name*: a second Spark must not present the
first one's open work as lost, and ids are reused. *A copy identical to its file is dropped silently*,
compared after reading the file through the same writer, because an older file may spell the same graph
differently (`E3-T24`).

**Verified.** Ten tests in `CrashRecoveryTests`, every store a scratch folder, a crash faked through
the store's liveness check. Removing the write from `RefreshHistory` failed six; ignoring the liveness
check failed `ARunningSessionsCopyIsNotOffered`. **Then a real crash**: Spark launched with
`--collapse 2` wrote a working copy carrying its own process id, `Stop-Process` left the copy behind,
and the next start showed the banner, photographed. The test's files were removed afterwards; the
recovery folder ended as it began, empty.

**What went wrong on the way, all caught before commit.** The first run's build failed on CA1822
(`Discard` touched no instance data) and a test result was read from it anyway — the rule that a
failed build followed by a result is not a result, applied late; `Discard` now does nothing on a store
that keeps nothing, which is also correct. The banner read *"a graph that was never saved had changes
that were never saved"*, seen only in the screenshot; an unsaved graph now has its own sentence. The
full UI suite failed `TheRibbonKeepsOnlyTheRunControls`, which excludes banner buttons by name and now
excludes these two as well — the same argument it already accepts, not a new ribbon exception. And a
second real-app check planted a copy with PowerShell 5.1's `ConvertTo-Json`, which serialises a
`Get-Content -Raw` string as an object with its path metadata; the store correctly ignored the malformed
file, so that screenshot showed nothing. The genuine crash above is the stronger check and it passed.

### 2026-09-11 — The kernel's long loop takes a cancellation token (`E3-T12` step A)

**What.** `Tessellation.Tessellate` and `ToMesh` gained overloads taking a `CancellationToken`,
checked at entry, per refinement span and per grid row; the token-free forms delegate unchanged. The
row asked that a token tripping inside tessellation leave the shape unmodified, and it does by
construction: surfaces are immutable, and `ToMesh` throws before `Build`, so nobody ever holds half a
mesh.

**Verified.** `TessellationCancellationTests`, deterministic rather than timed: one test cancels from
inside the sink on the first vertex and asserts the grid stops within a row. **With the row check
removed, the same tessellation ran on to 260,612 vertices** — the whole capped grid — and the test
failed. The other two assert an already-cancelled token does no work and that the token-free form
still makes the same mesh. Then the gates, **3,131 tests over ten executables**.

**Two analyzers objected, and both are now written down ([N154](NOTES.md)).** RS0027 forbade the
overload beside an optional-parameter form; it guards a published library's future overloads, Spark
publishes nothing, and it is off beside RS0026 for that stated reason. xUnit1051 then made every
existing test call to `ToMesh` an error, because the method now has a token overload — sixteen calls in
a file nobody had touched. The repository complies rather than suppresses, so they were patched from
the compiler's own list of locations; a text search would also have hit `Solid.ToMesh`, which shares
the name, has no token overload, and would not have compiled.

**Step B is next**: the evaluator's token does not yet reach any library node.

### 2026-09-11 — The evaluator's token reaches the nodes that ask for it (`E3-T12` step B, closed)

**What.** `NodeImporter` treats a `CancellationToken` parameter as no port, so a node's key cannot
change because its method started accepting one; `NodeInvoker.ForCancellableMethod` compiles an
invoker that passes the evaluation's token where the method declared it; `NodeDefinition` keeps it as
`InvokeCancellable`, separate from `InvokeScript`, which is how a code block is told apart; `Call`
prefers the script invoker, then this one, then `Invoke`. `Spark.Nodes.Core.Surface.ToMesh` declares a
trailing optional token and forwards it to step A's overload.

**The decision** ([D24](PRD.md#13-decision-log)). An overload of a node method would have been a second
node with the same ports, renaming both through the importer's disambiguation and breaking every graph
using the existing one; so the signature changed, recorded with the repository's first `*REMOVED*`
baseline line, and it counts as a minor change because no key, port or file moves.

**The defect it found** ([N155](NOTES.md)). The first full run had two unrelated engine tests failing:
the code-example generator walked parameters assuming one port each, ran off the end at the token, and
aborted the import of the whole first-party library. The new tests had not seen it because they
imported a fixture of their own - which, separately, the importer refused, since it does not import
nested types; the fixture is now top-level.

**Verified, and two mutations each caught by exactly the test aimed at it.** `CancellableNodeTests`,
four tests; the engine suite at 565. With `Call` ignoring the new invoker, the two delivery tests fail;
with the token turned back into a port, `ATokenParameterIsNotAPort` fails and the delivery tests
correctly still pass, because the invoker fills the token without an argument slot. **One mutation run
had to be thrown away**: after restoring the source I ran tests against binaries still built from the
mutation, and the first combined filter matched no tests at all (xUnit ANDs `-class` with `-method`).
Then the gates, **3,135 tests over ten executables**.

**The row closes with its stated exception**: OpenCascade operations cannot be interrupted from managed
code once started, and the evaluation help topic now says so beside what does stop.

### 2026-09-11 — The evaluation cache gains a managed-memory budget (`E3-T9`)

**Half of it was already there, and the register had said otherwise.** Reading `EvaluationCache`
before writing anything showed two ceilings, not one: an entry count and `DefaultNativeBudget`, which
weighs a resident `Brep` through `BrepResidency.NativeBytes` and the shim's `spark_occt_shape_bytes`.
It landed on 2026-08-31 (`5ac4367`). The 2026-09-09 audit wrote *its ceiling is a count*. Third time
today a re-check has been wrong in the same way — it described the code it expected rather than the
code on disk.

**What was genuinely missing was managed size.** A mesh of two million triangles cost one entry of
4,096 and nothing else. `DefaultManagedBudget` (1 GB) is a third ceiling over an estimate from counts -
vertices and faces, control points, points, list elements - that errs high, which the cache's own
remarks already call the safe direction. **It never asks a resident `Brep` its counts**: those read the
managed arrays, and for a resident shape reading them materialises it, the conversion ADR-0021 exists to
avoid - the estimate would have created the memory it was estimating.

**Verified.** Five tests in `EvaluationCacheManagedBudgetTests`, which learn a value's weight from the
cache rather than restating the formula, so the estimate can be tuned without rewriting them. With the
managed ceiling unenforced, `TheCacheEvictsOnManagedBytesWithTheCountNowhereNearItsCeiling` failed;
with a resident shape weighed by its counts, a residency whose `Materialise` throws tripped
`AResidentShapeIsNotMaterialisedToBeWeighed`. Then the gates, **3,140 tests over ten executables**.

**The register, corrected in passing**: `E13-T18` is blocked on the toolchain like `E13-T21`, since its
fix is C++ in the shim. `E3` has no half-built row left.

### 2026-09-11 — The viewport can say what is under a pixel (`E9-T8` step A)

**Nothing picked in the viewport.** Every `HitTest` in `Spark.UI` is the 2D canvas; a plain left
press in `ViewportControl` is `CameraDrag.None` and does nothing. `E2-T15` had left the tools in the
kernel - `Ray`, `BoundingVolumeHierarchy.FirstHit` - and nothing used them.

**The ray is built, not inverted.** `Camera.RayThrough(x, y)` takes the look-at basis the view matrix
is made from and spreads the vertical field of view over the aspect ratio. Inverting `ViewProjection`
would also work, and would lean on a matrix inverse at a far-to-near ratio of forty thousand, where
single-precision inverses go soft. **What keeps the two honest is the first test**: points projected with
the renderer's own `ViewProjection` lie on the rays through their own pixels, out towards the corners.

**The picker.** `ViewportPicker.Pick` puts each package's box in a BVH and lets `FirstHit` prune on
entry distance. The exact test is Moller-Trumbore for triangles, both windings because the renderer
draws both sides, and five pixels at the candidate's depth for edges and points - a line is a pixel
wide, and asking for an exact hit on one is asking the user to miss. The boxes are inflated by that
tolerance at their far side so a line on a box's edge is never pruned before its test runs.

**Verified.** Five tests in `ViewportPickerTests`, then two byte-exact mutations, each built and
restored: flipping the ray's vertical sign failed the agreement test and the triangle pick, and zeroing
the tolerance failed only `ALineIsPickedWithinAFewPixels`. Then the gates, **3,145 tests over ten executables**.

### 2026-09-11 — A click on geometry selects the node that drew it (`E9-T8` closed)

**Step B is the click.** A plain left press in `ViewportControl` used to be `CameraDrag.None` and do
nothing. It is now a click until it is released; released within four layout units of where it
started, `PickAt` asks `ViewportPicker` what is under it and the control raises `GeometryPicked`.
Any modifier keeps the press a camera gesture, so nobody orbiting selects by accident.

**Two sizes of pixel, one conversion.** The camera is sized in device pixels on the GPU path and in
layout units on the software one. `PickAt` scales the point by the camera's own size over the
control's bounds, which is right on both, and scales the five-pixel tolerance the same way.

**From key to node, in the view model.** A view may not name the engine's types (`E8-T11`), so
`MainWindowViewModel.SlotDrawing(GeometryKey)` parses the key's node id back and asks
`CanvasGraph.SlotOf`. The window calls `Canvas.SelectOnly`, and the one selection event does the
rest: the inspector shows the node and the viewport outlines what it drew (`E9-T9`). A click on
nothing selects nothing and leaves the selection alone.

**Verified.** Three tests in `ViewportPickSelectionTests`, the middle one the whole chain without a
window: a camera aimed at one of the demo's point markers, the ray through the centre pixel, and
the slot of the node that drew it. An off-by-one in `SlotDrawing` failed all three. Then the gates,
**3,148 tests over ten executables**, and the running application, by screenshot before and after: a
click on one of the demo's point markers turned *Nothing selected* into `Display.FromGeometryColour`,
selected on the canvas and shown in the inspector.

**Seen in passing, not chased.** The markers of the selected node looked the same in the after
screenshot as before, so `E9-T9`'s selection outline either does not show on point markers or is too
subtle to see at that size. It is not this row's claim; it is worth a look when `E9-T9` is next open.

### 2026-09-11 — Tessellation is parallel inside the scene builder (`E9-T7` step A)

**It was eager and serial.** `SceneBuilder.Collect` tessellated as it walked each value -
`surface.ToMesh`, `BrepKernel.Current.Tessellate`, and `CurveDrawable`'s constructor - on the thread
that called `Add`, one value after another.

**Lazy first, then parallel.** A surface, solid, curve or mesh now becomes a drawable that keeps its
geometry and its bounds, because the bounds are all the marker radius needs before anything is
drawn. The expensive half is a `Prepare` pass at the top of `Build`, run with `Parallel.For` up to
`MaximumParallelism`. Emitting stays serial and in key order, so the packages are exactly the
one-thread build's. A solid the kernel cannot tessellate is moved to `UnrenderableCount` in that pass,
where it is first known, and `Keys()` leaves out a key that drew nothing.

**Why the kernel is safe with it.** Checked before writing a line: nothing serialises tessellation
globally - `OcctKernel`'s lock guards only installing the provider - and the one place two threads
could meet, the same resident solid twice in a list, is the case `E12-T20` made safe. The geometry's
only lazy cache is `Mesh.Topology`, an atomic reference write.

**One visible difference, deliberately.** A surface's and a solid's contribution to the scene's extent
is now its own bounding box rather than its tessellation's, since the extent is needed before the
tessellation exists. It moves the marker radius by a hair and nothing else.

**Verified.** Three tests in `SceneBuilderParallelTests`. A parallel build of spheres, circles and
points over six keys equals the serial build buffer for buffer. That the pass is parallel at all is
observed, not timed: two surfaces meet at a barrier inside it. Forcing the pass onto one thread failed
the barrier test on its timeout; skipping the pass in a parallel build failed both. Then the gates,
**3,151 tests over ten executables**.

**One number in that gate run was wrong, and it was not this change.** The OCCT tests reported
4,259 seconds against 22 in the two runs before. They do not reference `Spark.Viewport`, so they
cannot reach `SceneBuilder`; run again on their own they took 17 seconds. Wall-clock time lost to
the machine, recorded here so a slow run next time is not taken for a new one.

### 2026-09-11 — The engine reports each node as it finishes (`E9-T7` step B1)

**Nothing reported a node until the whole run was done.** `SparkSession.EvaluateAsync` hands back one
`EvaluationResult` at the end, so the viewport waits for the slowest node in the graph before it can
draw the fastest.

**One place to report from.** Every node that produces output - evaluated fresh or served from the
cache - ends in `Run.Complete`; `Fail` and `MarkSkipped` are the other two endings and have nothing to
draw. So `Complete` reports `NodeCompleted(Node, Outputs, FromCache)`, after it has released the run's
lock, on whichever scheduler thread ran the node: a slow listener holds up that thread and nothing
else.

**A parameter, not an event.** `GraphEvaluator.Evaluate` gains an overload taking an
`IProgress<NodeCompleted>?`, and the old signature delegates with none. An event on the evaluator, or a
listener kept on `EvaluationContext` - which `NextRun()` carries from one run to the next - would
outlive the run it was meant for, and a viewport fed by a superseded run draws the wrong graph.

**Verified.** Three tests in `NodeCompletedReportTests`, with a synchronous recorder because
`Progress<T>` posts to a synchronisation context and a test reading it would race its own reports: a
chain reports each node once, in dependency order, carrying the values the result holds; a second run
over the same cache reports all three as cached; a failed node and the node it left without an input
report nothing, while an unrelated node in the same run does. Removing the report failed all three -
the third because the unrelated node then went unreported; reporting from `Fail` as well failed only
the third. Then the gates, **3,154 tests over ten
executables**.

### 2026-09-11 — The viewport draws a node's geometry as the node finishes (`E9-T7` closed)

**Step B2 is the publishing half.** `SparkSession` gains `IProgress<NodeCompleted>?` overloads of
`Evaluate` and `EvaluateAsync`, the old signatures delegating with none. `MainWindowViewModel`
hands each run a `GeometryStream`: it tessellates a finished node's preview ports through a
`SceneBuilder` of its own, outside any lock, puts the packages in the scene - which takes its own lock
- and raises `GeometryStreamed`. The window posts that to the UI thread as a repaint, because it is
raised on whichever thread ran the node.

**A snapshot of the keys, taken before the run.** `CanvasGraph.PreviewPorts()` reads the live canvas
graph, which the UI can edit while a run is in flight, so the stream is given a map from node to
preview keys built on the calling thread and reads nothing else.

**The full publish stays the authority, three ways.** The stream is closed before it, under the lock a
report publishes under. A report from a run a later one has superseded - still finishing on a worker
thread - is dropped by generation. And **keys a report streamed are retired like published ones**:
found while writing it, not by a test - a run superseded after streaming a node's geometry, with the
node then deleted, would have left that geometry on screen for good, because only a completed run's
keys were ever retired.

**Verified.** Two tests in `StreamedGeometryTests`: the demo's points are in the scene, and the view
has been told, before `EvaluateAsync` returns; after it, the scene is the full publish. Deterministic
rather than timed, since the session reports from inside the evaluation. Running the session without
the listener failed the first; telling the view without putting anything in the scene failed it too.
Then the gates, **3,156 tests over ten executables**.

**One UI test turned flaky, and the test was the thing at fault.**
`UndoRedoTests.TheRunAfterAnUndoRecomputesNothing` failed once in the gate run and once in four
runs after it. It committed an edit - which starts an automatic run - and then called
`EvaluateAsync` on top. Whenever the edit's run got past its last cancellation check before the
second one cancelled it, the second found everything cached, was applied last and reported nothing
computed: correct, and a failure. B2 widened the window by taking the preview-key snapshot before
the session cancels the previous run. The test now awaits the run the edit starts, as its undo half
already did. **In passing**, a superseded run no longer tessellates geometry it is about to drop:
`GeometryStream` checks for a newer run before building as well as before publishing.

**In the running application**, by screenshot: the demo draws its hundred points in one buffer set,
as before. Its run takes 275 ms, too quick to watch geometry arrive while it runs - so streaming is
shown by the tests, and the screenshot shows only that nothing it touched is broken.

**`E9` has no open row.** Picking (`E9-T8`), parallel tessellation and streaming (`E9-T7`) all landed
today.

### 2026-09-11 — Settings (`E8-T12` closed)

**The row was bare, and half of it was already built.** *Settings, Open* - no note, and no criterion in
`docs/EPICS.md`, only E8's scope line naming *settings, autosave and crash recovery*. There was no
settings class. There were three preferences that persist, through `PreferenceFile` (`E8-T59`), each
set from a different place: the update check from a Help-menu tick, the code font from a list in the
properties pane, and tidying on Enter from a checkbox beside it. `PreferenceFile`'s own remarks argue
against a settings framework until something needs one, and nothing does. So the criterion was written
first - *the preferences Spark remembers are in one Settings window, and each is saved as it changes* -
and met with a window, not a framework.

**One writer per preference.** `SettingsViewModel` goes through the main view model's `CodeFontName`
and `FormatsOnLineBreak`, which the properties pane binds, and through the same `UpdatePreference` the
Help menu's tick reads. A second instance over the same file would have held a stale answer and skipped
a write it needed, and two surfaces would have disagreed about what is remembered. Turning the update
check on in Settings moves the Help tick and checks at once, as the tick does.

**No OK, no Cancel.** Every preference already writes itself as it changes, so the window says that
rather than offering a button that would pretend otherwise. It is code-only, like the About box, from
*File > Settings...* and `Ctrl+,`.

**Verified.** Four tests in `SettingsTests`, in a collection that runs alone - the code font and the tidy
switch are application-wide statics that code-block tests read while they run - and with every
preference pointed at a temporary file, so a test run never changes what the person running it chose;
`MainWindowViewModel.UseCodeFontPreference` is the internal hook that makes that possible for the font.
Not writing the update preference failed the two tests that read it back; the window not wiring its tidy
switch failed the window test. **One surprise, kept because it was real**: the first time that first
mutation ran, the tidy test failed too. The window test had failed before closing its window, and the
open window took the next test in the collection with it. The window is now closed in a `finally`;
the same mutation then failed exactly the two, and the class passed ten runs in a row. Then the gates, **3,160 tests over ten executables**, and the window opened in the running
application.

### 2026-09-11 — Curve/curve intersection in closed form (`E2-T11` step A)

**The seed was not there.** The row says to *extract `CurveIntersection` and `CurveGeometry` as the 2D
seed*. Neither is in this tree, and the docs name `CurveGeometry` only as the topology member
`Edge.CurveGeometry`, which is something else. Nothing in `Spark.Geometry` intersects two curves at
all - its intersection members are for boxes, the BVH, rays and intervals. So it is built from the
curve API, and in three dimensions from the start, which is the part the row called new work.

**Closed form first, because it is the oracle.** The general intersector (step B) will bracket and
refine, and a refinement can only be trusted against an answer that cannot be wrong. So step A is
arithmetic: line/line (skew, parallel, colinear, end to end), line against a circle or an arc (in its
plane or piercing it), and circles and arcs against each other (one plane - crossing, touching outside
and inside, concentric - crossing planes, and two arcs of one circle sharing a stretch). Tangency is
decided by comparing distances to the tolerance before a square root is taken, so a grazing line is one
point. An arc answers only where it reaches.

**Internal for now.** `AnalyticCurveIntersection.TryIntersect` and its result types stay internal, so
the public API moves once, in step B, with the general case behind one entry point.

**Verified.** Nineteen tests in `AnalyticCurveIntersectionTests`, every answer checked with
`Curve.PointAt` on both curves, which the intersector does not use. Three byte-exact mutations, each
built and restored: skew lines taken as meeting, and an arc taken as its whole circle, each failed their
case. **Inside tangency put on the wrong side survived** - the test put the larger circle first, and on
that order the right branch and the wrong one give the same point. It now asks both ways round, and
the same mutation fails it. Then the gates, **3,179 tests over ten executables** - with one UI test
failing once in that run, 1 of 1,381, which four more full runs of the same tree did not reproduce.
Step A is internal geometry no UI test reaches, so it is committed; the gate run did not keep the
failing test's name, and now does. Reading for the cause found a real ordering hole in how runs are
applied, which is the next step - with its own test, and without claiming it was this failure.

### 2026-09-11 — The newest run wins, not the last to finish (`E8-T86`)

**A failure that would not come back, and what reading found instead.** One UI test failed once in
`E2-T11` step A's gate run - 1 of 1,381 - and four more full runs of the same tree passed. The gate
command had kept only each executable's totals, so which test it was is not known. It does not keep
only totals any more.

**The hole, which is real whatever that failure was.** Every constructor that opens a graph starts a
run, so a caller's own run racing that one is ordinary. `MainWindowViewModel.EvaluateAsync` applied
results in the order they reached its apply gate, and a run that had already finished when a later
one superseded it could reach the gate second - putting an older graph's results, and its geometry,
over a newer one's. The constructor's own remarks put it as *the last one to finish wins*. Streaming
(`E9-T7`) made runs a little longer, which makes that more likely, not less.

**The rule.** Each run already took a generation number for streaming. The view model now also
remembers the newest generation it has applied, and a result older than that is dropped - not
applied, not published, no `EvaluationCompleted` - with its stream closed.

**Verified, deterministically.** One test in `NewestRunWinsTests`, through an internal hook that holds
a run between evaluating and being applied: an older run is held; the graph is edited in Manual mode;
a newer run computes the edit and is applied; the older one is let go, and the view still reports what
the newer run computed. Letting the older result through again failed it. Then the gates, **3,180 tests
over ten executables**, with every executable's output kept.

**Not claimed**: that this was the test that failed. It is the one ordering defect reading found, and
it is closed with a test that fails without the fix.

### 2026-09-11 — The general curve/curve intersector (`E2-T11` step B1)

**Bracket, then refine.** `GeneralCurveIntersection` samples each curve into 128 chords over its own
domain. The second curve's chord boxes, each grown by a tenth of its length and the tolerance, go into
the `BoundingVolumeHierarchy` from `E2-T15`, which already answered box queries; each chord of the first
curve asks it which chords are near. Every near pair starts a Gauss-Newton refinement of `a(s) - b(t)`
from the chords' closest approach, kept only if it lands inside both domains within the tolerance.
Where the two tangents are parallel the step goes along the first curve alone and the second follows by
closest point - which is what carries a tangency or an overlap to a point on both.

**Points, touches and overlaps.** Candidates within the tolerance are one point. A run of candidates
joined by curve that stays on the other curve is a **touch** when it spans less than one sample spacing
- refinement near a tangency settles a few hundred-thousandths apart each time - and is reported as its
best point; otherwise it is an **overlap**, with its ends found by bisection. So an overlap shorter than
one sample spacing is reported as a point: the price of sampling, written down rather than discovered.

**The seam, found by the oracle.** On the first run the general path gave two points for circles
touching - outside and inside alike - where the closed form gives one. Both touches sit at angle zero,
which on a circle is also 2π: refinement found the touch once near the start of the domain and once
near the end, a little apart as a tangency always is, and in parameter order they were as far from
each other as two candidates can be. For a closed curve the last run and the first are now tried
across the seam, and when the stretch between them is short and lies on the other curve they are one
touch. The grazing line had passed all along: its touch is not on a seam.

**The closed forms are the oracle.** On all sixteen pairs step A answers in closed form, the general
path gives the same points - to the tolerance, or to its square root where the curves only touch - and
the same overlaps. Beyond them: a line through an ellipse, two NURBS curves crossing where both pass
through the same points, and a straight NURBS curve overlapping a line.

**Verified.** Byte-exact mutations: no refinement failed 3 tests; runs never joined failed 7 - every
tangency and every overlap; every run reported as a point failed 4. **Keeping duplicates survived**, and
rightly: duplicates sit next to each other and the run grouping merges them anyway, so the explicit
merge is an economy - one distance instead of three closest-point queries - now commented as one. Then the gates, **3,199 tests over ten executables**.

### 2026-09-11 — Curve/curve intersection becomes public (`E2-T11` step B2)

**One entry point, and the routing is the whole of it.** `Curve.IntersectWith(Curve other, in Tolerance
tolerance = default)` answers in closed form when `AnalyticCurveIntersection` has one, and by the
sampled path otherwise. The answers were already tested in steps A and B1; what is under test here is
that a closed-form pair really gets the closed form - to the last bit - and every other pair the
sampled path.

**What is published.** `CurveIntersectionPoint` and `CurveOverlap` are public record structs, publishing
what `BrepEdge` does. `CurveIntersections` became a plain sealed class: a record would have published a
copy constructor and an equality contract that nothing asked for. The `PublicAPI.Unshipped.txt` entries
were taken from the RS0016 messages themselves, which name each symbol in the file's own format -
nothing typed by hand to drift from what the analyzer means.

**The first gate run failed, and it was right to.** `GeometryJsonTests.EveryPublicGeometryTypeHasASample`
holds every public type in `Spark.Geometry` to a JSON sample or an exclusion argued in the test, and
the three result types had become public with neither - an omission, which is exactly what that test
exists to turn into a decision. They are excluded, each with its reason: an answer to a question about
two curves, recomputed from the curves, which are what a file saves. The gate named the test because
it now keeps each executable's output.

**Verified.** Four tests in `CurveIntersectWithTests`; always taking the sampled path failed the
closed-form routing test. Then the gates again, **3,203 tests over ten executables**.

### 2026-09-11 — Curve/curve intersection as nodes (`E2-T11` closed)

**Step C is two nodes.** `Curve.IntersectWith(curve, other)` returns the points, and
`Curve.OverlapWith(curve, other)` each stretch the two share, as a piece of the first curve trimmed
to its overlap - so an overlap arrives in a graph as geometry, not as a pair of intervals nobody can
draw. The help topics and the generated code examples came from the live library by rule, so the node
coverage, code-example and help-topic tests passed without being touched; the node library's public
API file took the RS0016 entries.

**Verified.** Three tests in `CurveIntersectionNodeTests`, run through the engine rather than by
calling the methods, because what a graph user gets is what the importer and the marshaller make of
them. Returning no points failed the first; cutting the overlap at the other curve's parameters failed
the second. Then the gates, **3,206 tests over ten executables**.

**`E2-T11`, all of it**: closed forms for lines, circles and arcs in 3D, the general case sampled,
pruned and refined and checked against them, one public entry point, and the nodes.

### 2026-09-11 — A k-d tree over points (`E2-T16` step A)

**What the row assumed was not quite so.** It asked to *extract and generalise `KDTree`*, *needed for
welding, dedup and point queries*. There was no `KDTree` anywhere, and no seed in the docs. And welding
does not need one: `Mesh.Welded` already merges through a spatial hash that checks twenty-seven
neighbouring cells. The caller the Dynamo inventory actually names is `Point.PruneDuplicates`, which
*wants the `KDTree` of E2-T16 rather than an O(n^2) loop*.

**The tree.** `PointKdTree` is implicit: one index array, arranged so the median of every range - on
the axis its depth chooses - sits at the range's middle, placed by median-of-three quickselect so a
sorted row of points is not the worst case. Three questions: the nearest point, the k nearest, and
everything within a radius. **Deterministic by design** - a tie goes to the lower index, the k nearest
come back by distance and then index, a radius query in ascending order - because a caller
deduplicating points needs the same answer on every machine.

**Verified.** Thirteen tests in `PointKdTreeTests`, each query against a linear scan over random clouds
of a thousand points, plus exact duplicates, a row of collinear points, a pile of coincident ones and an
empty tree. Three byte-exact mutations - pruning the far side too eagerly, building on one axis while
searching on three, leaving the radius boundary out - each failed. Then the gates, **3,219 tests over
ten executables**.

### 2026-09-11 — Point.PruneDuplicates on the k-d tree (`E2-T16` closed)

**A public door, not a friend assembly.** The tree stays internal to the kernel. The node library
could have been given access to it, but the importer treats that library exactly as it would a
third-party package, and a third-party package could not reach an internal type. So the kernel
gained `Point3d.PruneDuplicates(points, tolerance = 0)`, which uses the tree, and the node
`Point.PruneDuplicates(points, tolerance = 0.001)` calls that - with a typed list port, so the whole list
arrives rather than one point at a time (the trap `PlaneFitNodeTests` names).

**Judged against what was kept.** A point is removed only when a point already kept lies within the
tolerance. In a chain of points each a little closer than the tolerance to the next, the first stays,
the second goes, and the third stays, because what it was close to is gone. That makes the answer
depend on nothing but the order of the input.

**Verified.** Five tests in `PointPruneDuplicatesTests`, the first holding the tree to the O(n^2) loop
it replaces on a dense random cloud, and one through the engine in `PruneDuplicatesNodeTests`. Letting
removed points remove their neighbours failed the chain test; ignoring the tolerance failed three - the
cluster, the chain and the scan. Then the gates, **3,225 tests over ten executables**.

### 2026-09-11 — PointCloud, and GeometryGroup declined (`E2-T21` closed)

**Each had to earn its place against a list.** The row's note was empty; PRD FR-51 names both types
beside `Mesh`; the Dynamo inventory has neither. A graph already carries a list of points and a list of
mixed geometry, so the question for each was what it could do that a list cannot.

**`PointCloud` could.** It keeps its bounding box rather than walking every point for it, and it
answers nearest and within-a-radius through the `E2-T16` k-d tree - built once, on the first question,
rather than a scan per question. A scan of a million points is fine once; a thousand probes against it
is a billion distances. It prunes duplicates and transforms, immutably, round-trips through
`GeometryJson` as its points, and the viewport draws it as its points.

**`GeometryGroup` could not, and is declined with the reason.** A list already holds mixed geometry,
and a transform wired to a list already reaches every member through replication. A group type would
be a second way of saying what a list says, and a second thing for every node to accept.

**Verified.** Tests in `PointCloudTests` and `PointCloudSceneTests`, and a JSON sample that holds a
point twice, so a round trip that quietly deduplicated would fail. Three byte-exact mutations - the box
from the first point only, a transform that moves nothing, a JSON writer that drops duplicates - each
failed. Then the gates, **3232 tests over ten executables**.

### 2026-09-11 — Region and the planar booleans (`E2-T13` step A)

**Most of the planar layer was not there, and one piece was.** `Point2d`, `Vector2d` and the bridges
`Plane.To2d` and `Plane.To3d` existed; there was no `Curve2d`, no region, and Clipper2 - pinned in the
package manifest as the kernel's one permitted third-party dependency - was not referenced by anything.

**A region, bridged through a plane.** `Spark.Geometry.Planar.Region` is made from closed polylines
lying in a plane and handed back as closed polylines, so a graph never meets a 2D coordinate: the layer
supports, it does not compete. A hole is decided by nesting - the caller's loops are normalised with
even-odd fill - so a loop inside another is a hole whichever way round it was drawn. Two regions need
only be coplanar to combine; the second is re-measured in the first's frame, and regions in different
planes are refused, since their boolean is not a region.

**Clipper2, from one file.** Every use of it is in `Planar/ClipperBridge.cs`, internal, as the package
manifest asks - nothing public mentions a Clipper type, so the dependency stays replaceable. Its
precision in decimal places comes from the tolerance. Its API was read from the package's own DLL by
reflection before a line was written, because 2.0.0 ships without its documentation file. The
architecture test that holds the kernel's dependency ceiling kept passing, as it was written to; only
its remark, which said Clipper2 was not referenced yet, was brought up to date.

**Verified.** `RegionTests`, with areas as the oracle: two 2 x 2 squares overlapping in a corner have a
union of 7, an intersection of 1, a difference of 3 and a symmetric difference of 6. Four byte-exact
mutations - intersection answered as union, a hole counted as inside, different planes combined, a
coplanar region taken in the wrong frame - each failed. Then the gates, **3239 tests over ten
executables**.

### 2026-09-11 — Offset and simplify (`E2-T13` step B)

**The rest of FR-60's pipeline, through the same one file.** `Region.Offset(distance, join,
miterLimit)` grows a region, or shrinks it when the distance is negative - far enough, and it is empty -
with corners joined round, mitred or square. `Region.Simplify(tolerance)` drops the vertices that barely
bend an edge. Both go through `ClipperBridge`, which is still the only file in the kernel that names a
Clipper type.

**A test of simplify needs something to simplify.** The first case written used a vertex exactly on an
edge, and would have passed with simplify doing nothing: making a region already removes exactly
collinear points. It uses a vertex a hair off the edge instead.

**The first run was red, and rightly.** The round-corner case came out 15.1335 against 4 + 8 + π =
15.1416: Clipper approximates each arc with a polygon, and its default tolerance for how far that polygon
may stray is coarse. The bridge now passes its own - the region's linear tolerance, but never finer than
a hundred-thousandth of the offset distance, so a large offset does not become hundreds of thousands of
vertices nobody can see.

**Verified.** `RegionOffsetTests`, areas as the oracle: a 2 x 2 square grown by one is 4 + 8 + π with
round corners and 16 with mitred ones, and shrunk by one it is empty; the centroid of an L-shape and of a
square with an off-centre hole. Five byte-exact mutations - a miter given as a round join, a negative
offset that grows, Clipper's default arc tolerance, a simplify that changes nothing, a hole weighed as
solid in the centroid - each failed. Then the gates, **3247 tests over ten executables**.
### 2026-09-11 — Curve2d waits for its consumer (`E2-T13` closed)

**Step C was a decision.** The row says `Curve2d` is *required for BRep trim curves in UV space*, and
`BrepTrim`'s own remarks say a trim carries no pcurve because the type does not exist. So the question
was which code would read one. None in the managed kernel: trims are used only as topology - the loop
views, `Brep` validation, `Brep.Join`'s index offsets - and a genuinely trimmed face is tessellated
behind the OCCT seam, where the provider keeps its own pcurves.

**A type built for no caller is the mistake the codebase already names.** `PreferenceFile`'s remarks
put it: the moment to build the thing is when there is a second caller, not before. `Curve2d` is filed
as `E2-T64`, to be built with the first managed consumer - a trimmed-face tessellator or a
`BrepBuilder` that accepts trimmed faces - as lines and NURBS in UV. `E2-T13` closes on what it
delivered: `Spark.Geometry.Planar`, with `E2-T14` closed beside it. The one line of code that named
the old row - `BrepTrim`'s remark on the pcurve it does not carry - now names `E2-T64` and says why
the type waits.

### 2026-09-11 — Extension methods shown on the type they extend (`E5-T9` closed)

**Nearly all of it was already there.** An extension method is a static method whose first parameter
is its receiver, so the importer could already build its ports, invoke it, file it and write its code
example - it only refused to. `Classify` no longer excludes extension methods, and `OwnerName` keys one
as `Receiver.Method`, so a package's `CurveExtensions.Bend(this Curve curve)` is found under
`Curve.Bend`, where a user looking for something to do to a curve looks.

**The edges, decided rather than left open.** A receiver that is an array or a constructed generic
keeps the declaring class's name, since a key is not a type system. A receiver passed `in` or `ref` is
still excluded, by the rule for such parameters. A key colliding with a member the receiver's own type
declares is separated by the ordinary overload rule - its port names - so neither hides the other and
neither depends on declaration order; two packages never collide, because the package is part of the
key. The first-party library has no extension methods, so no built-in node changed.

**Verified.** Three tests in `ExtensionMethodImportTests`, with fixture types imported together: the
extension appears under its receiver and nowhere else and is no longer excluded; its receiver is its
first input and it evaluates; a colliding pair gets two distinct keys. Keying on the declaring class
again, and excluding extensions again, each failed. Then the gates, **3250 tests over ten
executables**.

### 2026-09-11 — Generic methods, closed over object where a canvas can use them (`E5-T10` closed)

**The answer was already on file.** `E5-T3`, marked Done, specified generics as *excluded unless closed
instantiations are named, or the method is rank-polymorphic identity-like and closed over `object`,
which works because `SparkList` is object-based*. Neither half existed; the importer simply excluded
every generic method.

**The half with a clear rule, built.** A generic method whose type parameters are all unconstrained and
all appear in an input is imported closed over `object`. The node still records the method as
declared - so its documentation and the two-way coverage diff find it - and only its ports and
invocation use the closed form.

**Two refusals, each for a reason a user would recognise.** A constrained type parameter is refused,
because `object` would break the constraint the author wrote: `where T : IComparable<T>` means the
method compares. A type parameter no input mentions is refused, because nothing on a canvas could
decide it: `Make<T>()` closed over object makes an object. **Named instantiations wait** for the first
author who asks - they need a new public attribute.

**An older test said the opposite, and was right for its time.** `NodeImporterTests` asserted that a
plain `Identity<T>(T value)` is excluded as generic - the blanket rule. That method is now exactly what
gets imported, so its fixture became a constrained one, which is still refused; and both refusals now
begin *generic type parameter*, so an exclusion list says what kind of member it is about.

**Verified.** Four tests in `GenericMethodImportTests`: a list reversed and a first item taken through
the engine, and both refusals, by name. Allowing constrained parameters, allowing uninferable ones, and
closing over `string` instead of `object` each failed. Then the gates, **3254 tests over ten
executables**.
### 2026-09-11 — The graph-construction API, closed on the evidence (`E3-T21`)

**Open because nobody had gone back to it.** The row asked for a public graph-construction API, *needed
by the CLI, by tests, and by collapse-to-custom-node*. `Spark.Engine.Graph` already exposes `AddNode`,
`RemoveNode`, `TryConnect` - which returns a `ConnectionResult` carrying the port compatibility and a
diagnostic rather than throwing - `Disconnect` and `SetLiteral`. The CLI reads a `.spark` file into a
`GraphDocument` that builds its graph through exactly those; collapse-to-custom-node builds its inner
graph through them in `CustomNodeLibrary` and `CanvasCollapse`; and the tests build graphs with them
everywhere, fourteen in `GraphTests` alone. Nothing was missing, so nothing was written.

### 2026-09-11 — The canvas shows a slow run reaching its nodes (`E3-T14` step A)

**Half of it was already there.** Since `E9-T7` the engine reports each node as it finishes and the
viewport draws that node's geometry at once; the canvas, though, changed only when the whole result was
applied, so a long run looked like a frozen graph with a live viewport beside it.

**The state the design language already named.** §7.4 has an *Evaluating* state - an `accent` ring,
travelling, with a progress glyph, and a static ring with `…` under reduced motion. It is now
`CanvasNodeState.Evaluating`: a run still going after 150 ms marks every node it has not finished, each
node's report clears its own mark, and the applied result - the authority, as for geometry - clears
whatever is left. Frozen nodes are never marked, since they are not going to run.

**The delay is the design, not a tuning.** Dragging a slider starts a run per pointer move. Marking at
once would flash a ring round every node on every move; a run that finishes inside the delay marks
nothing and asks for no repaint. The view model never touches a canvas node off the UI thread: reports
arrive on the evaluation's threads, so it raises a coalesced `EvaluationProgressed`, and the window posts
`ShowProgress` and a repaint.

**Drawn in the static form for now**, the ring ahead of any error ring the previous run left - a node
being worked on has no settled state yet - and the `…` glyph. The travelling stroke is step B.

**Verified.** Two tests in `EvaluatingStateTests`, made deterministic by a hook that holds one node's
report inside the run and a delay set to zero or an hour, never raced. A report that does not clear its
node, reports never recorded, an applied result that leaves the marks, and no delay at all each failed.
Then the gates, **3256 tests over ten executables**.

### 2026-09-11 — The evaluating stroke travels (`E3-T14` closed)

**§7.4's only animation, and the only repeating one in the product.** The evaluating ring from step A is
now, on screen, a single 2 px `accent` dash a quarter of the way round the outline, its offset advancing
on a 900 ms lap. Every stroke is timed from one epoch, so nodes evaluating together travel together
rather than each starting its lap when it happened to be marked.

**Frames only while something moves.** The canvas asks the top level for the next animation frame only
when a stroke travelled in the frame it just drew, so a canvas with nothing evaluating draws once and
rests - an idle graph costs nothing, which is the point of drawing by hand.

**Two budgets in the design language, and the stricter one holds.** §7.4 said the stroke stops below 55%
zoom; §10.2, written for the canvas as a whole, stops every per-node animation below 60% or above 400
visible nodes, and the canvas already enforced it through `CanvasLevelOfDetail.AllowsAnimation`. Using
that satisfies both, and §7.4 now says so rather than disagreeing with §10.2. An image export is a still
and draws the static ring.

**Verified.** Four tests in `EvaluatingStrokeTests`: the phase at four moments, and whether a frame
animated at working zoom, zoomed out, and with nothing evaluating - asserted through the headless render
path, which runs although it draws nothing (N124). A one-second lap, the budget ignored, a travelling
stroke that asks for no next frame, and a screen frame treated as a still each failed. Then the gates,
**3260 tests over ten executables**.

### 2026-09-11 — The `.sparkz` bundle packs and opens (`E3-T20` step A)

**Promised by an ADR and never built.** ADR-0017 kept the `.spark` file plain JSON so graphs diff and
merge, and named the cost: what a graph needs lives beside it, so emailing only the `.spark` sends a
graph without its libraries. The bundle was the fix, and all that existed was a `.gitattributes` line.

**The bundle recreates the pair rather than replacing it.** `SparkBundle.Pack` zips a manifest, the
`.spark` file and its package folder, each under its own name; `Unpack` opens that into a folder and
hands back the graph's path, with the package folder beside it exactly where Save As, the Packages
window and the package gate already look. Nothing that reads a graph had to learn to read a zip. A pack
writes beside its destination and moves into place, so a failed one never leaves a truncated bundle
under the name somebody is about to send.

**A bundle is a file from somebody else, so opening one checks before it writes.** A file that is not a
zip, a zip with no manifest, a newer bundle format, and a manifest naming a graph that is not there are
each refused by name - and so is any entry that would land outside the folder, the zip-slip, which
refuses the whole bundle because every entry is checked before the first is written.

**Three things ADR-0017 lists are not carried yet, each for a reason** recorded in the row: assets have no
folder yet, custom node definitions have no file home a graph points at, and a thumbnail needs a
renderer a command-line pack does not have. The bundle's format version is what lets an older build
refuse the bundle that adds them, instead of opening it without them.

**Verified.** Eight tests in `SparkBundleTests`. Removing the zip-slip check, packing half-finished
downloads, opening a newer format, trusting a manifest's missing graph, and writing entries while still
checking each failed. Then the gates, **3268 tests over ten executables**.

### 2026-09-11 — `spark pack`, and a bundle wherever a graph goes (`E3-T20` step B)

**ADR-0017 named the command, and now it exists.** `spark pack GRAPH.spark` writes `GRAPH.sparkz` beside
the graph, or wherever `--out` says, and prints what went in.

**The other verbs did not have to learn what a bundle is.** `run`, `check` and `export` open a `.sparkz`
into a temporary folder and read the graph found there; its package folder is beside it, so the package
gate asks about a bundle's assemblies exactly as it asks about a folder beside a graph - a bundle is not
a way round the question of whether its code may run. The folder is removed when the verb is done, and
messages keep the path the person typed rather than the temporary one. A refused bundle is an
`IOException`, which `Main` already reports in one line.

**Verified.** Six tests in `PackVerbTests`: a bundle runs value for value as the graph it holds, the
default name, `check` on a bundle is silent, the temporary folder is gone afterwards, a refusal is the
kind `Main` reports, and `pack` with no graph says what to type. Reading a bundle as though it were a
graph, leaving the temporary folder behind, and naming the default bundle `tower.spark.sparkz` each
failed. Then the gates, **3274 tests over ten executables**.

### 2026-09-11 — The application opens a bundle and shares one (`E3-T20` closed)

**Where ADR-0017 said the bundle had to be.** *It only works if it is discoverable, and if it is buried in
the CLI people will hit this before they find it.* File ▸ Open now takes a `.sparkz` - first in the
picker's list, so it is not behind a filter nobody changes - and File ▸ Share as bundle… makes one.

**Opened as a file, not as text.** A graph's trust, its packages and its banners are all keyed on where
it lives, so `TryOpenBundle` unpacks the bundle into a folder of its own and opens the graph there as
the file it is: its code blocks are asked about, and its packages gated, exactly as for a graph and
folder somebody had unzipped by hand. The folder is named from the bundle and a hash of its bytes, so the
same bundle opened twice reuses one folder, and the status bar says where it is, because Save writes
there.

**Shared from the file.** Share as bundle… saves first when the graph has no file or has changes, then
packs the file and its package folder beside it - the bundle is made from what is on disk, never from
what only the canvas holds.

**Verified.** Five tests in `BundleWindowTests`, each settling the model's own first run before looking
at the diagnostics pane. Opening a bundle as text with no file, a fresh folder on every opening, a
refused bundle thrown at the window, and a shared bundle named `tower.spark.sparkz` each failed. Then the
gates, **3279 tests over ten executables**. TODO item 9 is done.
