### 2026-09-11 — `--open` takes a bundle too (`E3-T20` step D)

**Found while planning how to see step C in the running application.** File ▸ Open took a `.sparkz`, but
the startup door - `--open`, and so a double-click once the file type is registered - read whatever it was
given as graph text, and a bundle is a zip. It now unpacks a bundle into its own folder first, and
everything after that sees the ordinary file, so the package record, the trust decision and the package
gate apply to it unchanged. The folder is named by a new internal constructor, so the test opens its
bundle into its own folder rather than the user's profile. The startup door reading a bundle as a graph,
and the named folder ignored, each failed the new test - the second by doing exactly what the
constructor exists to prevent, unpacking the test's bundle into the real profile's bundle folder, which
was deleted by hand afterwards. Then the gates, **3280 tests over ten executables**.

### 2026-09-11 — The Dynamo parity manifest (`E11-T23` step A)

**837 rows, generated from metadata, not typed from memory.** DYNAMO-COVERAGE was a hand count in
prose and tables, and its §7 proposed the fix: a checked-in manifest with a row per ProtoGeometry
member, checked on every build. The raw inventory was never checked in, so the first job was to
recover it the way the document says it was taken - from the public **metadata** of `ProtoGeometry.dll`,
types and signatures only, nothing decompiled - with a small reader over `System.Reflection.Metadata`.

**Calibrated before a row was written.** Two copies are installed. Revit 2026's, the reference surface
FR-81 names, reproduces the document exactly under one counting rule - public methods including
overrides, public properties and enum values; not constructors or accessors - giving 51 types, 837
members, 618 methods, 215 properties and 4 enum values, and every per-type count in §3. Revit 2024's has
49 types and 756 members, and was not the source.

**Seeded without guessing.** T-Splines `Needs a decision` (Q12); §5's refusals `Not planned`, each with its
section's reason; 89 `Done` where the member exists by the same name on the mapped Spark type, marked as
matched by name and not yet reviewed; and the remaining 472 `Unassessed`.

**It caught the document's arithmetic on its first run.** §5 says 93 members are refused. Its own lists add
to 104, and the four primitive solids carry 14 parameter-recovery properties, not 11: 107, and a committed
surface of 561 rather than 575. The document now says so in place, rather than being silently rewritten.

**Three checks in `Spark.Docs.Verify`**, which still references no Spark project - `Spark.Geometry.dll` is
read from its build output as metadata: the rows are well formed; the totals agree with the document's §2
and §3; and every Done row names a member Spark declares, the rename-catcher, whose failure message says
*present, never equivalent*, as §7 asked. It refuses to pass with no Done rows at all. A renamed member, a
refusal with no reason, a deleted row and an unknown status each failed. Then the gates, **3283 tests
over ten executables**.

### 2026-09-11 — Format versions, closed on the evidence (`E3-T19`)

**The row was written when there was one version, and there are five.** Notes and groups made version 2,
code blocks 3, a node's title and colour 4, and the package list 5. Each was added without changing or
removing anything before it, and each file is written at the lowest version that can read it - which is
what lets an untouched old graph re-save byte for byte. A newer file is refused whole, and older ones are
read by the current reader, which tests already assert for versions 1, 2 and 4.

**The migration path has never had a caller.** No version has yet changed the meaning of anything an
earlier one wrote, so there has been nothing to migrate, and writing the machinery now would be the code
for no caller that this project's own rule refuses. The rule for the first change that is not additive
stays in the row: a JSON-to-JSON migration, never against typed models, never deleted, with a golden-file
test. No code changed; the suite stays at **3283**.

### 2026-09-12 — Five decisions from the client, and four blocked items cleared

**Not a code step beyond two workflow files, and the most valuable half-hour of the run so far**: five
of the six things waiting on a person are now answered, and each answer is recorded where the next
session will find it rather than in a conversation nobody can read.

**Spark is released open source (`D25`), and that settles the licensing.** The client asked the right
question — *we are not making Spark open source, so what is the licensing concern?* — and the honest
answer is that it was never about our source. The LGPL duty rides with OCCT's binaries, which we ship
either way. What had teeth was §5: if `spark_occt` were a derivative work rather than a work that uses
the Library, the licence would reach into code we own. Public source makes both readings land in the
same place, so `Q13` stops being six questions for counsel and becomes two publish-step chores worth
doing anyway — ship the shim's source, attach an OCCT source archive.

**Nothing is signed (`D26`).** No certificate is bought, `E12-T9` is withdrawn and `E13-T17` closes with
it. The consequence is written down rather than left to be rediscovered as a bug report: SmartScreen
warns once, the per-user unelevated install keeps Windows from also demanding administrator, and the
SHA-256 beside each artefact is what a careful user checks instead.

**Actions is stopped in the tree, not only in the settings (`E13-T19`, `E13-T20`).** Switching it off in
the repository settings had left three workflows that would all fire the moment anybody switched it back
on. `ci.yml` and `nightly.yml` are now `workflow_dispatch` only. **They are dormant rather than deleted,
and that follows from `D25`**: a public repository's minutes are free, so the four rows blocked on CI —
`E1-T19`, `E1-T21`, `E8-T15`, `E11-T14` — unblock themselves at release with no redesign. What the local
gates cannot replace is said plainly in `E13-T20`: a clean-room build, and the ubuntu leg that once
caught a defect Windows could not.

**STEP is verified by a third party (`E13-T12`).** The client exported a `.step`, imported it into
**AutoCAD**, and worked on it with no issues. That was always the acceptance test — *a third-party
viewer, never our own reader* — so the row closes and `R12` retires in practice. IGES, AP242, assemblies,
names, colours and units are not claimed by it.

**Our own solid kernel: asked, examined, declined (`D2` unchanged).** The client asked whether Spark
could implement its own solid geometry and drop both OCCT and Clipper2. Three findings answered it. The
motive was licensing and self-reliance, and `D25` removes the licensing half. The cost is this project's
own recorded finding — exact surface-surface intersection, tolerant topology, sewing, fillet and STEP are
a multi-year research problem. And `IBrepKernel` already abstracts all 21 operations, so a kernel of our
own would be a second provider rather than a rewrite, which makes the question one that can wait for
evidence instead of a decision today. **Clipper2 was separated from it explicitly**: Boost-licensed, pure
managed, no obligation, one internal file — it carries none of the weight the question was about.

**One thing left with the client**: `Q12`, whether T-Splines is in the parity commitment, which is the
denominator of every coverage figure. The recommendation on file is to exclude it and say so publicly.
The OpenCascade reinstall is also theirs to run, by hand, when the machine is free.

No code changed beyond the two workflow files, so the suite stays at **3283**.

### 2026-09-12 — `E11-T23` step B: the reverse direction, and the 89 name matches reviewed

**Reconciled first, and the tree was ahead of the journal.** The journal said `IN PROGRESS` on
step B with a concrete *Next action*, and `git status` showed the step substantially written:
`DynamoParityChecks.cs` carrying `EveryPublicMemberIsNamedExcusedOrCounted`, an untracked
`tests/corpus/dynamo-parity-exclusions.tsv`, and the 89 reviewed rows already in the manifest.
The write-ahead did exactly its job — nothing had to be re-derived. What was left was the
verification, the documents and the commit, which is the half a dead session loses.

**What the check does.** Of every public member `Spark.Geometry` declares, either a parity row
names it, or a rule in the exclusions file excuses it, or it is counted against a budget. Three
things about that are deliberate:

- **It excuses by rule and never member by member.** 790 of 877 members are named by no row, and
  a file of 790 hand-written excuses would be precisely the drifting artefact
  [DYNAMO-COVERAGE §7](DYNAMO-COVERAGE.md#7-how-this-document-is-kept-true) exists to prevent —
  the `DocGenerator` failure in a new file extension. So: five member-name rules for .NET plumbing
  (`Equals`, `GetHashCode`, `ToString`, `Deconstruct`, `op_*`), and 42 whole types Dynamo has no
  counterpart for, each carrying the §2 or §3 sentence that already said why.
- **A type some parity row names cannot be excused wholesale**, and the check enforces that rather
  than trusting it. Without that rule the exclusions file is a way to make the check green.
- **The residue is checked for exact equality, not as a ceiling.** 278 members sit on types that
  *do* map to a Dynamo type, so each is either a member an `Unassessed` row will name once it is
  assessed or a genuine gap. A ceiling would let the number sit where it is for ever; exactness
  makes it fall as the review proceeds and makes a rise a failure. Same rule `bench/budgets.jsonc`
  applies to performance: a measurement with no budget beside it is not a guard.

**The counting rule had to be made the same on both sides.** `SparkGeometryMembers` was counting
constructors, property accessors and other special-name methods, which is why an earlier count
said 1,021 members. The manifest's own rule — methods, properties, enum values and operators, not
constructors and not accessors — is the one that reproduces DYNAMO-COVERAGE's published totals, so
the reverse direction now uses it too, and the number is **877**. Two counts of "the public
surface" that differ by 144 is not a detail either side can keep to itself.

**The review of the 89 found one row where the name lied**, which is the whole argument for having
marked them rather than shipping them. `PolySurface.Surfaces()` had matched `Brep.Surfaces()`;
Spark's returns the untrimmed surface table in face-index order, Dynamo's returns the trimmed
faces. Demoted to `Unassessed` with that reason, and the faithful equivalent needs pcurves a trim
does not carry yet (`E2-T64`). The other 88 hold, their reasons rewritten from *matched by name;
not yet reviewed* to what was actually checked — and 24 of them are `ToString`, `Equals` or
`GetHashCode`, now saying so rather than counting as if they closed a gap. [N156](NOTES.md).

**Verified.** The new check watched red four ways before it was believed: a type exclusion deleted
(residue climbs past the budget), a type a parity row names excused wholesale (refused by name and
by count), a rule with no reason, and a rule that excuses nothing any more. Green after each was
put back. Then the gates: `dotnet build Spark.slnx --no-incremental -warnaserror` clean with zero
warnings, `dotnet format --verify-no-changes --severity warn` clean, and **3,284** tests over
**ten** executables with zero failures and zero skips — one more than the 3,283 this step started
from, which is the new check.

**Two stale things fixed on the way past**, both found by reading rather than by a test. The
exclusions file's own header said *783 of 870*, written before the counting rule was tightened;
it now says 790 of 877, and the difference is exactly the accessors. And *Current state* carried a
fragment of a long-dead `E8-T13` table row — `ecovery\`, written from …` — left by a bad edit some
sessions ago, breaking the table it sat in. Removed.

**`E11-T23` closes.** All four checks the row asked for exist: well-formedness, the totals, the
rename-catcher, and the reverse direction. The register now has a guard in both directions, and
what remains on the parity rows is assessment rather than machinery.

**Cost.** One session, no surprises in the code, and most of the time in the documents — the
review's 89 rows and the 42 type rules are prose that has to be right, because the next reader
consults them with confidence or the register is worse than nothing.

### 2026-09-12 — `E2-T44` step A: the 33 topology rows assessed

**Assessment, not implementation, and that was the whole point of the slice.** With the parity
register guarded in both directions there is finally a worklist, and §3.5 is the tractable end of
it: 33 members over six types, 6 `Done` by a name match and 27 `Unassessed`. Every one now carries
a real status and what was actually checked.

**19 reachable, 14 not** — and the number matters much less than the shape. *What is there*: the
three tables (`Brep.Faces()`, `Edges()`, `Vertices()`) and `Brep.VertexPoint`; `BrepEdgeView.Curve`
for `Edge.CurveGeometry`; `BrepEdge.Start` / `End`; `BrepEdgeView.AdjacentFaces`;
`BrepFaceView.Loop`; `BrepLoopView.Trim`; `BrepLoopView.Kind` for `Loop.IsExternal`; and
`BrepTrim.IsReversed`.

**What is not is a single gap, twelve times over.** Spark's topology stores each relationship
exactly once and in one direction — face names loops, loop names trims, trim names edge, edge names
vertices — so every member that asks for the reverse has nothing to answer it: `Vertex.AdjacentEdges`,
`Vertex.AdjacentFaces`, `Edge.CoEdges`, `Loop.Face`, `CoEdge.Loop`, `CoEdge.Partner`,
`Face.Edges` / `Face.Vertices`, and `CoEdge.Next` / `Previous` / `StartVertex` / `EndVertex`, which
are cheaper because trims are contiguous. Filed as **`E2-T65`**, with the argument the code already
makes: `BrepEdgeView.AdjacentFaces`'s remarks say a back-pointer array would be a second description
of the same fact, so the answer is an index built on demand, not fields on the records. **A parity
row must not be allowed to undo `E2-T22`** — an object graph would satisfy all twelve and would be
the wrong trade, and the row says so in writing rather than leaving the next session to rediscover it.

**The finding: `Face.SurfaceGeometry()` is not `BrepFaceView.Surface`.** It looks like a match —
same idea, a `Surface` from a face — and it is not: Dynamo returns the **trimmed** face, and
`BrepFaceView.Surface` returns the **untrimmed** surface the face is a window onto. That is exactly
the difference [N156](NOTES.md) had found the day before under `PolySurface.Surfaces()`, found
twice in two days on two different rows. **It is the same root cause and it will keep recurring**
until pcurves land (`E2-T64`): Spark's surface table is untrimmed, Dynamo's face *is* the trim. The
row is `Planned`, not `Done`.

**The reverse-direction check earned itself in its first week.** Naming 13 Spark members flipped
three types — `BrepFaceView`, `BrepLoopView`, `BrepEdgeView` — from *excused wholesale* to *named by
a row*, and the check refused the file by name and by count, exactly as it was written to. Those
three exclusions are deleted; their remaining unnamed members moved into the residue, which **rose
from 278 to 287**. A rise is what the budget exists to flag, so the cause is written into the
budget's own reason rather than absorbed: the next reader sees a rise with an explanation beside it,
or a rise with none, and those mean different things. `BrepShellView` keeps its exclusion — Dynamo
has no shell type — and its reason no longer points at a rule that has been deleted. `BrepLoopKind`
keeps its exclusion but its reason was wrong: it said Dynamo does not expose loop kind, and Dynamo
exposes it as `Loop.IsExternal`; the *type* has no counterpart, which is a different claim.

**Verified.** All four parity checks green, including §3.5's per-type counts after the table grew a
column — the check reads the first two columns by regex, so a measured *Reachable* column could be
added without touching it. `dotnet build --no-incremental -warnaserror` clean with zero warnings,
`dotnet format --verify-no-changes` clean, and **3,284** tests over **ten** executables with zero
failures and zero skips. No new tests, because no new behaviour: this step moved a register and the
documents that read it.

**Cost.** Short, and almost entirely reading — the assessment is 27 judgements about what two
libraries mean by a member name, and the only way to make it worth anything is to write down what
was checked rather than that it was checked.

### 2026-09-12 — `E2-T65`: the topology read backwards, without a back-pointer

**The whole design question was already written down in a remark, and it was right.**
`BrepEdgeView.AdjacentFaces` has argued since it was written that a back-pointer array would be a
second description of the same fact that somebody has to keep in step, and that a caller wanting
the reverse repeatedly should build the index once and keep it. `E2-T44`'s assessment then produced
twelve parity members that want exactly that reverse — which is precisely the pressure that turns
an index-based topology into an object graph one convenience member at a time. **The remark was
followed rather than re-argued**: `BrepAdjacency` is that index, built from a `Brep` in one pass,
held by the caller, and stored nowhere in the model.

**Four of the twelve needed no index at all**, and noticing that was worth more than the code it
saved. A loop's trims are contiguous from `BrepLoop.FirstTrim`, so `CoEdge.Next`, `Previous`,
`StartVertex` and `EndVertex` are arithmetic on `BrepLoopView` — Dynamo answers the same four with
pointers between objects, and here they cost nothing and are stored nowhere. A gap is not always as
deep as the count makes it look.

**What it is.** CSR arrays — offsets plus values — for vertex→edges and edge→trims; flat arrays for
trim→loop and loop→face. Where the relationship is stored the answer is a `ReadOnlySpan<int>` into
the index and costs nothing; where it is derived (`FacesAt`, `EdgesOf`, `VerticesOf`) it is a fresh
array, because deriving means visiting several stored relationships and removing repeats.
**`PartnerOf` returns -1 rather than throwing** when an edge is not used by exactly two trims: a
naked edge is a legitimate model, and a caller walking every trim of an open sheet should not have
to guard each call with the question the method already answers.

**`BrepEdgeView.AdjacentFaces` was deliberately left scanning.** Re-pointing it at the index would
mean building one per call, which is worse than the scan it replaces — so there are now two ways to
ask the same question, and two ways to ask a question means two answers unless something says
otherwise. `TheIndexAndTheScanAgreeOnEveryEdge` says otherwise, over every edge of three fixtures,
and each method's remarks now name the other and say when to use it.

**The fixture is a plate with a square hole**, and it earned its keep immediately. A box has one
loop per face and two trims per edge, so it cannot see either mistake that matters; the plate has a
face with an inner loop and eight edges that are all naked. Mutating the implementation to claim
only a face's first loop turned **four** tests red, including the index-versus-scan agreement.

**Watched red three ways** before any of it was believed: the self-loop guard removed from the
vertex→edge counting pass (one test — the edge that starts and ends at one vertex), a face claiming
only its first loop (four), and `StartVertex` reading its edge's direction instead of its trim's
(one, and only on a cylinder's seam face, which is the one place the two differ).

**Two checks caught this change without being asked to**, and they are the ones worth mentioning.
`GeometryJsonTests.EveryPublicGeometryTypeHasASample` failed because a new public geometry type has
no round-trip sample — `BrepAdjacency` is now excluded with the reason that writing a derived index
would be writing the same fact twice, which is the reason the model does not store it either. And
the residue budget rose a second time, 287 → 293, because `BrepAdjacency`'s own `Of` and five counts
sit on a type parity rows name and so cannot be excused. That is the second legitimate rise in a
day, and [N157](NOTES.md) is what it taught: an exact-match budget is a good guard and a noisy one,
and its running cost is a sentence of prose per change.

**Verified.** 25 new tests. `dotnet build Spark.slnx --no-incremental -warnaserror` clean with zero
warnings, `dotnet format --verify-no-changes --severity warn` clean, and **3,309** tests over
**ten** executables with zero failures and zero skips — up from 3,284. The four parity checks green
with §3.5 at **31 of 33**.

**`E2-T44` closes with it.** The two members still out of reach are `Face.SurfaceGeometry()` and
`CoEdge.ParameterCurve`, and no amount of topology work delivers them: they need pcurves, which is
`E2-T64` and waits on a managed consumer.

**Cost.** One session for the twelve, which is what a gap that is genuinely one gap costs. The
assessment the day before is why — twelve rows filed separately would have been twelve small
arguments about back-pointers, and filed together they were one.

### 2026-09-12 — `E2-T42` step B: `NurbsSurface`, `PolySurface`, and the row closes

**Short, and the value was in three refusals to take an easy match.**

**`IsPeriodicInU` and `IsPeriodicInV` are not `IsClosedU` and `IsClosedV`.** They look like it, they

meet in space — and periodic is a property of the knot vector and of the control net wrapping
smoothly. A closed surface with a seam is closed and not periodic. That is [N156](NOTES.md)'s trap
for the third time in two days, and the third time it was seen coming rather than found afterwards,
which is the only sign the note did any good.

from `Solid` by *closure*, which is tolerance-dependent, so under that scheme a healing operation can
change an object's type. Spark has one `Brep` and asks `IsSolid`. A row can be satisfied by a design
decision rather than by code, and saying so is more useful than either a `Done` naming some unrelated
member or a `Not planned` implying the capability is absent.

**`UnconnectedBoundaries()` became reachable on the day it was assessed.** A naked edge is an edge
exactly one trim uses, and until `E2-T65` built `BrepAdjacency` an edge did not know its trims. Had

date matters as much as its contents.

**§3.3 closes at 36 of 106**, with 25 of the remainder `PanelSurface`'s standing refusals. The
residue budget fell again, 291 → 285.

**What the two steps together have made unavoidable.** Twenty rows across §3.3 now say `Planned`

doing no work, removed by the rule that catches rules doing no work.

**Verified.** The four parity checks green with the residue budget exact at 285 — unchanged across
both `E11-T30` and this step, which is what says the reverse direction is still reading
`Spark.Geometry` alone. Build clean with zero warnings, format clean, **3,309** tests over **ten**
executables with zero failures and zero skips.

### 2026-09-12 — `Chamfer` gets a test, and `E13-T22` is found by writing a node that needed it

**The step set out to do two small things and one of them turned into a kernel defect.**

**The small one first.** `IBrepKernel.Chamfer` had **zero** call sites in the suite — every other
kernel operation had between one and nine — while `E2-T43` had marked two parity rows `Done` against
it hours earlier. It now has two tests. `ChamferingTakesAWedgeOffEveryEdge` asserts a **closed form**:
chamfering a cube of side *a* by *d* removes a prism from each of the twelve edges and a piece from
each of the eight vertices, so `V = a³ − 6d²(a − 2d) − 20d³/3`, which for a 4-cube at 0.5 is exactly
176/3. **The first draft asserted a range, 60 to 63.5, from a half-derivation that dropped the corner
term — and the real answer, 58.666666666666664, fell outside it.** Doing the arithmetic properly was
the difference between a test that checks OCCT and one that checks that OCCT returned a number.
`AChamferTooLargeForTheSolidIsRefused` pins the refusal at `SPK1081`, the same code a fillet that
does not fit gives.

**The other one.** The client ran `--graph solids` and could not tell whether the hollowed box had
been hollowed — because `Solid.Hollow` calls `Shell(solid, [], …)`, an empty face list, so the void is
sealed and the outside is the outside of the original box. **A demonstration nobody can see is not a
demonstration.** So: a `Solid.HollowOpen(solid, openTowards, thickness)` that opens the face whose
normal best matches a direction — a rule rather than an index, for the reason `FilletAll` already
gives about edges — wired into the demo so the wall would show.

**It does not work, and the reason is not in the node.** The test that caught it asserted volume on a
**3 × 3 × 6 block**, because opening a z-face and opening a side give different volumes there and the
same volume on a cube. Asking for the top gave the side's figure. A probe over all six faces:

| managed face | normal | volume when shelled | what that means |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | (0,0,−1) | 26.896 | a z-face |
| **1** | **(0,0,+1)** | **24.256** | **a side** |
| **2** | **(0,−1,0)** | **26.896** | **a z-face** |
| 3, 4, 5 | ±x, +y | 24.256 | sides |

**The managed `Brep` numbers its faces in the order `BrepPrimitives.Box` wrote them; OCCT numbers
them in its own explorer order; and `OcctBrepKernel` passes the caller's ints straight through.** It
is a *permutation*, not corruption — exactly two of six behave like z-faces, so a real face is opened
every time, just not the one asked for. `E13-T22`.

**Nothing shipped is wrong, and that is why nobody saw it.** Every caller in the product passes an
empty list meaning *all of them*: `FilletAll` rounds every edge, `Hollow` opens none. **A permutation
of a whole set is that set**, so the mismatch cancels exactly at every shipped call site — and at
every existing test, all of which passed `[]` too. The suite had complete coverage of the operations
and none of the argument. [N159](NOTES.md) is the general form, and it is not really about OCCT: an
`int` is the one thing that will cross a seam without anybody noticing it has.

**So `Solid.HollowOpen` was written, tested, found broken and deleted in the same step**, and the demo
graph is back to `Solid.Hollow` with a comment saying why the box looks solid. A node whose documented
contract is *opens the face that looks this way* must not ship opening a different one; that is worse
than the invisible hollow it was meant to fix. The fix needs the shim to expose a stable face
identity, and the shim cannot be rebuilt while the OpenCascade install is gone (`E13-T21`).

**The defect is pinned, not merely filed.** `SolidNodeTests.AFaceIndexDoesNotSurviveTheCrossingIntoOcct`
and `TheMismatchIsAPermutationAndNotCorruption` assert the **wrong** behaviour on purpose and say in
their remarks that they are **expected to go red when `E13-T22` is fixed**, at which point the fixer
should delete them and write the positive assertions. A task row can be missed on a reading; a test
cannot be missed on a build.

**Four parity rows gained a caveat**: `Solid.Fillet`, `Solid.Chamfer`, `PolySurface.Fillet` and
`Solid.ThinShell` all cited index-based selection as the Spark equivalent, and now say that only the
whole-set form is correct today.

**Verified.** 74 tests in `Spark.Geometry.Occt.Tests`, up from 69, with **zero skips** — which is what
says the provider really ran rather than the suite quietly passing without it. Build clean with zero
warnings, format clean, **3,314** tests over **ten** executables with zero failures and zero skips.
**One caveat, recorded rather than smoothed over**: the pass immediately after the example graph was
regenerated showed a single UI failure that two subsequent full passes did not reproduce, and its
cause was not established. It is noted here so that a recurrence is a second sighting rather than a
first.

**What this step is really evidence for.** The screenshot was the client's, the question *what should
I test* was theirs, and the answer that mattered — a kernel defect three commits deep — came from
refusing to accept a picture as proof of a claim I had written into the register that morning.

### 2026-09-12 — The dashboard becomes a generator and a gate (`E10-T17`, `E11-T31`)

**What.** The client's instruction: *keep the dashboard updated whenever EPICS, TASKS or TODO is
updated, **without fail***. Recorded in AGENTS.md's standing instruction and its document table —
and then built into something that can actually hold, because the page it applies to was
hand-written HTML carrying about forty derived numbers.

**Why the instruction forced a redesign rather than a habit.** *Without fail* is not a property
hand-maintained numbers can have. This repository has the scar on file: `DocGenerator` was 1,478
hand-maintained entries that drifted until 101 of 108 public constructors rendered blank. So
`scripts/build-progress.py` now derives every number on each run — from TASKS, the parity
manifest, DYNAMO-COVERAGE's section headers, the journal's *Current state* and git — and
`ProgressDashboardChecks` fails the build when the page disagrees with the register. AGENTS.md's
own sentence is the whole argument: **a rule nobody enforces is a preference.**

**It re-derives, it does not re-render.** The generator writes the numbers it used into a JSON
island at the foot of the page; the check parses `docs/TASKS.md` and `dynamo-parity.tsv` *itself*
and compares. Green therefore means two independent readings of the register agree with the page —
not that a script is deterministic, which is all a byte-comparison of a re-run would have proved.
Same shape as `E11-T23`, deliberately.

**Two traps, both hit while writing the parser, both now in the code as comments.** The status
column is *prose* as often as it is a word — `Blocked 2026-09-11 on the toolchain`, `Done, in the
half that is reachable` — so it is normalised on its leading clause, and **an unrecognised cell
fails the test rather than being quietly bucketed**. And the column is not at a fixed index: E13's
table carries an `Est` column the other twelve do not, so reading position 2 counted seventeen
estimates as seventeen statuses. Each table's own header is read now.

**The split that keeps it readable.** Every *number* is derived; every piece of *narrative* — what
a milestone means, what is waiting on a person — lives in the script's `NARRATIVE` block.
Generated prose is prose nobody reads.

**Verified, and the gate was proven to fire before it was trusted** ([N18](NOTES.md)'s standard):
closing `E2-T30` in TASKS without regenerating turned two tests red, naming *the register has 359,
the dashboard says 358* and the command that fixes it. Reverted, green again. Build clean with
zero warnings, format clean, **3,319** tests over ten executables — 3,314 plus this row's five.

**One caveat, recorded rather than smoothed over, and it is a second sighting.** The first full
pass showed **a single `Spark.UI.Tests` failure** whose name was not captured; two further full
passes of that executable were clean. The entry of 2026-09-12 for `E13-T22` records exactly this
shape once already, and `E11-T27` is the open row for it — Avalonia's `Dispatcher.UIThread` is
process-global, so a pure view-model test can race a session test. **That is now twice**, which is
the thing this paragraph exists to make visible; it is not evidence that this step broke anything,
and it is not evidence that nothing is wrong.

indistinguishable), and **these indices are safe where a `Brep`'s are not**, because a mesh index is

`MakeWatertight` is a voxel remesh nobody has costed.

**`MakeWatertight` is not `Welded`, and writing that down was half the value of the pass.** Welding
merges coincident vertices; it does not fill a hole, and `MeshTopology.IsClosed` only reports the
answer. Marking it `Done` would have been [N156](NOTES.md)'s trap a fourth time in four days.

**Two harness corrections, both the register lying in the safe direction** — and they are why this

- **`Spark.Geometry.Io` was not on the rename-catcher's delivering list**, so `Mesh.ImportFile` and

**The residue budget went *up*, 285 to 292, on a step that assessed 60 rows — and that is the

reasoned about: `MeshTopology` 9, `MeshFace` 5, `GeometryJson` 1, each probed by re-excusing it
alone and reading the number; naming eight more `Mesh` members took 8 off. **A rise has two causes
that look identical from the outside**, and only the history written into the budget row at the time
tells them apart — so §7 now says so, instead of asserting that a rise means drift.

### 2026-09-13 — `E2-T46`: §3.8's 89 infrastructure rows assessed, and a solid that cannot be moved

**The step.** The fifth subsystem assessment, and the last one that is not curves or values. 89
members over 8 types, of which **56 were already refused** under §5's rules; the 33 that were open
are `Geometry`'s 29 and `DesignScriptEntity`'s four. §3.8 rewritten with a measured *Reachable*
column: **24 of 89**.

**A reading rule had to be settled before any row could be written, and it is now in the section.**
Spark has no `Geometry` base class and will not acquire one — ADR-0002's value types are `readonly
struct`s and a common base would box every one. So **a `Geometry` row is `Done` when Spark delivers
the capability on the types that carry it, and the section says which types are missing.** Anything
stricter refuses the design instead of measuring it; anything looser is the register lying again.

**The transformation family is 14, not 12.** The section's own list — `Transform` ×2, `Translate`
×3, `Rotate` ×2, `Scale` ×4, `Mirror`, `Scale1D`, `Scale2D` — has always summed to 14 under a heading
that said 12. All 14 are `Done`, through `Transform` factories applied by each type's
`TransformedBy`; three of them (`Scale(Plane, …)`, `Scale1D`, `Scale2D`) are a **composition** —
change basis, scale, change back — which is three calls for Dynamo's one and is exactly what §3.8's
`By*` façade recommendation exists for.

**And then the finding, which is the worst thing this register has turned up: a `Brep` cannot be
moved.** `TransformedBy` is on `Curve`, `Surface`, `Mesh`, `PointCloud`, `PolyCurve`, `PolyLine` and
all seven analytic surfaces, and **not on `Brep`**. `IBrepKernel` has no transform operation and
`Spark.Nodes.Core` has no node. A user can union two solids, fillet every edge, hollow the result and
write it to STEP — and cannot translate it by a vector. **It has been true since M6 and nothing
reported it**: no test, no node, no user. [N161](NOTES.md) records why the register could not have
found it either, and what to do instead — when a row is `Done` because *some* types carry the member,
enumerate the ones that do not, in writing. Filed as `E2-T70`, with the ADR-0021 trap attached: a
`Brep` may be resident in the provider, so a transform is not a matrix multiply over the managed
arrays, and doing it that way produces a shape whose two halves disagree.

**The second finding is one gap wearing four names.** `ClosestPointTo`, `DistanceTo`, `DoesIntersect`
and `Intersect`/`IntersectAll` all fail for the same reason: **Spark's queries take a *point*, never
another geometry.** The point case is not merely present but hard-won — `E2-T62` and `E2-T63` spent
two entire steps making `Surface.ClosestPoint` correct on a fold. Geometry-to-geometry is absent, and
the same hole shows in the intersectors: curve/curve is exact (`E2-T11`), solid/solid is the
kernel's, and **curve/surface and surface/surface have no member anywhere**. Surface/surface is
ADR-0002's research-grade problem and belongs behind the seam; curve/surface is not, and is the half
a managed implementation should own. Also `E2-T70`.

**Three members refused on principle, filed as a new §5 rule [j].** `IsAlmostEqualTo(Geometry)` and
`Approximate()` take **no tolerance**, so they compare against an ambient one — which is precisely
the ground §5 [f] already refuses `GeometryExtension.EqualsTo(a, b)` on while accepting
`Equals(x, y, tolerance)`. **Only the form is refused**: `EqualsWithin(other, in Tolerance)` exists on
eight value types. `ContextCoordinateSystem` is refused on §5 [c]'s different ground — a context frame
is a fact about where a value was *created*, so it needs identity and history, and two `Point3d`s
with the same coordinates are the same value.

**A fifth under-claim, and they have now appeared in every single assessment.**
`DesignScriptEntity.Tessellate(IRenderPackage, TessellationParameters)` was listed as *planned*; the
shape Spark built is the same shape one assembly earlier — `Tessellation.Tessellate(surface,
ITessellationSink, tolerance)`, with `MeshBuilder` implementing the sink and `SceneBuilder` consuming
it. §5 [e] got the reason right (geometry has no screen awareness) and the status wrong.

**The residue moved further than it ever has: 292 → 319.** Naming `Transform.Translation` and five
siblings means `Transform` is a type the register has claimed, so it may no longer be excused
wholesale and its other **28** members come into the count; `Tessellation` added 2 the same way, and
naming `Curve.BoundingBox`, `PolyCurve.Segments` and `CoordinateSystem.ToTransform` took 3 off. Each
contribution measured by re-excusing one type at a time and reading the number, not reasoned about.
**This is the price of a claim, not drift** — excusing `Transform` wholesale while saying it answers
fourteen Dynamo members was the contradiction the check exists to catch, and it caught it.

**The readable-failure change from the previous step paid for itself immediately.** The residue check
reported *two* problems at once — `Transform` excused while named, and the budget off by one — in a
single run. Under `Assert.Empty` the second would have been truncated to `has 2···` and the first
would have been the only thing visible.

**Three more stale numbers corrected**, all re-measured with the same throwaway metadata probe:
`Spark.Geometry`'s members named by no parity row (747 → **735**, against 894 declared), the rows
naming one (180 → **202**, naming **159** distinct members), and the exclusions file's rule count
(39 over 34 types → **37 over 32**).

**Verified.** The four parity checks green with the residue budget **exact** at 319; §3.8's per-type
counts agreeing with the manifest and its *Reachable* column measured from it; `docs/progress.html`

**Cost.** One session, no production code changed. §3.8 rewritten, 33 manifest rows written, two more

### 2026-09-13 — `E2-T70` step A: a solid can be moved, and a mirror no longer turns one inside out

**Why this and not `E2-T41`, said plainly because the queue says otherwise.** `E2-T46` found a
*defect* rather than a bookkeeping error — a `Brep` could be unioned, filleted, hollowed, tessellated
and written to STEP, and could not be **moved** — and a defect found today outranks the sixth audit
pass, which nothing blocks and which will still be there tomorrow. The register work is not delayed
by this; `E2-T41` is next either way.

**What landed.** `Brep.TransformedBy(in Transform)`, plus `Solid.Translate`, `Solid.Rotate` and
`Solid.Mirror` as nodes, and `MeshFace.Reversed()`. Points, edge curves and face surfaces move;
**every index is left exactly as it was**, because an affine map does not change what is connected to
what.

**Three decisions, each of which could have gone the other way.**

*It materialises a resident shape, and the answer was already written down.*
`BrepResidency.Materialise`'s own remarks name *a transform* as one of the structural demands that
read a shape out of its provider, so this is the design being honoured rather than a corner cut. The
alternative — asking the provider to transform the shape it holds, which keeps residency and its
fidelity — is **not available**: `IBrepKernel` has no transform operation, and `E13-T21` blocks
adding one while the shim cannot be rebuilt. That is now in the XML docs rather than left for the
next person to rediscover.

*It needs no provider.* Moving a solid is a construction, not an operation, so it works in a build
with no OpenCascade at all — which matters, because everything else on the `Solid` node palette does
not.

*A non-uniform scale on analytic geometry is refused, by inheritance rather than by catching.* A
cylinder scaled 2× in x is an elliptic cylinder and there is no type for one. The refusal arrives
from the **edge circle** rather than from the cylindrical face, because curves are moved before
surfaces — both would refuse, and the first to notice explains. Written into the test rather than
engineered away.

**The part that is not obvious: orientation, and it caught a live bug elsewhere.** A transform whose
`Determinant` is negative reverses handedness, so each surface's own normal — the cross product of
its parameter directions — ends up pointing the opposite way relative to the moved shape. Every
`BrepFace.IsReversed` therefore has to flip, or a mirrored box is inside out. **What makes it
dangerous is that nothing else notices**: every index is still in range, `Validate()` is still empty,
`IsSolid` is still true. Only the normals are wrong.

**Asking whether `Mesh.TransformedBy` did the equivalent showed that it did not.** It moved the
vertices, inverse-transposed the normals correctly, and left every face wound backwards — so a
mirrored mesh had winding disagreeing with its own normals: negative volume, `FaceNormal` answering
inwards, black in the viewport. That has been live since M5 and nobody reported it, for the same
reason the missing `Brep` transform went unreported: mirroring is rare, and every cheap check passes.
Fixed with `MeshFace.Reversed()`. [N161](NOTES.md) now carries the general form — **orientation is a
property no index checks and no validator validates**, so it survives every structural test a model
has.

**Verified, and the gates were proven to fire rather than trusted** (AGENTS.md step 7).
`AMirroredSolidIsNotInsideOut` and `AMirroredMeshIsNotInsideOut` were run with the
`Determinant < 0` branch replaced by `if (false)` in both files: **both went red**, then green again
when restored. Eight new tests in all — a translated box read back off its vertices *and its bounding
box*, because a model whose points moved and whose planes did not still passes every index check; a
rotated cylinder whose edges, trims, loops and shells are unchanged; a mirrored box whose every face
normal points away from the centre, checked directly rather than through a tessellated volume, which
would need a kernel; a rotation that flips nothing; the non-uniform-scale refusal, with a uniform
scale beside it to show the refusal is about the shape rather than about scaling; `MeshFace.Reversed`
on a triangle and a quad; and — in `Spark.Engine.Tests`, where the residency double lives — a
**resident** solid moved without the caller materialising it first, asserting one materialisation and
`IsResident` false on the result.

**The parity guard fired on this step's own code, which is the first time it has.** The residue check
went red at 321 against 319 on the first build after `Brep.TransformedBy` and `MeshFace.Reversed`
were written, naming both. They are **counted rather than named**, and consistently: the parity rows
for the transformation family name the `Transform` *factory*, because §3.8's whole argument is that
Spark has one mechanism where Dynamo repeats a member per type — so `Curve.TransformedBy`,
`Surface.TransformedBy`, `Arc.TransformedBy` and now `Brep`'s are all counted. The exclusions history
says so.

Build clean with zero warnings, **3,328** tests over ten executables (3,319 plus this step's nine),
zero failed and zero skipped, format clean, docs harness green including the four parity checks and
the dashboard's two gates. The `Solid` help topic gained a *Moving a solid* section with a worked
example, the mirror caveat, the refusal and the materialisation cost.

**Cost.** One session. Two members of public API, three nodes, one help section, eight tests, and a
bug fixed that was not the one being looked for.
### 2026-09-13 — `E2-T41` step A: §3.2's 82 `Curve` rows, and the trim family gets a survivor

**What.** Every one of `Curve`'s 82 parity rows assessed member by member against the delivering
assemblies — the public-API baselines of `Spark.Geometry`, `Spark.Api`, `Spark.Geometry.Io` and
`Spark.Nodes.Core`, never this document ([N160](NOTES.md)). **40 `Done`, 20 `Planned`, 14 `Needs a
decision`, 8 `Not planned`.** It began at five `Done` and 77 `Unassessed`, so the question that
mattered — *is the largest type in the inventory mostly a gap* — had never actually been asked. It
is not. §3.2 rewritten with a measured *Reachable* column for `Curve` and blank for the ten concrete
types that are step B, because a number nobody derived is how a register starts lying.

**The three calls, and why none of them was deferred.** A pass that assesses eighty rows and leaves
every hard one open has not assessed anything.

1. **§5 [i]'s duplicated trim family has a survivor: the `Parameter*` set.** §5 [i] has said since
   the document was written that `Curve`'s `TrimBy*` methods duplicate its `Parameter*` methods
   name-for-name and that Spark ships one set — and then that the family was *uncounted*, because
   which set survives had not been decided. It is decided: [i] itself names `Parameter*` as the
   primary, the capability is assessed on those rows, and the eight `TrimBy*`/`SplitBy*` members are
   refused and **counted**. §5's refused total goes 113 → 121 and the committed surface 555 → 547.
   `SplitByPoints` has no twin in either set and was assessed on its merits rather than swept up.
2. **§6.3's four length parameterisations are half answered.** `DistanceAtParameter` and
   `ParameterAtDistance` are arc length — which is what §3.2 has assumed since the curve contract was
   designed against it — and are `Done` on `Curve.LengthAt` and `Curve.ParameterAtLength`. **What
   `SegmentLength` measures is still not deducible from metadata**, so the six members carrying that
   word are `Needs a decision`. If it is arc length they duplicate members Spark already has; if it
   is a chord walk they do not, and claiming them on the first reading is [N156](NOTES.md)'s trap.
3. **`ApproximateWithArcAndLineSegments` is not refused under §5 [j], though its signature
   qualifies.** [j] refuses `Geometry.Approximate()` for taking no tolerance, and it can, because the
   capability has a tolerance-taking home in Spark to be refused *in favour of*. A biarc
   approximation has no home at all, so refusing this one would file a real gap under a rule about a
   parameter list. It is `Needs a decision`.

**What surprised me.** **Nine of the surviving trim and split family are `Done`, and seven by
composition** — `Curve.Trimmed(in Interval)` is abstract on the base, so `ParameterSplit(t)` is
`Trimmed` twice and `SplitByPoints` is `ClosestParameter` and then `Trimmed`. `E2-T7` recorded *no
`Split`* as a deliberate M1 exclusion and that is still true of the **member**; the **result** has
been reachable since the contract was written, and §2's rule makes the result the subject. Every
such row says *composed* in its reason, because a composition claimed silently reads exactly like
drift.

**The finding is `ToNurbsCurve()`.** Spark has **no curve-to-NURBS conversion anywhere** — not on
the base, not on a type, not as an extension — while `Spark.Geometry.SurfaceConversion` has converted
five of the eight analytic *surfaces* exactly since M5. `Line`, `Arc`, `Circle`, `EllipseCurve` and
`PolyLine` all have exact NURBS forms and not one is written, so the half of the kernel built first
is the half missing the conversion. Twenty gaps in all, filed as **`E2-T71`** in five families:
NURBS conversion, planarity (`IsPlanar` and `Normal`, which also block the two `Extrude(double)`
overloads — they wait on the curve's own normal, not on the kernel), chord stepping, extension, and
projection/pull.

**[N161](NOTES.md) earned itself twice in one step, and the second time by disagreeing with the
first.** `Curve.ToString()` is `Done` and `Surface.ToString()` is `Planned`, and the rows look
identical. The rule is to enumerate the types that do *not* carry the member: for curves the
enumeration is **empty** — all seven concrete types override it, so a `Curve`-typed value prints
itself — and for surfaces only `NurbsSurface` does. Nothing but the enumeration tells them apart.
The same rule made `IsPlanar`'s row name the four curve types that cannot answer it.

**Residue 321 → 318, the first fall since `E2-T42` step B, and the direction is the story.**
Thirteen `Spark.Geometry` members named by the new rows, against ten dragged in by two types the rows
now claim: `CurveOffset`, because `Curve.Offset` names `CurveOffset.Offset`, and `ExtrusionSurface`,
because `Curve.Extrude` names the **type** for the reason `Surface.ByRevolve` names
`RevolutionSurface` — a construction is a constructor and constructors are not counted. `E2-T46` ran
a pass of almost exactly this size and the residue rose **27**. Same shape of work, opposite sign,
and the difference is entirely whether a section's `Done` rows land on types the register had already
accounted for. Written up as **[N162](NOTES.md)**, because it is worth knowing before planning the
next pass rather than after running it.

**Verified.** Build clean with zero warnings, **3,328** tests over ten executables, zero failed and
zero skipped, format clean. The docs harness green on all fourteen checks — `EveryRowIsWellFormed`,
`TheManifestAgreesWithTheCoverageDocument` reading §3.2's per-type counts straight out of the

**exact** at 318. The dashboard regenerated from `scripts/build-progress.py` and its two gates green.
No code changed: this is a register step, and the only thing it could break is the register.

**Cost.** One session. 82 rows, one new task, one note, five documents, and a decision §5 had been
carrying since the day it was written.
### 2026-09-13 — `E2-T41` step B: the ten concrete curve types, and §3.2 closes at 111 of 187

**What.** The 105 rows step A left: `Line` 6, `Arc` 14, `Circle` 8, `Ellipse` 8, `EllipseArc` 9,
`Helix` 7, `NurbsCurve` 15, `PolyCurve` 21, `Polygon` 9, `Rectangle` 8. With step A's 82 that is
**§3.2 assessed in full — 187 rows, 111 reachable**, the largest section in the register and the last
of the geometry sections. `E2-T41` closes.

**Three of the ten types are complete**, which no section has produced before: `Ellipse` 8 of 8,
`EllipseArc` 9 of 9 and `Rectangle` 8 of 8. Two of those three are **the same Spark type** —
`EllipseCurve` answers both Dynamo ellipse types, because an ellipse over a sub-domain is not a second
type — and the third is not a type at all, which is §3.2's own argument paying off.

**Two decisions, and neither was dodged.**

1. **`Helix` goes in** (`D27`, `E2-T73`). It has been `Needs a decision` since the document was
   written — absent from FR-48, never argued against — and the section said plainly that either it
   goes into FR-48 or its absence is recorded as deliberate. The argument that decided it is that a
   helix **travels at a constant speed**, so `LengthAt`, `ParameterAtLength`, `PointAtLength`,
   `DivideEqually` and `DivideByLength` are all closed form and exactly right. That is true of only
   five of the seven types Spark already has; the ellipse needed Gauss–Legendre and Newton for the
   same members. It is the cheapest type this hierarchy can gain, it needs no kernel, and AEC users
   draw it.
2. **`Rectangle` and `Polygon` stay `PolyLine` factories** — recorded as built rather than left as an
   argument. **The price is now visible in the rows, which is the point of recording it**:
   `Rectangle.Width` and `Height` are `Done` as `PolyLine.SegmentAt(0).Length` and
   `SegmentAt(1).Length`, because a rectangle that is a closed polyline has no width property. That
   is the trade the section chose.

**A rule this section had to state, because sixteen rows turned on it.** §2 counts composition, and
step B pushed hard enough on that to need a boundary: **composition means the caller passes members'
results to another member, and it stops counting when the caller has to compute the quantity the
member exists to compute.** `Line.ByTangency(curve, t)` is `Done` — `Curve.PointAt` and
`Curve.TangentAt` feed `Line.FromStartPointDirectionLength`. `Arc.ByCenterPointStartPointEndPoint` is
`Planned` — getting there means working out the sweep angle from two radii, and the sweep angle is
what the constructor is for.

**Three findings, and each is one missing idea rather than a list** (`E2-T72`, 29 rows).

- **There is no curve fitting of any kind.** `Line`, `Arc` and `Circle` each carry a
  `ByBestFitThroughPoints` and not one is written — while `Plane.FromBestFit` fits a plane and
  `NurbsCurve.FitPoints` fits a spline. The machinery and the appetite are both in the kernel
  already; the three closed-form fits are simply absent.
- **Spark's only fillet takes two lines.** `CurveOffset.FilletLines(Line, Line, radius)` is the whole
  of it, and four rows want the generalisation — `Arc.ByFillet`, `ByFilletTangentToCurve`,
  `PolyCurve.Fillet` and `CloseWithLineAndTangentArcs`. Claiming any of them on `FilletLines` would
  be [N156](NOTES.md)'s trap, so each row says what it actually takes.
- **A NURBS curve cannot be periodic**, and `NurbsCurve.IsPeriodic` is [N156](NOTES.md)'s trap for
  the **third** time, after `Surface.IsPeriodicInU` and `Face.SurfaceGeometry()`. `KnotVector` is
  clamped — `CreateClamped` is its only factory — so three rows wait on the same missing knot vector.
  A fourth, `ByPointsTangents`, is the *same* tangent-constrained interpolation `E2-T66` wants on
  `NurbsSurface`: one algorithm short on both sides of the kernel, not two.

**What surprised me, and it is a correction rather than a discovery.** [N162](NOTES.md) was written
in step A, this morning, and it ended with a prediction: *a section whose capabilities are
constructions will cost*. Step B is exactly that section — 105 rows, almost every one a constructor —
and the residue **fell 15**, from 318 to 303, the largest move the number has made. The prediction
was wrong and the reason is worth more than the prediction: `Line`, `Arc`, `Circle`, `EllipseCurve`,
`PolyLine` and `PolyCurve` were **already in the register**, so thirty rows naming their factories
landed on members the assembly declares. One type came off the excused list —
`Spark.Geometry.Planar.Region`, because `Polygon.ContainmentTest` is `Region.Contains` and
`Polygon.Center` is `Region.Centroid` — and it brought twelve members against twenty-seven named. The
corrected rule is that a pass costs what its `Done` rows' **types** cost, and nothing else. N162 keeps
the failed prediction in place above its correction, because a note that quietly rewrites its own
reasoning teaches nothing about how the reasoning failed.

**One row is reachable under both readings of an ambiguous word, which is rare enough to note.**
`Polygon.Center()` — Dynamo does not say whether it is the area centroid or the mean of the corners,
and the two differ. Spark has both: `Region.Centroid()` and the average of `PolyLine.Points()`. So the
register does not have to resolve which Dynamo means, and saying which would be a guess.

**Verified.** Build clean with zero warnings, **3,328** tests over ten executables, zero failed and
zero skipped, format clean. The docs harness green on all fourteen checks: every row well formed,
§3.2's eleven per-type counts read straight out of the rewritten table and agreeing with the manifest,
the rename-catcher confirming all 53 new `Done` rows name members a delivering assembly really
declares, and the residue budget **exact** at 303. Dashboard regenerated and its two gates green. No

**Cost.** One session, with step A. 187 rows, two new tasks, one decision in the PRD, one note and

### 2026-09-13 — `E2-T40`: the value layer re-measured, and the register is finished

**What.** §3.1's 78 remaining rows — `Point` 7, `Vector` 17, `Plane` 10, `CoordinateSystem` 28,
`BoundingBox` 15, `UV` 1 — assessed member by member against the delivering assemblies. **§3.1 is
113 of 133.** With it, **no row of the 837 is `Unassessed`**: `Done` 392, `Planned` 124, `Not
planned` 123, `Needs a decision` 198. §2's headline table is rewritten from those numbers rather
than checked against them, and it moves from **99 of 575 (17.2%)** to **392 of 545 (71.9%)**.

**This is the section that was supposed to break the pattern, and it did not.** The other six all
started from *0 reachable*, so an assessment could only move them up and a gain proved nothing.
§3.1's 99 was a real count — made by hand, in prose, a year ago — and it was the number the whole
document rested on. The write-ahead said plainly, before any of the work: *expect over-claims here
where every other section had under-claims, and say so if the 99 does not survive.* It did not
survive: it was **14 low**. Seventh section, seventh under-claim.

**Where the 14 went, because the pattern has three named mechanisms and this section shows all
three.**

- **Six on `CoordinateSystem`'s transformation family.** The section argues at length — correctly —
  that Spark splits Dynamo's `CoordinateSystem` into an orthonormal frame and a `Transform` carrying
  the algebra, and then **counts the split as six missing members**. `Rotate`, `Mirror`, `Translate`,
  `PreMultiplyBy`, `PostMultiplyBy` and `Determinant` are all on `Transform` and all reachable. This
  is [N158](NOTES.md)'s finding reaching the one section that predates it.
- **Six on `BoundingBox`.** `MinPoint`, `MaxPoint`, `ByCorners` and `IsEmpty` were never counted at
  all, and `ByGeometry` ×2 became reachable **the moment there was geometry to bound** — the
  sentence calling them uncovered was written when Spark had no curves, surfaces, solids or meshes.
  `ToCuboid` and `ToPolySurface` are the *same* member, `BrepPrimitives.Box`, because Spark has one
  `Brep` and open-or-closed is a property rather than a second type.
- **Two on the cylindrical and spherical frame constructors**, which this very task closed on
  2026-09-10 and whose prose still said *planned* — [N160](NOTES.md) exactly: read the assembly,
  never the document.

**One member answers ten rows, and it is worth naming.** `GeometryJson.Serialize` and `Deserialize`
are Spark's whole serialisation surface (FR-57), where Dynamo has a `FromJson`/`ToJson` pair on every
type. Five types' worth of rows, `Done` on two members.

**Two rows settle by being reachable under *every* reading of an ambiguous signature**, which is
rare enough to be worth the pattern name. `BoundingBox.IsEmpty()` is §6.3's *degenerate, zero-volume
or never-initialised* — `BoundingBox.Empty`, `Volume` and `IsValid` answer all three.
`CoordinateSystem.ByCylindricalCoordinates` is *positioned there* or *oriented to those directions* —
`FromOrigin` and `FromOriginXAxisYAxis` answer both. The ambiguity stands; it just decides nothing.
`Polygon.Center` in §3.2 was the first of these.

**Two refusals, counted.** `Vector.IsAlmostEqualTo` joins §5 [j] — the same member on the same
ground one type down, taking [j] from three to four — and `CoordinateSystem.ByOriginVectors`'s
explicit-Z overload is refused on §3.1's own argument, that Spark **derives** Z and an independent Z
is how a caller gets a left-handed frame by accident. `CoordinateSystem.IsEqualTo` is deliberately
**not** refused beside `IsAlmostEqualTo`, and the difference is the whole of [j]: *almost* equal with
no tolerance has to get one from somewhere unstated, and exact equality does not.

**`Q17` is filed, and filing it is the point.** Does Spark want an `OrientedBox`? §3.1 said it was
*recorded as an open question* — in prose, in a coverage document, which is nowhere a decision gets
taken. Six rows turn on it, and they are the only `Needs a decision` rows left in §3.1 and §3.8
outside the T-Splines. The recommendation is yes and later, with the type and `ByMinimumVolume`
separated, because a minimum-volume box is not a box in a given frame but a **search** for the frame.

**Residue 303 → 270**, the largest fall it has made, and **no type came off the excused list** —
every type this section touches was already claimed. It now measures what it says: with nothing
`Unassessed` left, these 270 are not members some future pass will name. They are Spark's own
surface, which is most of them, or a gap in the register. **From here a rise is the only thing that
can mean anything**, and it means exactly what the check was built to catch.

**[N163](NOTES.md)** is the note this step earned: seven passes, seven under-claims, three
mechanisms, and the reason the error can only run one way — an over-claim turns the rename-catcher

### 2026-09-13 — `E2-T70` step B: a curve can be cut by a surface

**What.** `Curve.IntersectWith(Surface, in Tolerance)`, returning `CurveSurfaceIntersections` —
points that each carry the parameter on the curve **and** the `UV` on the surface. It is the half of
`E2-T46`'s *every query takes a point, never another geometry* that a managed implementation should
own: curve/curve has been exact since `E2-T11` and solid/solid is the provider's, and curve/surface
had **no member anywhere**. `Curve.IntersectWithSurface` is the node. `E2-T70` closes.

**How, and the one idea that makes it work.** A surface has no signed distance of its own, which is
why this is harder than curve/plane. One is **built**: at each of 128 samples along the curve,
`Surface.ClosestPoint` gives the nearest point and its parameters, and the displacement from it to
the curve point, dotted with `Surface.NormalAt` there, is a signed quantity that changes sign exactly
where the curve passes through. A sign change is a **hypothesis**, not an answer — the nearest point
jumps across the surface's medial axis — and what confirms it is the refinement: Newton on
`C(t) − S(u, v) = 0`, three equations in three unknowns, Jacobian columns `C′(t)`, `−S_u`, `−S_v`,
solved by Cramer's rule with a **relative** singularity test. Absolute would call every
well-conditioned system on a millimetre-scale surface singular.

**A singular Jacobian is a tangency rather than a failure.** It means the curve's direction has
fallen into the surface's tangent plane, and the fall-back is bisection on the bracketed signed
distance — which cannot converge quadratically and cannot diverge either.

**The anchor found a design error, which is what anchors are for.** The test computes the exact
line/plane intersection — one division — over a hundred pseudo-random cases and requires the general
path to match it **to a nanometre**, a thousand times tighter than the default tolerance. It failed
at once, and the reason was a line I had written deliberately: the refinement stopped as soon as the
residual was inside the tolerance. **The tolerance decides what counts as *meeting*; it does not
decide how accurately the answer is *reported*,** and conflating the two hands back a point that is
only as good as it had to be. Newton converges quadratically, so running it until the residual stops
improving costs two or three more evaluations and lands near machine precision — and the **best**
point seen is kept rather than wherever the loop stopped, which is `Surface.ClosestPoint`'s own rule
([N137](NOTES.md)) earning itself a second time. Had the assertion been written at the tolerance, the
member would have shipped a thousand times less accurate than it can be, and nothing would have said
so.

**One test was wrong and the code was right, which is worth recording.** A circle of radius five
standing across a cylinder of radius three was asserted to cross it twice. It crosses **four** times:
the circle is `(5 cos t, 0, 5 sin t)`, its distance from the axis is `5 |cos t|`, and `5 |cos t| = 3`
has four roots in a turn. The test now carries that arithmetic in its name and its summary, because
the next person to read it will have the same first instinct.

**What it will not do, stated on the member and in the help topic.** A tangency that touches zero
without changing sign between two samples is missed — the same bargain
`GeneralCurveIntersection` makes and states. A curve lying *in* the surface is not a set of points,
and comes back as `LiesOnSurface` with no points rather than as whatever samples were taken. And a
crossing beyond the surface's **patch** is not a crossing: a `Plane` is infinite and a
`PlaneSurface` is the rectangle you asked for.

**Surface/surface is deliberately absent.** ADR-0002 makes it the research-grade problem and it
belongs behind `Spark.Api.IBrepKernel`. So `Geometry.Intersect(Geometry)` stays `Planned` in the
register: a member that has to answer every pair cannot be `Done` while one pair is missing. The row
now says which pairs work and which does not, instead of saying *nothing at all*.

**The one source-level cost, and it is small.** `IntersectWith` is now an overload pair, so
`curve.IntersectWith(null!)` no longer compiles without a cast. That falls on a call nobody makes
outside a test, and the one test that made it says so in its summary.

**Verified.** Build clean with zero warnings, **3,340** tests over ten executables (3,328 plus this
step's twelve), zero failed and zero skipped, format clean. The two tests that matter —
`LineAgainstPlaneAgreesWithTheClosedForm` and `LineThroughASphereGivesTwoPointsADiameterApart` —
were **proved to go red** by disabling the Newton refinement and watching them fail, then restored.
The help topic's worked example is itself pinned by a test, because the topic claims every example on
it was run; and the help-sample compiler caught the first draft of it, where a second fenced block
referred to a variable declared in the first. Residue **270 → 277**, raised with the reason in the
exclusions history: a rise from new code, and the first one since the manifest had no `Unassessed`
row left that could have been hiding it.

**Cost.** One session, after three register steps. Two public types, one public member, one node, one
help section, twelve tests, and a design error caught by an assertion written tighter than the
contract required.

### 2026-09-13 — `E2-T73`: `Helix`, the eighth curve type

**What.** `Spark.Geometry.Helix` over `Curve`: a point turning about an axis at a fixed radius while
rising along it at a fixed rate. Its `GeometryJson` serialisation both ways, a `Helix.ByAxis` node,
a section of the `concepts.curves` help topic with a worked spiral stair, and 26 tests. Filed this
morning out of `E2-T41` step B on decision `D27`; closed this evening.

**Why it is worth a line in this log beyond *a type was added*.** This is the **first step of the
run that builds what the register found rather than measuring it**. Seven passes moved the headline
before today, every one of them by discovering that Spark was already further ahead than its own
prose claimed ([N163](NOTES.md)). `Helix`'s seven rows are `Done` because the type was written:
§3.2 goes from 111 to **118 of 187**, the headline from 392 to **399 of 545**, and `Helix` becomes
the eleventh ProtoGeometry type answered in full — the first of the eleven this register asked for
and then watched get built.

**The shape of the type, and every choice in it was already made somewhere in this layer.** State is
a `Plane` — origin on the axis at the helix's start, x axis pointing at the start point, normal the
axis direction — plus a radius, a pitch and a positive sweep, with
`C(θ) = O + r·cosθ·X + r·sinθ·Y + (pitch/2π)·θ·Z`.

1. **A negative sweep flips the plane** rather than running the domain backwards. That is `Arc`'s
   convention, and the reason is structural: the whole of `Curve` — `CheckParameter`, `LengthAt`,
   every division — relies on `Domain.Min < Domain.Max`. Turning the other way about an axis is
   turning the same way about the opposite one, and **the pitch survives the flip unchanged**,
   because the rise reverses along with the direction it is measured in. Worth checking rather than
   believing, and it was.
2. **`AxisPoint` is reported beside the start, not where the caller put the origin.** Only the axis
   *line* is in the curve: the start point fixes the height at angle zero, so an origin anywhere
   else on the same line names the same helix and there is nothing to preserve. `Arc.StartAngle`
   already reports in the frame the curve holds rather than the one it was handed.
3. **A zero pitch is refused and the message names `Arc`.** A helix that does not rise is a circular
   arc and Spark has one — the same argument as `Circle.Trimmed` returning an `Arc`, that a circle
   which is not closed is not a circle. A **negative** pitch is *not* refused: that is handedness,
   and unlike a negative sweep it cannot be reached by flipping anything, because flipping the axis
   reverses the turn and the rise together.

**The branch that would have shipped wrong, and it is not the one the write-ahead expected to be
hard.** `TransformedBy` scales the radius by the **radial** factor and the pitch by the **axial**
one, and they are different numbers: a transform that stretches along the axis leaves a helix a
helix and changes only its rise. `CircularArcs.TransformFrame` — which `Circle` and `Arc` both use —
returns the radial factor and nothing else, because a circle has no second one to want. Taking it
for both is the easy mistake **and it hides itself**: under a uniform scale the two are equal, so
the result has exactly the right shape and the wrong height, and passes every test that does not
stretch along the axis. `AStretchAlongTheAxisChangesThePitchAndNotTheRadius` and
`AMirrorGivesAHelixOfTheOppositeHand` were both **proved red** with the axial factor replaced by the
radial one, and `ANegativeSweepGivesTheSameCurveTurningAboutTheOppositeAxis` was proved red with the
plane flip removed. Two branches, not one.

**How the arc length is anchored, and what it is deliberately *not* anchored on.** A helix's speed is
`sqrt(r² + (pitch/2π)²)`, which is what the type computes — so asserting that against `Length`
asserts the implementation against itself. The anchor is the **summed chord length of 400,000
samples of `PointAt`**, which contains no closed form anywhere in it and converges on the true
length from below; it agrees to nine figures, and the test also asserts that it is *below*, because
a chord sum that exceeded the curve would mean the sampling was wrong rather than the length. A
second, independent statement of the same fact: a helix **unrolls to the hypotenuse** of a right
triangle whose legs are the arc turned and the height climbed. And the trap the write-ahead named
was real — **every curve except the ellipse travels at a constant speed, so a division test cannot
tell a right answer from a plausible one** (`E2-T7` learnt it once already), so the division tests
check against the analytic arc length and are never the evidence for it.

**What surprised me, and it is the most useful thing in this entry.** Adding
`Spark.Nodes.Core.Helix` beside `Spark.Geometry.Helix` — the same pairing that already exists for
nine other names — **broke `Helix` in every code block in the application**, and the build was clean
and all 3,368 tests passed. A code block's prelude imports both namespaces, so every shared type
name is `CS0104` unless `ReferenceCatalog.NodeLibraryImports` pins it, and that list is **a literal
array written by hand** whose comment read *the nine that collide with `Spark.Geometry`*. There were
ten.

What caught it was the **help-sample compiler**, three documents later, and only because the help
topic for this step happened to include a worked example naming the type. **Had the façade shipped
undocumented, it would have shipped broken**, and the report would have come from a user. This is
written up as [N164](NOTES.md), and the general form is worth stating: *a list that enumerates a
relationship between two artefacts, maintained by hand, is wrong the moment either changes, and its
failure is silent by construction because the list is what would have to notice.* Three guards of
exactly that shape already exist in this repository — `ConstructorParityTests`,
`SolutionMembershipTests`, the exact residue budget. The fourth did not, and the gap was a
`private static readonly string[]`. `CodeBlockLibraryReachTests.EveryCollidingNameIsPinned` now
derives the colliding set by reflection; proved red by deleting the `Helix` pin.

**Residue 277 → 284**, a rise of seven from new code, and the arithmetic is the check working
exactly as designed: `Helix` declares fourteen public members, six are named by the parity rows,
`ToString` is excused by rule, and the seven counted are the `Curve` overrides — `Domain`,
`IsClosed`, `LengthAt`, `ParameterAtLength`, `Reversed`, `Trimmed`, `TransformedBy`. **That is
member for member what `Circle` and `Arc` already contribute**, because the parity rows for the
curve contract name `Curve.Domain` and `Curve.LengthAt` — Spark puts the contract on the base class
where Dynamo repeats it per type — so each concrete curve's override answers no Dynamo member of its
own. A rise of any other size would have meant the type had grown a member with no row behind it.

**Left for `E2-T71`, and it turned out to be a sharper question than it looked.**
`Spark.Geometry.Occt.ModelWriter` has no word for a helix, so it falls to the `default` branch and
exports one by interpolating 64 samples with `Approximated` set. The first draft of this entry said
that was the sharpest case yet for `Curve.ToNurbsCurve` **because a helix has an exact rational
form**. *It does not*, and the proof is three lines — written up as [N165](NOTES.md) and corrected
in the four documents that had already repeated it. A NURBS curve's coordinates are `X(t)/W(t)` and
`Z(t)/W(t)` with all four piecewise polynomial. A helix needs `z = c·θ` and `x = r·cos θ` at once,
so `θ(t) = Z(t)/(c·W(t))` would have to be rational **and** `cos(θ(t))` rational with it — and a
transcendental function composed with a non-constant rational map is never rational. So the
64-sample approximation is **a limit to label rather than a gap to close**, and the real consequence
is for the shape of `ToNurbsCurve` itself: every other curve Spark has converts exactly and this one
cannot, so the member has to say which answer it gave rather than handing back a bare `NurbsCurve`
a caller will assume is exact.

**Cost.** One session. One public type, one node, one help section, one note, 26 tests, two branches
proved red on purpose and a third defect found in a subsystem this step had no business touching.

### 2026-09-13 — `E2-T71` step A: curve to NURBS, and what a conversion result may claim

**What.** `Curve.ToNurbsCurve(in Tolerance)`, virtual on the base, returning a new public
`NurbsConversion` — the NURBS curve and whether it is the *same curve* or an approximation to it.
Exact overrides on `Line`, `PolyLine` and `NurbsCurve`; a base fallback that interpolates a
tessellation and says so. `Spark.Geometry.Occt.ModelWriter` now asks the curve instead of inferring
the answer from its own control flow. Eight tests.

**Why the signature is not Dynamo's, which is the only interesting decision in the step.** Dynamo's
`Curve.ToNurbsCurve()` returns a `NurbsCurve`. Spark's returns a result, and [N165](NOTES.md) —
written yesterday evening, correcting a claim I had made in four documents — is the reason. Seven of
Spark's eight curve types are exactly representable as NURBS. `Helix` is **provably not**, at any
degree, with any knot vector. A member that returned a bare curve would collapse those two outcomes
into one value, and the difference between them is the difference between a downstream boolean that
is right and one that is merely plausible. So the flag travels with the answer. It is the shape
`CurveIntersections` and `CurveSurfaceIntersections` already have, and the flag `ModelWriter` had
already found it needed.

**Why `NurbsCurve` overrides it rather than inheriting.** Left to the base, asking a NURBS curve for
a NURBS curve would sample it, interpolate the samples, and hand back an approximation of the exact
thing that was passed in — reported as an approximation, so not even silently. It is the sort of
loss that only shows up after a model has been round-tripped a few times, and the override costs one
line.

**What the tests are careful about, in two directions.**

- **An exact conversion is asserted as exact**, bit for bit at every sampled parameter, not within a
  tolerance. A tolerance-sized assertion passes for a conversion that is merely a very good
  approximation, which is precisely the distinction `IsExact` exists to make — [N165](NOTES.md)'s
  lesson pointed the other way round.
- **Agreement is a fact about the set of points, not about the parameters.** Above degree 1 an exact
  conversion does *not* visit the curve at the same parameters, because a rational quadratic walks a
  conic by a projective function of the angle. `SurfaceConversion`'s remarks have said this at length
  since `E2-T19`. Degree 1 is the exception — `Line` and `PolyLine` keep their parameterisation —
  and that is pinned by a test rather than left as a happy accident, because a later change to the
  knot vector could take it away without failing anything else.

**The branch proved red is `IsExact` itself.** Flipping the base fallback to report `true` fails
three tests. Without that, a flag that is always `true` on the paths the other tests exercise is
decoration.

**What I found in `ModelWriter`, and it was wrong in both directions.** Its `AddCurve` switch had a
`default` label that called a private `ToNurbs` helper, and *that helper* set `Approximated = true`.
So the flag meant **"the switch fell through"**, not "the conversion was approximate". A curve that
converts exactly but has no case above — which is now every `PolyLine`, since the ABI has no word for
one — was exported perfectly and reported as approximate; and a case added to the switch would have
been reported as exact whether it was or not. The flag is now `|= !converted.IsExact`, which is the
question it was always trying to ask.

**And the same helper was sampling at a flat 64 points.** On a three-turn helix that is a chord every
16 degrees and a deviation of roughly **two per cent of the radius** — not a rounding error, and
measured nowhere. It is now a sag derived from the curve's own length through `Tolerance.ForScale`,
which is what that method exists for: Spark's coordinates are unitless, so a constant sample count is
wrong for a model in kilometres and wrong for one in microns. The OCCT suite runs in the same 19
seconds it did before.

**Residue 284 → 289**, and one judgement inside it worth recording. The five are `NurbsConversion`'s
two members and the three per-type overrides; `Curve.ToNurbsCurve` itself is named by the row it
satisfies and costs nothing. **`NurbsConversion` is counted rather than excused**, where
`CurveIntersections` and `CurveOverlap` are excused types with the same justification written beside
them. The precedent is split — `E2-T70` step B counted `CurveSurfaceIntersections` on that identical
reason — and I followed the later choice deliberately: counting is the conservative direction,
because a counted member stays visible in a number somebody reads every build, and an excused one is
