invisible for ever. That is [N163](NOTES.md)'s argument for an exact budget rather than a ceiling,
applied to the decision of what goes into it.

**Cost.** One session, after the `Helix` step. One public type, one virtual and three overrides, one
help section, eight tests, and a flag in a neighbouring assembly that had been answering a different
question from the one its name asked.

### 2026-09-13 — `E2-T71` step B: the rational curves, and one copy of the quarter-circle

**What.** `Arc`, `Circle` and `EllipseCurve` now convert to NURBS exactly.
`SurfaceConversion`'s private rational-arc helper became an internal `RationalArcs` that both the
surface and the curve layers call. Five tests.

**The work was moving the arithmetic, not deriving it.** `SurfaceConversion.Arc` has produced an
exact rational quadratic for a circular sweep since `E2-T19` and everything hard about it was
already settled and already commented: the control point between two span ends is at the **tangent
intersection**, radius `r / cos(θ/2)` — *outside* the arc — and not at the arc's midpoint; the weight
is `cos(θ/2)` and not `cos θ`; and a sweep past a half turn must be split, because the middle weight
reaches zero at π and the control polygon turns inside out beyond it. Writing that a second time
inside `Circle.ToNurbsCurve` would have been three chances to lose one of those three facts, and the
two copies would have disagreed first about a degenerate sweep, where nobody looks.

**The shared copy justified itself inside the same step.** Replacing `cos(θ/2)` with `cos θ` — the
error the original comment warns about by name — reddens the new curve tests **and eight surface
tests**: cylinder, cone, sphere, torus, and the normals check. That is the whole argument for one
derivation, demonstrated rather than asserted.

**`EllipseCurve` cost nothing beyond the circle.** An ellipse is an affine image of a circle, and an
affine map carries a rational B-spline to a rational B-spline — so the control points, the weights
and the knots are a circle's, mapped through the ellipse's frame with `x` scaled by one radius and
`y` by the other. There is no elliptical construction in the codebase to get wrong, which is worth
more than the lines it saved.

**`Arc` and `EllipseCurve` needed one thing the circle did not: the knots slid back.** Both are
parameterised from their *own start*, not from the plane's x axis, so the control points are built
at their angles in the frame and the knot vector is then shifted by `-startAngle`. Sliding a knot
vector is an affine reparameterisation and leaves the curve untouched. Get it wrong and the result is
the right shape sitting at the wrong parameters — which nothing but the domain would notice, so the
domain is what the test asserts.

**Two tests were wrong and the code was right, and one of them was worth the trip.** The first was an
ordinary slip: I checked the ellipse's radii by evaluating at a parameter I expected to be the end of
an axis, forgetting that the parameterisation is not preserved. It is now stated as the ellipse's own
equation, `(x/a)² + (y/b)² = 1`, which names both radii, separates them, and needs no parameter at
all. The second is more interesting. `AConvertedCircleIsNotTheSameParameterisation` sampled an
**eighth** of the way round — and failed, reporting that the two agreed. They do: an eighth of a full
circle is the **middle of the first of four spans**, and a knot span's midpoint maps to its arc's
midpoint by symmetry. I had picked one of the nine parameters where the rational parameterisation and
the angle coincide. The test now checks a tenth, *and* pins the nine agreements, because they are a
fact about the construction rather than a coincidence and a future change to the span count would
move them.

**Residue 289 → 292** — three overrides, priced exactly as step A's three and as `TransformedBy`'s
always have been, because the parity row names the member on the base. **`RationalArcs` itself adds
nothing**, because it is internal and this number reads the public surface only. That is worth a line
in the exclusions history: moving arithmetic into an internal helper is free in this measure, so the
six overrides across the two steps are the entire price of putting one virtual on `Curve`.

**Cost.** One session, straight after step A. One internal file, three overrides, five tests, and
two test bugs — one of which taught me something about the curve I was converting.

### 2026-09-13 — `E2-T71` family (2): planarity, and the plane a curve lies in

**What.** `Curve.IsPlanar(in Tolerance)` and `Curve.PlaneOf(in Tolerance)`, both virtual on the
base, with overrides on `Line`, `Arc`, `Circle` and `EllipseCurve`. Thirteen tests. It closed five
register rows: the two it is named for, `PolyCurve.BasePlane`, and the two `Extrude` overloads that
were waiting on a curve-wide normal.

**The decision in the step is the name, and it went against Dynamo.** Dynamo exposes
`Curve.Normal` as a property. Spark already has `Curve.NormalAt(parameter)` — the **Frenet** normal,
which points at the centre of curvature and changes along the curve — and a curve-wide `Normal`
beside it would be two unrelated quantities under names one letter apart. That is precisely the kind
of collision a parity register should *catch* rather than import, so the member is `PlaneOf`,
returning the whole frame. Dynamo's `Normal` is `PlaneOf()?.Normal`, and returning a `Plane` rather
than a `Vector3d` means `PolyCurve.BasePlane` is answered by the same member instead of needing its
own.

**Two members, because there are two questions.** *Is there a plane containing this curve* and
*which plane is it* are not the same question, and a **straight line** is where the answers diverge:
it lies in infinitely many planes, so it is `IsPlanar` **true** and `PlaneOf` **null**. Returning one
of the infinitely many would be inventing a rotation the caller did not ask for and could not
predict. That makes `null` mean two things — no plane, or too many — and `IsPlanar` is the member
that separates them. It reads oddly for about ten seconds and is then obviously right, so it is said
out loud in the remarks, in the help topic and in a named test rather than left to be discovered.

**The implementation is one line of arithmetic and one line of judgement.** `Plane.FromBestFit`
returns a plane for *any* set of points whatever — so fitting one and returning it would report every
curve as planar, a helix included. What decides the answer is how far the curve strays from the plane
that was fitted to it, measured against the caller's tolerance. That is the branch, and deleting it
reddens three tests.

**The test that matters is a curve that is nearly planar and is not.** A wildly non-planar curve
fails even a broken implementation, by luck — the fitted plane is so bad that any check passes. The
case that separates working from broken is a cubic with one control point lifted by a hundredth on a
curve ten across: planar at a tolerance of 0.1, not planar at 1e-6. The same curve answering
differently under two tolerances is ADR-0010 stated as a test rather than as a principle.

**One name I invented and caught before committing.** The first draft of the two `Extrude` rows named
`Spark.Geometry.CurveOffset.Extrude` as the member they compose onto. There is no such member — the
extrusion members are the `ExtrusionSurface` *type* and `IBrepKernel.Extrude`, which the direction
overloads already name. I checked because [N160](NOTES.md) says a register has to read the assembly
every time rather than its own prose, and this is the second time in two days that rule has caught
something in a row I was writing rather than in one I was reading.

**Residue 292 → 300**, and the shape is now worth naming rather than re-deriving each step: **adding
a virtual to `Curve` costs one residue per overriding type per member.** `E2-T71` has added three
virtuals across three steps and paid six, three and eight. That is the price of putting a contract on
a base class inside a register built around a per-type inventory, it is not drift, and the
alternative — writing rows for the overrides — would be claiming eight Dynamo members that do not
exist. The exclusions history now says so once, in place of saying it three more times.

**Left undone, and named rather than forgotten.** `CurveOffset.Offset` still asks the caller for a
plane normal where Dynamo infers it. It could now infer it, and that is a change with a
compatibility question in it rather than an oversight, so it is a row of its own.

**Cost.** One session. Two virtuals, eight overrides, thirteen tests, one help section, and one
invented member name that lasted four minutes.

### 2026-09-13 — `E2-T72`'s first idea: curve fitting, of which Spark had none

**What.** `Line.FromBestFit`, `Circle.FromBestFit` and `Arc.FromBestFit`, with a constructor beside
each and a node beside each. `LeastSquares` gained `TryFitLine` and `TryFitCircle`. Fourteen tests.

**It was one step because the machinery was already built.** `LeastSquares` has been internal since
`E2-T40` step B; `Plane.FromBestFit` is on it; `Curve.PlaneOf` started using it this morning. The
file's own remarks have named `Circle.FromBestFit` and `Line.FromBestFit` as future callers since the
day it was written, which is the reason the fit lived in a helper instead of inside `Plane` — and
that decision paid for itself today rather than in principle.

**The line fit is the plane fit read the other way round.** A plane fit wants the direction the
points vary *least* along; a line fit wants the direction they vary *most* along. Both are
eigenvectors of the same covariance matrix. The plane fit can take a row of the covariance's
adjugate directly, because the smallest eigenvector is the adjugate's range when the fit is exact —
there is no such trick for the largest, so the largest eigenvalue comes from the closed-form
**trigonometric solution of the symmetric 3×3 characteristic cubic** and the eigenvector is then a
column of `adj(C − λI)`. Still exact arithmetic, still no iteration and no convergence tolerance,
which is the property that made the plane fit worth writing this way in the first place.

**The two refusals are mirror images, and that is why both belong in one file.** A plane fit refuses
**collinear** points — they lie in infinitely many planes. A line fit refuses points with **no
preferred direction** — a ring, a ball — because every line through their centroid fits as well as
every other. Same shape of ambiguity, opposite end of the spectrum, one degeneracy rule.

**The circle fit is the one with a decision in it, and I measured the decision rather than citing
it.** A circle through scattered 3D points is two fits: the plane first, then the circle within it.
For the second, the *algebraic* (Kåsa) fit minimises `Σ(|p−c|² − r²)²`, which is linear in the
unknowns and therefore a 3×3 solve — and is **exact** for points that genuinely lie on a circle,
whatever arc they cover. What it is not is unbiased: under noise, on a **short arc**, it
systematically under-estimates the radius, because squaring the distance weights the far points
hardest and a short arc has no far side to balance them. So the algebraic answer seeds a
Gauss–Newton refinement of the *geometric* residual, `Σ(|p−c| − r)²`, which is the thing anybody
fitting a circle actually means.

**Removing that refinement makes a 20° arc of radius 10 with a 0.5% wobble come back as radius
9.58**, and leaves every other test in the file green. That is the textbook bias reproduced in this
repository, and it is why the test that decides the implementation is a short noisy arc rather than
a full circle (where symmetry cancels the bias) or exact points (where there is no bias to find).

**Two of my tests were wrong before the code was, and the second was instructive.** The first draft
of the noise test used a wobble of ±0.1 on a 20° arc of radius 10 — and reported a mean fitted
radius of **11.93**. That is not a bug: the *sagitta* of that arc, how far it bulges from its own
chord, is 0.15, so the noise was two thirds of the entire signal the radius is recovered from. The
radius is genuinely indeterminate there, and no implementation rescues it. **A test tuned past that
point measures the conditioning of the problem rather than the quality of the code**, and the fixed
test says so in a comment so the next person does not tighten it back.

**Residue unchanged at 300** — the first step in five that cost nothing. Every new public member is
named by the row it satisfies, and `Circle.FitInPlane`, the half `Arc.FromBestFit` shares, is
internal. Worth noting beside the last three steps' rises: a step that adds *members named by rows*
is free, and a step that adds a *virtual on `Curve`* costs one per overriding type.

**And a pinned screenshot moved.** `MainWindowViewModelTests.TheCreationBoxOrdersEqualMatches...`
pins the exact screenful the client once photographed for the query `circ`, and it now has six
entries rather than five, because `Circle.FromBestFit` is a `Circle` create node and sorts first
alphabetically. That is the ordering rule working. I updated the expectation and added a note saying
the list grows with the library — the cost of pinning a real screen rather than a fixture, which is
a cost worth paying and worth naming.

**Cost.** One session. Two internal fitting routines, three factories, three constructors, three
nodes, one help section, fourteen tests, and two test bugs of my own that taught me more about the
problem than the code did.

### 2026-09-13 — `E2-T72`'s second idea: the general two-curve fillet

**What.** `CurveOffset.Fillet(first, second, radius, normal, tolerance)` rounds the corner where any
two curves cross, returning the arc and the two curves trimmed back to meet it. A `Curve.Fillet`
node over it, aliased to Dynamo's `Arc.ByFillet`. Ten tests.

**The step turns on a stopping point that had expired.** `FilletLines` handles two lines and says in
its own remarks why it stops there: *a fillet between two general curves is a tangency problem solved
by iteration, and it needs curve-curve intersection to know where the corner is at all — neither of
which exists yet*. That was true when it was written. `Curve.IntersectWith` landed in `E2-T11`, and
the iteration is this step. **A comment explaining a limit is a claim with an expiry date on it**,
and the register is what made me re-read this one rather than inherit it.

**The method is offset plus intersect, and both halves already existed.** The fillet's centre is the
point at distance `radius` from *both* curves — which is exactly where their offsets cross. There are
**four** such points, one per combination of which side each curve is offset to, and all four are
genuine tangent centres. Only one rounds off the corner the user can see. **The nearest to the
crossing wins**, which is a rule rather than a consequence, so it is stated in the remarks and pinned
by a test that puts two lines through a full cross and checks the answer is the diagonal one.

**And the crossing is a seed, not the answer.** `CurveOffset.Offset` has exact branches for `Line`,
`Circle` and `Arc` and falls back to fitting a curve through sampled offset points for everything
else — so a centre read straight off two offsets is accurate to the *fit*, and a fillet is a promise
about **tangency**, which is precisely what an approximate centre breaks. The centre is refined by
Newton on `distance(c, first) = radius` and `distance(c, second) = radius`. The gradient of a
distance-to-curve is the unit vector from the closest point, so the Jacobian is two rows of two and
the step is a 2×2 solve, taken in a basis of the plane so the answer cannot drift out of it.

**The test I wrote for that refinement proved nothing, and removing the branch is what told me.**
The first draft used an arc against a line — and both of those offset *exactly*, so the seed was
already the answer and the test passed with the refinement deleted. That is the failure mode
AGENTS.md step 7 exists to catch, caught by doing step 7 rather than by reasoning about it. Rewritten
against a **`NurbsCurve`**, which has no exact offset branch, it fails the moment the refinement goes.

**And my test geometry was wrong before that.** The arc-and-line case originally put the line at
`x = -5` against a circle of radius 5 — which *touches* at `(-5, 0)` rather than crossing. A tangent
pair has no corner, and the fillet rightly could not be built; the error surfaced as *three collinear
points do not define a circle*, four frames deep. The message was accurate and unhelpful, and the
geometry was mine.

**Two failures in the full suite traced to one line.** `[SparkNodeAlias("Curve.Fillet")]` on the
method `Curve.Fillet` is an alias naming its own node, and `ShippedAliasTests.NoAliasCollidesWithARealNodeName`
says exactly that: *aliases that name a live node and can never be reached*. A crash-recovery test
failed alongside it, asserting a banner that named a file and getting the no-file wording instead. I
first thought I had broken the recovery test on its own — a stash-and-compare said so — but the
comparison was confounded: the class run in between had cleaned the per-test store. With the alias
removed the recovery test has been green through four runs including two full suites. I am recording
that as *traced to the alias* rather than as *proved*, because the mechanism connecting a duplicate
node registration to a lost graph origin is plausible and I did not isolate it.

> **Corrected the next day's first step, and the caution above was not enough.** That recovery test
> failed again in `E2-T72`'s third step with no alias anywhere near it. It was **never** related to
> the alias: `CrashRecoveryTests.ACopyThatDiffersFromItsFileIsOfferedByName` leaves **two**
> leftovers — the helper that produces the text crashes a session and leaves a fileless copy of its
> own — and then asserts which of the two the banner describes. The two are written milliseconds
> apart and the order is not stable, so it failed about one run in ten. The four green runs I cited
> were luck, and *traced to* was a conclusion I should not have drawn from them: a test that fails
> one run in ten will look fixed by any change at all, four times running, about two thirds of the
> time. The fix is in that step's entry.

**Residue unchanged at 300**, the second step running. `CurveOffset.Fillet` is named by the row it
satisfies and the three helpers under it are private.

**Two rows got smaller rather than closed**, and saying which is worth more than leaving them
`Planned` with their original reasons. `Arc.ByFilletTangentToCurve` is this solve with a third row
and the radius as a third unknown. `PolyCurve.Fillet` is this member over `PolyCurve.Segments` with
the joins rebuilt — bookkeeping rather than algorithm, plus §6.3's undeducible second flag.

**Cost.** One session. One public method, three private helpers, one node, one help section, ten
tests, two test bugs of my own, and one alias that broke two suites.

### 2026-09-13 — `E2-T72`'s third idea: a NURBS curve that closes smoothly

**What.** `KnotVector.CreateUniform` and `KnotVector.IsUniform`;
`NurbsCurve.FromPeriodicControlPoints` with a constructor beside it; `NurbsCurve.IsPeriodic`.
Twelve tests. `E2-T72` is finished — all three of the ideas `E2-T41` step B found.

**The row is `IsPeriodic` not being `IsClosed`, and everything else follows from taking that
seriously.** A closed curve's ends meet. A periodic curve's ends meet **smoothly**, with the
derivatives agreeing up to `degree - 1`. A clamped curve whose last control point sits on its first
is closed and is *not* periodic, and it has a visible kink at the seam. That curve is in the test
file as the **control**: it passes every assertion about positions — both curves' ends coincide to
1e-9 — and fails every assertion about derivatives. Without it, a test suite about periodicity is a
test suite about closure wearing a different name, which is [N156](NOTES.md)'s trap and would have
been its third outing after `Surface.IsPeriodicInU` and `Face.SurfaceGeometry()`.

**It needed no new evaluation code, and finding that out before writing any was the useful part.**
The previous step's *Next action* predicted the opposite: *the basis-function span search and the
domain check both assume a clamped vector today, and both are in `NurbsCurve`'s hot path*. I checked
that claim first, because a step that touches the hot path is a different step from one that does
not — and it was wrong. `KnotVector`'s constructor asks for non-decreasing finite knots and a
non-empty domain and **never asked for clamped**; `FindSpan` binary-searches the interior spans and
its only concession to clamping is a loop over repeated end knots that simply does not run. So a
periodic curve is the textbook construction — an unclamped uniform vector with the first `degree`
control points repeated at the end — and every existing member evaluates it correctly **without
knowing there is a seam**. Which is also the reason the derivatives agree: the seam is an ordinary
interior span, and there is nothing there to be discontinuous.

**And it found a latent defect that had been predicted in a comment and not guarded.**
`NurbsCurve.IsClosed` compared the first and last *control points*, under a remark that read *a NURBS
curve can be closed by repeating its first control points at the end (a periodic vector) or by
placing the last control point on the first, and only the second is visible in the data*. That
sentence names the case the implementation cannot see — and the implementation shipped anyway,
correctly, because nothing could build a periodic curve. The day one existed, `IsClosed` called a
curve that plainly closes open, and a test I had just written caught it. **A comment that says what
a member cannot see is a test that was never written.** It now recognises both constructions, and is
**cached in a field**, because `Curve.CheckParameter` reads `IsClosed` on every evaluation and the
honest repair — comparing `StartPoint` with `EndPoint` — would have cost two curve evaluations per
`PointAt`.

**The flag is a separate factory rather than a `bool` parameter**, which is Dynamo's shape and not
Spark's. `NurbsCurve(points, degree)` is clamped; `FromPeriodicControlPoints(points, degree)` is
periodic. A flag that decides *which of two constructions happens* is a second construction, and a
reader of the call should not have to look up what `true` meant. `ConstructorParityTests` then
insisted the constructor mirror **all three** of the factory's parameters including its defaults —
same shape, not merely usable — which is a sharper rule than I had remembered and is right.

**A flake I mis-diagnosed yesterday, settled properly.** `CrashRecoveryTests.ACopyThatDiffersFrom...`
failed again, with no alias anywhere near it. The previous entry recorded it as *traced to* a
duplicate node alias on the strength of four green runs; that was luck. The real cause is in the
test: the helper it uses for its *text* gets that text by crashing a session, which leaves a
**second** leftover with no file — so the store holds two, and the test asserts which one the banner
describes. They are written milliseconds apart and the order is not stable. It now empties the store
between the two, and asserts `OfferRecovery()` returns **exactly one**, so a stray copy fails loudly
instead of flaking. Both entries carry the correction. **A test that fails one run in ten looks
fixed by any change at all, four runs running, about two thirds of the time** — which is the reason
ten consecutive green runs is this repository's standard for a flake and why four was never evidence.

**Residue unchanged at 300**, the third step running. `KnotVector` is an excused type and the two
`NurbsCurve` members are named by their rows.

**Cost.** One session. Two knot-vector members, one factory, one constructor, one property, one
cached repair to a member I did not set out to touch, twelve tests, and a flake that had been in the
suite longer than any of today's work.

### 2026-09-13 — `E2-T71` family (3): chord stepping, and division from a parameter

**What.** `Curve.DivideByChordLength(chord)` and an overload taking a start parameter;
`Curve.DivideEquallyByChord(segments)`; an overload of `DivideByLength` taking a start parameter.
Three nodes over them. Fourteen tests. Four register rows.

**A chord is not an arc length, and everything here follows from that.** `DivideByLength` walks the
curve with a tape measure. A chord step asks: from where I am, which point ahead is `d` away *as the
crow flies*? On a tight curve that point is much further along than an arc step of the same size. The
anchor is a circle, where both answers are closed forms this repository does not contain — a chord of
`d` on radius `r` subtends `2·asin(d/2r)`, an arc step of `d` subtends `d/r` — so the tests pin the
answer instead of restating the implementation. On a **line** the two agree exactly, which is worth
pinning and is also why a line can never be the case that decides anything here.

**The branch that matters is the bracket, and not the refinement.** Distance from a fixed point is
*not* monotone along a curve that bends back. Hand a solver the whole remaining domain and it will
find *a* point at the right chord distance — possibly the one most of the way round a circle rather
than the one just ahead — and the result looks like a plausible division that has skipped most of the
curve. So the curve is walked forward in arc-length steps of a quarter chord until the distance first
reaches it, and only then bisected. Replacing that walk with a single bracket over the whole domain
reddens three tests, including a unit circle divided by a chord of 1, where every step must advance
by sixty degrees and not by three hundred.

**`DivideEquallyByChord` is an outer solve, because no marching rule lands on the far end.** Walk
with a chord that is too small and the last step falls short; too large and it overshoots. So the
*chord* is what is solved for, bisected between `|start − end| / n` — a floor by the triangle
inequality — and `Length / n` — a ceiling, because `n` chords of `d` consume at least `n·d` of arc.
It can fail: the bisection assumes a longer chord reaches further, which a curve doubling back inside
one step breaks, and it **throws** rather than returning separations that are only nearly equal.

**One boundary cost a debug and was worth it.** Six chords of 1 close a unit circle exactly — and the
walk returned six points where seven were right. The sixth step lands on the end of the domain, where
the distance comes back as the chord less an ulp or two, so the step was refused and the loop came
back with a gap in it. That is the opposite of what `DivideEqually` promises for a closed curve, and
the fix is a relative slack at exactly one place: the sample that has run off the end.

**Residue 300 → 299, and the direction is new.** Every fall this number has made before came from an
*assessment* naming members that already existed. This one came from **building**: the two new member
names are covered by the rows they satisfy, and `Curve.DivideByLength` — which had been sitting in
the residue unnamed since it was written — is now named, because the overload answering the
from-a-parameter rows shares its name. **A step that added public API lowered the count**, which
sounds like a contradiction and is not: the residue counts members no row accounts for, and building
the from-a-parameter form is what finally gave an old one a row to belong to.

**I made the same mistake as two steps ago.** A `SparkNodeAlias` naming its own node —
`Curve.DivideByLengthFromParameter` on the method `DivideByLengthFromParameter`. `ShippedAliasTests`
caught it again, immediately and by name, which is the guard doing its job twice; the slip is mine
and is now recorded twice so the third time is harder to make.

**Two rows got harder rather than easier, and that is worth saying.** §6.3's
`PointsAtEqualSegmentLength` and `PointsAtSegmentLengthFromPoint` stay `Needs a decision`. Before
today, *segment length* had one plausible reading in Spark; now it has **two**, because both measures
exist and either would look right. A capability arriving can make a register row harder to answer,
and pretending otherwise would be the guess §6.3 exists to refuse.

**Cost.** One session. Four public members, three private helpers, three nodes, one help section,
fourteen tests, one off-by-an-ulp at a closed curve's seam, and one alias I have now written twice.

### 2026-09-13 — `E2-T71` family (4): extension, which Spark had none of

**What.** `Curve.Extended(atStart, atEnd)`, virtual on the base, with exact overrides on `Line`,
`Arc` and `Helix`. A node over it. Thirteen tests. Three register rows closed and two re-described.

**Its absence was load-bearing, which is the best argument for a member there is.**
`CurveOffset.Fillet` — written two steps ago — has to refuse a pair of curves that does not already
cross, because nothing in Spark could make them cross. `Trimmed` only ever narrows. That is now a
test: two lines that miss each other, a fillet that throws, both lines extended, the fillet made.

**A type that can continue itself does; everything else gets a straight tail.** A `Line` becomes a
longer line, an `Arc` and a `Helix` a wider sweep — all exact, and all cheap for the same reason the
last four steps have kept leaning on: those curves travel at a **constant speed**, so a requested arc
length is a division rather than an integral. A curve with no cheap continuation is extended along
its own end tangent and comes back as a `PolyCurve` with straight tails. That is always available,
always tangent-continuous, and — the part that matters — **visible in the returned type**, so the
difference is something the caller can see rather than something they have to know.

**`EllipseCurve` takes the tail on purpose, and writing down why is the point.** Its equation
continues perfectly well past its domain. Its *speed* does not stay constant, so turning *two units
of extension* into *how much more sweep* means integrating outside the range its own arc-length
machinery was built for. A worse version of the exact answer is not better than the honest linear
one, and an undocumented near-miss would have been the worst of the three.

**The branch that hides here is which end.** `atStart` and `atEnd` differ only in a sign, and a sign
error is invisible on a symmetric curve — a centred arc extended at the wrong end looks exactly like
one extended at the right one. So every test uses an **asymmetric** curve and asserts that the end
*not* asked for did not move. Swapping the two arguments reddens three tests, including the
fillet one, which is a pleasing way for a defect to surface: the fillet stops being possible.

**One clamp worth naming.** An arc extended past a full turn stops at a full turn. A sweep beyond
`2π` is a curve that passes through its own points twice; `Arc.FromPlaneRadiusAngles` refuses it, and
an extension that reached past it would have been smuggling a shape in through a side door. When both
ends are extended and the total would overrun, the surplus comes off the **end** rather than being
shared, because a caller extending both ends of an almost-closed arc means *close it* and the start
is where the arc is anchored.

**Residue 299 → 302**, three overrides, and the pattern named two steps ago now has four data
points — six, three, eight, three. It is also worth seeing beside the step immediately before it:
family (3) **lowered** this number by giving an old member a row, family (4) raised it by adding
overrides, and both were steps that wrote code. The number moves in both directions during
construction, which it could not do while the register was only being read.

**Two rows were re-described rather than left alone.** `PolyCurve.ExtendWithArc` and
`ExtendWithEllipse` still say `Planned`, but their reasons used to read *extension, which Spark has
none of on any curve type*. That is no longer true, and the rows would have been misleading in a way
nothing would catch. They now say what actually separates them: `Extended` **continues** the curve —
along its own tangent, or its own equation — where those add a shape the **caller** specifies by
radius and angle. Different constructions that sound alike, which is exactly the confusion a register
exists to prevent.

**Cost.** One session. One virtual, three overrides, one protected validator, one node, one help
section, thirteen tests — and no alias naming its own node, which after two in one day counts as
progress.

### 2026-09-13 — `PolyCurve.ToNurbsCurve`: the last conversion that need not have been approximate

**What.** `PolyCurve.ToNurbsCurve` converts exactly, by converting each segment, raising them to a
common degree and joining. Four tests. No new register row — `Curve.ToNurbsCurve` was already
`Done` — but its reason changed, because what it was `Done` *about* changed.

**The work is knot bookkeeping and the geometry is free.** Every curve type a polycurve can hold
already had an exact conversion after steps A and B, and `NurbsCurve.WithDegreeElevated` already
existed and was already exact. So this is: convert, elevate the lower-degree pieces, lay each
segment's knots onto its own unit of the polycurve's domain, and concatenate.

**The counting was done in the write-ahead rather than in a debugger, and that paid.** Two clamped
degree-`p` curves of `n₁` and `n₂` control points join to one of `n₁ + n₂ − 1` — the shared endpoint
counted once — which needs `n₁ + n₂ + p` knots. Taking all of the first vector and all but the
leading `p + 1` of the second gives `n₁ + n₂ + p + 1`: **one too many**. Dropping the first vector's
*final* knot lands it — **and that is the same edit that leaves the seam value at multiplicity `p`
rather than `p + 1`**. The off-by-one and the continuity are one correction. Writing it out before
writing code meant the first build was right, which is not how this usually goes.

**The branch proved red is the seam, and it is the kind that hides.** Repeat the seam knot once too
few and the curve is *smooth where the polycurve has a corner*. It still passes through every
vertex. It still has the right length to several figures. It still samples correctly everywhere
except within a knot span of the join. So the assertion has to be **at the corner** — the tangent
either side of the seam, a right angle for a right-angled join — and the test curve has to actually
have a corner, which a polycurve of tangent-continuous pieces does not.

**One segment that cannot convert makes the whole thing inexact.** A `PolyCurve` can hold a `Helix`,
and [N165](NOTES.md) says a helix is provably not a NURBS curve at any degree. Rather than claim an
exactness one segment cannot support, the member falls back to the base's sampling and reports
`IsExact` as false. An unclamped segment — a periodic curve used as a piece of a chain — takes the
same path for a different reason: the join arithmetic assumes clamped ends, and quietly producing a
wrong curve would be worse than an approximate right one.

**Which finishes something worth stating plainly.** Every curve type in Spark that *can* be
converted exactly to NURBS now is, and the single one that cannot is the one that provably never
will be. That sentence was not available this morning: `ToNurbsCurve` did not exist, the claim that a
helix converts exactly was written in four documents, and `PolyCurve` was on a list of things to get
round to.

**Residue 302 → 303**, the seventh type to override that one virtual, one each time. After seven
rises and one fall the number is doing nothing surprising, which is worth recording once and then
not again.

**Cost.** One session, and a short one. One override, one private helper, four tests, and an
off-by-one found on paper.

### 2026-09-13 — The tangent-constrained interpolation, and the decision no test of tangency can see

**What.** `NurbsCurve.InterpolatePointsWithTangents`: a curve through given points that leaves the
first in a prescribed direction and arrives at the last in another. Seventeen tests. The first
`NurbsCurve` node file, carrying `InterpolatePoints` as well, and a help section with two compiled
examples. `ByPointsTangents` moves to `Done`, and the register stands at **419 of 545**.

**It is `InterpolatePoints` with its end conditions replaced, and nothing else.** Two more control
points, two more rows. The derivative at either end of a clamped curve is a closed form in the first
two — or last two — control points, so the two new rows have two entries each and no derivative
basis was needed. The knots are the same averaging over the chord parameters with the first and
last repeated once; for a cubic that is Piegl and Tiller's Eq. 9.50, and the augmented-list form
gives it for any degree, so `AveragedKnots` was called rather than copied. The first build was
clean and the seventeen tests passed on their first run, which is the second step in a row where
the write-ahead did the debugging.

**The decision was the derivative's magnitude, and it is the failure no test of the stated property
can see.** A caller gives a direction. The solver needs a vector. The length is a free choice, and
*every* choice makes a curve exactly tangent to the direction asked for — a wrong one bulges or
flattens the ends and passes every tangency test there is. The rule taken, unit direction times the
total chord length, was written in the write-ahead and tested the only way it can be: five points on
a quarter circle of radius 10, the circle's own end tangents, and the result required to stay on the
circle *between* the samples.

**Three numbers, from mutating the implementation** (AGENTS.md step 7), now [N166](NOTES.md):

| Derivative used | Worst distance from the circle | Tangency tests |
|---|---:|---|
| unit direction × total chord length (shipped) | 0.0014 | green |
| the same, tripled | 0.29 | **green** |
| the end chords, directions ignored | 0.11 | seven red |

The middle row is the one that matters: a curve two hundred times worse and every assertion about
tangency still green. That is why the arc test exists, and why the magnitude rule is in the
member's remarks rather than left as an implementation detail a caller could not discover.

**Two points and two tangents are the cubic Hermite**, and the closed form — the ends, and a third
of the derivative in from each — is asserted control point by control point. It is the case with an
answer that does not come from the solver, and it also goes red under the tripled derivative, as it
should: the closed form fixes the magnitude too.

**The node layer had no NURBS node at all.** `InterpolatePoints` has been in the kernel since M3 and
was reachable from no graph. That is not a gap the register could see — it counts kernel members —
and it was found because the help rule asks for a worked example and an example wants a node to
name. One file, two nodes, the Dynamo names as aliases, `curves.md` §14.

**The curve work pauses here, on purpose.** The previous session's plan was that after this row the
curve work stops and `E2-T66`…`E2-T69` begin, and nothing found today argues with it: what remains
of `E2-T71` waits on the ray caster, and what remains of `E2-T72` is `PolyCurve` and `Arc`
bookkeeping on no critical path. The row stays open and says so. `E2-T66`'s `ByPointsTangents` on
`NurbsSurface` is now this solver applied along each parametric direction, with the magnitude rule
already decided.

**The eleventh collision, and this time the guard fired first.** Adding `Spark.Nodes.Core.NurbsCurve`
beside `Spark.Geometry.NurbsCurve` made `NurbsCurve` ambiguous in every code block, exactly as
`Helix` did in `E2-T73` — and the guard written after that, `EveryCollidingNameIsPinned`, failed the
run and named the fix in its message, on the same build rather than three documents later. One line
in `ReferenceCatalog.NodeLibraryImports`, and the help samples compiled.

**Residue unchanged at 303**, the fourth step running: the member is named by the row it satisfies,
and the node type lives in `Spark.Nodes.Core`, outside the count.

**Cost.** One session, and a short one. One member, one node file, seventeen tests, one help
section, one note, and a mutation script run twice.

### 2026-09-13 — The principal directions, and the test surfaces that could not see them

**What.** `Surface.PrincipalDirections`: the two directions a surface bends least and most in,
paired with the curvatures `PrincipalCurvatures` returns. Fifteen tests. Two nodes — the curvature
family had none — and a section in the solids help topic. `PrincipalDirectionsAtParameter` moves to
`Done`, and the register stands at **420 of 545**.

**It was nearly free, and it was.** `PrincipalCurvatures` formed the first and second fundamental
forms, took the two eigenvalues of the shape operator and discarded the eigenvectors. The forms now
live in one private helper that both members call, `PrincipalCurvatures` is three lines, and the
new member is the eigenvector solve on top: each direction is the null vector of a row of
`II − κI`, in the parametric basis, mapped into space through the first derivatives. **The row is
chosen, not assumed.** Near an umbilic one row of that matrix can vanish to rounding while the
other does not, so the one with the larger coefficients is used. The second direction is the
normal crossed with the first — the same vector in exact arithmetic, and exactly orthonormal in
floating point, which a second eigenvector solve would not be.

**The umbilic is written down rather than thrown.** On a sphere, on a plane, and at isolated
points on most surfaces, both curvatures are equal, every direction is principal and there is no
eigenvector to find. The member returns the normalised `u` derivative and the normal crossed with
it: a valid orthonormal pair of principal directions, chosen by the parameterisation rather than
the geometry, and the remarks say so because the return value cannot.

**The branch is the pairing, and the suite could not see the other failure until a saddle was
added.** Two mutations (AGENTS.md step 7). Swapping the two directions: the cylinder, the torus
and the saddle go red — the zero curvature no longer runs along the axis, the larger curvature no
longer goes over the tube — while every test of unit length, orthogonality and tangency stays
green, which is exactly why those tests are not the claim. Returning the parametric directions in
place of the eigenvectors: **the torus and the saddle go red, for different reasons.** Every
analytic surface in the suite — plane, sphere, cylinder, cone, torus, an extruded circle, a
revolved line, a ruled surface between two circles — is parameterised *along its principal
directions*, so `du` and `dv` are the right directions on all of them, and the torus fails only
because the shortcut pairs them with the wrong curvatures; the cylinder passes even that, since
its `u` direction happens to carry the smaller curvature. A suite built from analytic surfaces
cannot tell an eigenvector solve from a shortcut except through the pairing. The bilinear patch through four alternating corners is `z = xy`, the smallest surface
whose principal directions are the diagonals of its parameter square, and it is in the file for
that reason alone.

**Nothing else surprised.** A sphere's poles are degenerate and `PrincipalCurvatures` throws there
too, so the grid test samples strictly inside the domains, as the existing curvature grid test
already did. The curvature nodes take their parameters as fractions and return each pair as a
two-item list, which is the shape `Curve.Fillet` already returns three curves in.

**Residue unchanged at 303**, the fifth step running: the member is named by the row it
satisfies, and the helper record is private.

**Cost.** One session, and a short one. One member, one helper, two nodes, fifteen tests, one help
section, and a mutation script run twice.

### 2026-09-13 — `Surface.ToNurbsSurface`, and *exact* turning out to be two claims

**What.** `Surface.ToNurbsSurface` on the base, so a `Surface`-typed value can be asked at all,
and the three types that had no conversion — extrusion, revolution, ruled — now have one. A new
result type, `NurbsSurfaceConversion`. Twenty-four tests. The `Surface.ToNurbs` node, which took a
sphere and now takes a surface, and a section in the solids topic. Both `ToNurbsSurface` rows move
to `Done`, and the register stands at **422 of 545**.

**The three new conversions are each one idea.** An extrusion is the profile's NURBS curve with a
second row of control points translated by the sweep: degree `p × 1`, the profile's weights in
both rows. A revolution is Piegl and Tiller's A8.1 — each profile control point swept by the
rational circle, in its own plane perpendicular to the axis, at its own radius, with the weights
multiplying. A ruled surface is two rails brought to one degree and one knot vector and laid into
a net two rows deep. None of them needed new arithmetic: `RationalArcs` had the circle,
`WithDegreeElevated` and `WithKnotInserted` had the merge.

**The finding is that *exact* was two claims wearing one name, and the ruled surface is where
they come apart.** A ruling joins its two rails at **equal parameters**. An `Arc` converts to a
rational quadratic that traces the same curve and visits it in a different order — which the
curve side has documented since `E2-T71` and which nothing had yet *depended* on. So two rails
that are each exactly right rule a **different sheet**: correct along both edges, wrong
everywhere between them. `NurbsConversion` gained `PreservesParameterisation` beside `IsExact`,
the surface twin carries both, and a ruled surface is exact only when both rails keep theirs. A
ruled surface between a line and a circle reports itself inexact, and that is not a gap: it is
the honest answer.

**The base refuses rather than sampling.** There is no surface interpolation to approximate with
— `InterpolatePoints` is a curve member — so a fallback would have had to invent one, and a
silently invented approximation is the claim `NurbsConversion` exists to stop. Instead a
reflection test requires every concrete surface type to declare its own override, so a tenth
type cannot ship quietly wrong.

**Three mutations, and one of them corrected me** (AGENTS.md step 7):

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| the merge runs one way only | three red, by refusing |
| a ruled surface is exact when both rails are | two red |
| knots matched with `==` inside the merge | **green** |

The third is the one worth keeping. I had written that the merge's own tolerance was
load-bearing, and it is not: the comparison that protects it is
`KnotVector.Multiplicity`'s, which has taken a tolerance since it was written and says why in its
own remarks. Mutating *that* to `==` turns four control points into five — two knots a single unit
in the last place apart, and a zero-length span in both rails. The test now pins the count, the
remark names the right member, and this is the first test in the repository that proves that
tolerance earns its place. **A claim about which line matters is a claim, and this one was wrong
until it was mutated.**

**Two smaller things.** `ToNurbsSurface` takes a tolerance, as the curve member does, and it
reaches only the profile conversion — an extruded helix measured against its *profile* tightens
from 1e-1 to 1e-4 with it. Measuring that same deviation through `Surface.ClosestPoint` instead
reports 0.038 however fine the conversion is, because the seed grid is 16 × 16 and the helix
turns through 540°: the test measures on the curve, and says so, because an assertion that cannot
move is not an assertion.

**Residue 303 → 310**, ending six steps of no movement, and the whole rise is the price of an
honest answer: three members on `NurbsSurfaceConversion`, `PreservesParameterisation` on
`NurbsConversion`, and the `ToNurbsSurface` overrides on the three surface types the register does
not excuse wholesale. Returning a bare `NurbsSurface` would have cost nothing here and a great
deal later.

**Cost.** One session. One virtual, nine overrides, one result type, two internal curve helpers,
twenty-four tests, one help section, one node widened, and a mutation that made me rewrite a
paragraph I had already written.

### 2026-09-13 — `Surface.Offset`, which is exact where a curve offset is not

**What.** `Surface.Offset(double)` on the base, a new `OffsetSurface` type carrying the general
case, and four analytic overrides that return their own kind. Twenty-six tests, a serialization
case and its sample, a node, and a section in the solids topic. The row moves to `Done` and the
register stands at **423 of 545**.

**The finding is one sentence: an offset is exact for every surface, and a curve offset is not.**
I expected to be writing the surface analogue of `CurveOffset` — sample, fit, report a deviation —
and the write-ahead is where that turned out to be wrong. `CurveOffset` approximates because it
must return a `NurbsCurve`, and the offset of a polynomial curve is not polynomial: the
*representation* cannot hold the answer. `Surface` is not a representation. It is an abstract
evaluatable type, and `S(u, v) + d · N(u, v)` is a perfectly good surface. So `OffsetSurface`
holds the true offset, exactly, and approximation is deferred to the one place it is actually
forced: asking that surface for a NURBS form. Which it **refuses**, naming
`ApproximateWithTolerance` as the capability that would answer — a refusal that now points at the
next step.

**The cone is the decision worth recording, because the obvious shortcut is wrong.** A plane, a
sphere, a cylinder and a torus all offset to their own kind over the *same* parameter domain. A
cone does not. Its offset is the same infinite cone with the base radius grown by `d / cos α` —
but the patch ends move *along the axis* by `d · sin α` as well, so a `ConicalSurface` with the
original height range is the right cone trimmed in the wrong place. It would look right, have the
right type, and be a different patch. The cone therefore uses the general wrapper, which is
exactly right, and the reason is in the remarks rather than in a commit message nobody will find.

**Two mutations, and the second is the one the write-ahead predicted** (AGENTS.md step 7):

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| the general offset goes the wrong way | eleven red |
| the sphere shortcut subtracts instead of adding | four red |

The second matters because it leaves a **perfectly good sphere of the right radius** — every
test that measures a radius passes, and so does every test that checks the type. What catches it
is the test that compares each analytic shortcut against `OffsetSurface` over the same surface,
point for point. That is the comparison a careless cone shortcut would have failed, and it is why
the shortcuts are tested against the general answer rather than against expectations of their
own.

**Residue 310 → 319**, and all nine are `OffsetSurface`'s own public surface. A new surface type
costs its whole surface — the same arithmetic `RevolutionSurface` produced in `E2-T42` — and here
it is the right price, because the offset is exact *precisely because* it got a type of its own
rather than being fitted into a `NurbsSurface`.

**Cost.** One session. One virtual, one new surface type, four overrides, a serialization case,
twenty-six tests, one node, one help section.

### 2026-09-13 — The surface fit, and a measurement that had to be taken somewhere else

**What.** `Surface.ApproximateWithTolerance` and `NurbsSurface.InterpolatePoints`. Sixteen
tests, a node, two parity rows to `Done`, and the register at **425 of 545**.

**Two rows, one algorithm, and the order was forced.** An approximation of a surface is *sample
a grid and interpolate it*, so the grid interpolation had to exist first — and that is
`NurbsSurface.ByPoints`, a row I had not planned to touch. It is Piegl and Tiller's A9.4, which
is the tensor-product form of the curve interpolation Spark has had since M3: solve the banded
system along `u` for every row of the grid, then along `v` for every column of what that
produced. No new solver, no new knot arithmetic. `ChordLengthParameters`, `AveragedKnots` and
`SolveInPlace` went from private to internal, which is the whole of the plumbing.

**The branch is where the deviation is measured, and it is the only hard thing here.** An
interpolating surface passes exactly through the points it was built from. So a deviation
measured at those points is **zero for every grid, however coarse** — a two-by-two grid would
report a perfect approximation of a sphere, the refinement loop would exit immediately, and
every test asking *is the result close* would pass, because the result is close at the places
the test looked. The measurement is taken at the midpoints between samples instead, and moving
it onto the samples turns five tests red.

**A mutation corrected the write-up, for the second step running.** I had written that averaging
the chord parameters across the grid was load-bearing and that taking one row's would fail on
real data. Replacing the average with the first row's parameters leaves **every test green**.
The reason is that a tensor-product interpolation passes through its grid for *any* parameter
values that keep the system non-singular — the parameters change the shape *between* the
points, and nothing in this suite measures that against a reference surface. The averaging
stays, because it is the standard construction and the cheap alternative has no argument for
it, but the remark now says it is **unguarded rather than safe**, and says what a test would
have to do. Two steps running, a mutation has changed a paragraph I had already written; that
is the practice working rather than failing.

**`OffsetSurface` is why this member exists, and it is in the tests.** Yesterday's step gave
Spark a surface type with no exact NURBS form, which refuses to invent one and names
`ApproximateWithTolerance` in the refusal. That refusal now has something to point at: an
offset cone approximates to a ten-thousandth and the test asserts both halves — that the
conversion still throws, and that the approximation works.

**One small decision worth recording.** A grid with a collapsed row — the pole of a sphere — is
accepted rather than refused. The degenerate line has no chord lengths to contribute, so it is
skipped in the averaging and the other lines carry the parameterisation. Refusing would have
ruled out every surface of revolution, which is exactly the shape somebody sampling a surface
has.

**Residue 319 → 320**, the smallest rise this number has made while building, and the reason is
that both new members were asked for by name in the register. The one that costs is
`ApproximationSampleLimit`, the ceiling on refinement, which is Spark's own machinery on a type
a row names.

**Cost.** One session. Two public members, three helpers promoted to internal, sixteen tests,
one node, and a mutation that rewrote a paragraph.

### 2026-09-13 — Projection, and what actually bends

**What.** `Surface.Project`, for a point and for a curve. Seventeen tests, two nodes, the row to
`Done`, and the register at **426 of 545**.

**The row's whole point is that this is not `ClosestPoint`, and the test had to be tilted to say
so.** The closest point on a surface is the shortest way onto it; a projection is where you
arrive travelling the way you were pointed. On a plane square to the direction those are the
same place — so a test built on a flat ground plane would pass for an implementation that simply
returned the nearest point. On `z = x`, projecting straight down from `(2, 0, 6)` lands at
`(2, 0, 2)` and the nearest point is `(4, 0, 4)`, both computed by hand. The mutation that
answered with `ClosestPoint` turned seven tests red.

**The member is mostly reuse, which is the good kind of step.** A projection is a line crossed
with a surface, and `Curve.IntersectWith(Surface)` has existed since `E2-T70`. So the line is
sized from the surface's own bounding box, the hits come from an intersector that is already
tested, and the new code is the ordering and the bookkeeping.

**Two orderings that are easy to get wrong, and both are tested.** Hits come back ordered
**along the direction** from the point, not by distance from it — so a point inside a cylinder
gets the hit behind it first and the one ahead second. And a miss is an empty answer rather
than an exception, because a projection that misses is a fact about the geometry.

**The finding was a premise of mine that was wrong, and it took a failing test to see it.** The
curve overload first sampled the curve with `Tessellate`. A tessellation subdivides where the
**curve** bends — and a straight line does not bend, so it tessellates to its two ends. Its
shadow across a pipe, interpolated through two points, was the straight chord *through* the
pipe rather than a curve lying on it, and the test measuring the radius read 2.87 instead of 3.
**What bends is the shadow, not the curve, and the curve knows nothing about the surface's
curvature.** The sampling is therefore fixed and generous at 200 points — the same choice
`CurveOffset.OffsetSamples` made, for a reason I had to rediscover rather than read.

**The shadow breaks where it leaves the surface**, rather than being joined across the gap. A
line projected across a torus from above lands on the tube, misses over the hole, and lands
again: two curves, not one. Joining them would draw a curve across a place the surface is not,
and the mutation that joins them turns that test red.

**Three mutations** (AGENTS.md step 7):

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| answer with the closest point | seven red |
| return only the nearest hit | two red |
| join the shadow across gaps | one red |

**The curve case is approximate and says so.** The exact projection of a curve is a
surface-surface intersection, which Spark does not have — `Curve.Project` and
`Curve.PullOntoSurface` are the register's rows for that and stay open. But every point returned
was *found* on the surface rather than computed towards it, so what is approximate is only the
path between them, which is a much smaller claim than *this curve is approximately on the
surface*.

**Residue 320 → 321**, the one member being `ProjectionSamples` — the second public constant of
its kind after `ApproximationSampleLimit`, and both exist because a resolution had to be chosen
rather than derived, and a caller should be able to read it instead of guessing.

**Cost.** One session. Two overloads, one constant, seventeen tests, two nodes, and a premise
corrected by a number that was 2.87 when it should have been 3.

### 2026-09-13 — Every surface says what it is, and a loft that is honest about its count

**What.** `ToString` on the eight concrete surface types that lacked it, with a reflection
guard; and `RuledSurface.FromLoft`, the ruled loft over a sequence. Sixteen tests, a node, two
rows to `Done`, and the register at **428 of 545**.

**Two small rows in one step, because neither is an algorithm and both are the same shape of
gap** — a capability that is complete on one type and absent on the rest, which is
[N161](NOTES.md)'s subject.

**`ToString` is that note's example almost exactly.** Only `NurbsSurface` overrode it. A
`Surface`-typed value therefore printed its class name — `SphericalSurface` — which is not
wrong, looks entirely plausible in a debugger, and tells you nothing about *which* sphere. That
is why it survived: there is no failure to notice. Each type now names itself and something it
measures, and the guard is by reflection, requiring every concrete type to declare its own
override. Deleting one turns it red. It is the second such guard on `Surface` in two days,
after `ToNurbsSurface`'s, and the pattern is worth naming: **where a capability belongs to
every type, the test is a reflection sweep and not a list**, because a list is a thing to
forget to update.

**A second test earns its place by catching what the first cannot.** A reflection guard is
satisfied by an override copied from the type next door, which would then lie confidently. So
the descriptions must also begin with their own type's name and differ from one another.

**`ByRuledLoft` is a different result rather than a missing capability**, and that was already
in the register before this step — the assessment recorded in `E2-T42` that N curves give N − 1
ruled surfaces in Spark against one in Dynamo. Building it confirmed the reading rather than
overturning it: one surface would have to be either a `Brep` of N − 1 faces, which is
`Brep.Join`'s job, or a NURBS surface lofted through all the curves, which does not rule
straight between consecutive ones and is a different construction. The member returns the list
and the remarks say which alternative was rejected and why.

**The branch proved red is the pairing, not the count.** Pairing every curve with the first
still returns N − 1 surfaces, still returns `RuledSurface`s, and still passes any test that
checks how many there are. What catches it is the test asserting that surface *i* runs between
curves *i* and *i + 1* — by reference identity, so it cannot be satisfied by a coincidence of
geometry.

**Residue 321 → 341, and not one of the twenty is code this step wrote.** The eight `ToString`
overrides are excused by the member rule and cost nothing. What costs is *claiming two types*:
naming `PlaneSurface.ToString` and `RuledSurface.FromLoft` in parity rows takes both types off the
excused list, because a type a row names is a type whose whole surface the register has to account
for — so their other nineteen members arrived in the count. **That is the third time this exact
arithmetic has run**, after `E2-T42`'s `RevolutionSurface` and `E2-T45`'s `MeshTopology`, and I
walked into it again. The check caught it on the commit, which is what it is for.

**And the step committed red, which is its own lesson** ([N167](NOTES.md)). The verification was
chained behind a `grep` of the test output — and `grep` exits 0 when it *finds* something, so
matching `[FAIL]` reported success. The docs harness was failing for the reason above and the
commit went in anyway. Caught on the next run and fixed in the commit after; the rule is that a
runner's exit code is the gate and a grep of its output is a report.

**Cost.** One session, and a short one. Eight overrides, one factory, sixteen tests, one node.
`E2-T66` has one item left.

### 2026-09-14 — `Surface.Join` closes `E2-T66`, and three guards fire at once

**What.** `Brep.FromSurface` and `Surface.Join`. Seventeen tests, a node, two rows to `Done` —
and **`E2-T66` is closed**, eighteen members over six steps. The register stands at **430 of
545**.

**The row's own blocker is what the step removed.** `Surface.Join` had said, since `E11-T30`
assessed it, that `Brep.Join` concatenates BReps and the kernel's sew merges them but *a
surface has to become a face with a loop first, which is `BrepBuilder` work and not a
one-liner*. That was right, and it was also the whole step: `Brep.FromSurface` wraps a surface
as a single face bounded by its own four boundaries, which `IsoCurveU` and `IsoCurveV` already
give at the domain extremes. The join on top of it is three lines.

**What joining does and does not promise, said once.** It makes one shape out of several
sheets. It does **not** make them watertight: two surfaces meeting along an edge keep their own
copies of it, because merging coincident geometry needs a tolerance and is the kernel's sew —
which `Brep.Join`'s own remarks already said of vertices, and which is now said of this member
too, where a caller will actually read it.

**A degenerate boundary is dropped rather than refused.** A whole sphere's `v` extremes are its
poles, where the boundary is a single point; the loop closes with three edges. That is this
kernel's existing position rather than a new one — `RuledSurface` has always described a cone
as ruled between a circle and a degenerate point-curve — and keeping the zero-length edge turns
that test red. **The check needed a tolerance and not a comparison with zero**: a pole's
iso-curve has a length that is tiny rather than exactly nothing, and the first version
compared against `0.0` and kept all four edges.

**Three mutations** (AGENTS.md step 7):

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| the face is built reversed | eight red, every count still right |
| one edge wound the other way | refused by `AddLoop`, naming the position |
| degenerate boundaries kept | one red |

The second is worth noting because the failure is *better* than a test: `AddLoop` checks
closure when the circuit is added and says *the loop is broken at position 1: the previous edge
ends at vertex 0 and this one starts at 1*. That message was written into `BrepBuilder` long
before this step and it is exactly what a caller building a loop by hand needs.

**Three other guards fired on this commit, and every one of them was right.** The alias check
caught the node aliased to its own name — unreachable, and it would have shipped. Constructor
parity asked for `Brep(Surface)` beside `Brep.FromSurface`; that one is exempted with the
reason, because a second construction path into the type whose invariants are the most
expensive in the kernel to get wrong buys a call that reads no better. And the residue check
caught `Brep.FromSurface` itself. **Three guards, three different subsystems, one commit** —
which is the strongest argument for the ones written earlier this run.

**And the gates were run properly this time.** Yesterday's near-miss ([N167](NOTES.md)) was a
commit chained behind a `grep` of test output, which passes when the grep *finds* a failure.
Every suite here was run into a file and checked by its exit code, which is how the three
failures above were seen at all.

**`E2-T66` is closed.** Eighteen members, six steps: the curvature directions, `ToNurbsSurface`
on the base, the offset, the fit and the grid interpolation, projection, `ToString` and the
sequence loft, and the join. Every one of them was a row somebody had written a reason into
months earlier, and in four cases the reason turned out to name the whole of the work.

**Cost.** One session. One factory, two overloads, one exemption, seventeen tests, one node.

### 2026-09-14 — The four mesh primitives, and a mutation that proved nothing

**What.** `MeshPrimitives` with `Plane`, `Cuboid`, `Sphere` and `Cone`. Eighteen tests, four
nodes in a new `Mesh` node file, four rows to `Done`, and the register at **434 of 545**.

**`E2-T67` was skipped, and skipping it is the right call rather than an omission.** It was the
next row by number, and its own text says it is **blocked in practice by `E13-T21`**: mass
properties belong on `IBrepKernel`, a new kernel member means a new shim function, and the shim
cannot be rebuilt because the OpenCascade install is gone. The previous *Next action* had also
misnamed that row — it called `E2-T67` *`BrepPrimitives` has no sphere and no cone*, which is a
sentence from `E2-T66`'s text. Reading the row rather than trusting the note is what caught it.

**The row's own distinction turned out to be the whole design.** `E2-T45` filed these with the
observation that a mesh primitive is *not* a Brep primitive tessellated, because **its argument
is a subdivision count and not a tolerance**. That is exactly right and it decides everything:
these build their grids directly, they are quad-dominant, and the caller gets a net they can
index into rather than whatever density a tolerance implied.

**The branch is the seam, and my first mutation was too weak to prove it.** A sphere's last
column of vertices must *be* its first column. I mutated the ring loop to emit a duplicate
column — and every test stayed green, because the face indexing still wrapped with a modulo and
never referred to the duplicates. The mesh had unused vertices and identical topology. Only the
second mutation, which also changed the faces to *use* the copies, split the seam: four sphere
sizes red, each naming its naked-edge count.

**That is the second time in this run a first mutation proved nothing** — the other was
`E2-T66`'s knot tolerance, which turned out to be guarded somewhere other than where I claimed.
The lesson is the same both times and worth stating plainly: **a mutation has to change the
answer, not merely the code.** A mutation that leaves the output identical has tested the
mutation, not the test.

**A cuboid is deliberately not closed.** Its six sides do not share vertices, because a box's
edges are creases: one shared vertex would mean one normal where the surface has two, and every
renderer would round the corner off. So `IsClosed` is false for it, which is the truthful answer
about that vertex set, and `Mesh.Welded` is there for a caller who wants the other trade. Both
halves are in the remarks, because a reader who finds `IsClosed` false on a box will otherwise
file a bug.

**Three guards fired, and one of them was two days old.** The node type `Mesh` shadows
`Spark.Geometry.Mesh` and broke two existing node files that returned the kernel type
unqualified — which is the `NurbsCurve` collision of two days ago, in the same place, caught by
the same compiler. The code-block catalog needed `Mesh` pinned, which is the guard written after
`Helix` walked into it. And three aliases named their own nodes.

**Residue unchanged at 342.** `MeshPrimitives` is a new public type, but all four of its members
are named by the rows they satisfy, so the type is claimed and costs nothing — the opposite of
two steps ago, where naming one member of an excused type cost nineteen.

**Cost.** One session. One type, four members, four nodes, eighteen tests, and a mutation run
twice because the first one did nothing.

### 2026-09-14 — Two mesh queries, and a name that carries a decision

**What.** `MeshTopology.Edges()` and `Mesh.TriangleCentroids()`. Twenty-four tests, two nodes,
two rows to `Done`, and the register at **436 of 545** — which is **80.0%** of what Spark has
committed to.

**`Edges()` is the smallest member in its row and the data was already there twice.**
`EdgeCount` counts distinct edges by walking the twin array; `NakedEdges()` hands out the
unpaired ones. So the enumeration existed in two places and was exposed in neither. What the
member adds is the one rule that makes it correct: **emit a halfedge only when it has no twin,
or when its own index is the lower of the pair.** No set, no second pass.

**The branch is the count, not the contents, and that is the interesting part.** An
implementation that emits every halfedge returns *real* edges, with the right endpoints, in a
sensible order — and each interior one twice. Every test asking *are these edges* passes on it.
What catches it is asserting the count against `EdgeCount`, which is computed a completely
different way, so the two agreeing is evidence rather than a tautology. That mutation turns
nine tests red.

**`TriangleCentroids()` carries a decision in its name that Dynamo never had to make.** Dynamo's
meshes are triangles. Spark's `MeshFace` may have four corners — so a member called *triangle*
centroids has to say what it does with a quad, and the two answers are not equivalent. It
averages the corners the face actually has. The alternative, splitting quads into triangles
first, would return **more points than there are faces**, destroying the one property a caller
uses: that the result pairs index for index with `Faces()`. The name is kept because it is what
somebody coming from Dynamo will search for; the remarks say what it really is.

**The quad is the branch**, and the test is built so the value separates the two implementations
rather than merely the count: the fourth corner is at (9, 10, 20) while the other three are near
the origin, so ignoring it gives (1, 2, 0) against the correct (3, 4, 5). Five tests red.

**The alias guard fired for the third step running**, this time on `Mesh.Edges` aliased to its
own node name. Three steps, three collisions of the same shape — a node named for the kernel
type it wraps, then a method whose alias repeats the name the node already has. Each time the
guard named it exactly and the fix was one line.

**Residue unchanged at 342.** Both members are named by the rows they satisfy.

**Cost.** One session, and a short one. Two members, two nodes, twenty-four tests.

### 2026-09-14 — `Mesh.Explode`, and a decision the row left open

**What.** `Mesh.Explode`. Eleven tests, a node, the row to `Done`, and the register at **437 of
545**.

**The row said this was *the one the topology already answers*, and it was right.** A
connected-component walk over `MeshTopology.AdjacentFaces` — a queue, a visited array, and one
new mesh per component. The hard part had been done when the halfedge structure was built.

**What the row did not say is what *connected* means, and the two readings give different
answers.** Faces sharing an **edge**, or faces sharing a **vertex**? They agree on almost every
mesh and disagree on the one that matters: two parts joined at a single corner. This takes
edge-adjacency — it is what `AdjacentFaces` answers, and it is what a person means by a piece,
something you could pick up on its own. **The decision is in the remarks and pinned by a test**
rather than left for a caller to discover: the mutation that walks `FacesAroundVertex` instead
turns exactly one test red, and that test exists for no other purpose.

**The branch is the renumbering, not the split.** Each piece carries only the vertices its own
faces use, with the indices rewritten. A piece that kept the original vertex array would have
the right faces, the right geometry, render identically and round-trip — and report a vertex
count belonging to a mesh it is no longer part of. The only assertion that sees it is the count,
and that mutation turns three tests red.

**Two smaller things worth having decided.** A mesh already in one piece returns **itself**
rather than a rebuilt copy, which makes the common case free. And the optional channels —
normals, texture coordinates, colours — travel across by the same renumbering, so a coloured
mesh explodes into coloured pieces rather than losing what it had at the split.

**Residue unchanged at 342**: the member is named by the row it satisfies.

**Cost.** One session, and a short one. One member, two private helpers, eleven tests, one node.

### 2026-09-14 — Smoothing, and a true claim that nothing was checking

**What.** `Mesh.Smoothed` and `MeshTopology.VerticesAroundVertex`. Fourteen tests, a node, the
row to `Done`, and the register at **438 of 545**.

**The neighbour set was the missing piece, and it deserved a name.** `MeshTopology` could
answer *which faces touch this vertex* and *which edges exist*, but not *which vertices are
joined to this one* — which is precisely what Laplacian smoothing averages over. It could have
been a private loop inside the smoother. It is a public member instead, because it is a
question about topology rather than about smoothing, and the next member of this row will want
it.

**The boundary is pinned, and that is the decision the member makes.** A vertex on an open edge
has fewer neighbours and they are all on one side, so averaging drags it inwards. Smooth an
open grid a few times without pinning and it **shrinks away from its own outline** — while
looking perfectly smooth in the middle, which is why no test of the interior can see it. The
assertions are that boundary vertices have not moved at all and that the bounding box has not
changed; unpinning turns four tests red.

**And a mutation found an unguarded claim, for the third time in this run.** The remarks said
every pass reads the previous pass's positions rather than its own partial results, so the
answer does not depend on the order vertices happen to be stored in. That was **true** — and
nothing was checking it: mutating the loop to update in place left all thirteen tests green.
The fix is a test that pins it directly. At full strength, one pass must put each free vertex
*exactly* at the average of its neighbours' **original** positions, which an in-place update
cannot do because some neighbours have already moved. Fourteen tests now, and the mutation
turns the new one red.

**Three times this run a mutation has caught a claim nothing was testing** — the knot tolerance
in `E2-T66`, the parameter averaging in the surface fit, and this. Two of those were left as
documented gaps because no reasonable test existed. This one had an easy test and simply did
not have it, which is the better outcome and the more embarrassing one.

**One thing recorded rather than fixed.** A closed mesh has no boundary, so smoothing shrinks
it — that is what Laplacian smoothing does, not a defect, and there is a test asserting the
shrinkage so nobody reads it as one. Taubin's λ|μ smoothing is the answer if shrinkage ever
matters, and it is a different member.

**Residue 342 → 343.** `Smoothed` is named by its row; `VerticesAroundVertex` is not, because no
Dynamo row asks for it — Dynamo has no `MeshTopology`. It is Spark's own machinery on a type a row
names, the same category as the two sampling constants earlier this run.

**Cost.** One session. Two members, fourteen tests, one node, and a test written because a
mutation proved it was missing.

### 2026-09-14 — A polyline asked about itself, and my arithmetic corrected by the code

**What.** `PolyLine.SelfIntersections`. Eleven tests, a node, the row to `Done`, and the
register at **439 of 545**.

**The gap was structural rather than geometric, which the assessment had already said.**
`Curve.IntersectWith` takes *another* curve. Every intersection query in Spark takes the other
thing — so a curve could not be asked about itself at all, and the one shape that matters most
is exactly that: a closed outline that crosses itself, which is what a badly traced boundary
is. The geometry was already there; what was missing was the question.

**The branch is the closing segment, and it fails in the direction that hurts.** Consecutive
segments meet at their shared vertex by construction, so those pairs are skipped. On a **closed**
polyline the last segment is consecutive with the first — and an implementation that skips only
the `i, i + 1` pairs reports a plain rectangle as self-intersecting at its own first corner.
That is not an edge case; it is every well-formed outline anybody draws. The mutation turns
five tests red, including every regular polygon.

**The implementation corrected my arithmetic, which is worth writing down.** A test asserted
that a polyline doubling back crossed itself at `x = 3`; the member said 8/3, and the member
was right — the last segment runs from `(4, 4)` to `(2, -2)`, so it meets `y = 0` at two thirds
along, where `x = 4 − 4/3`. The test now carries that derivation in a comment rather than the
bare number, so the next reader can check the claim instead of trusting it. **A hand-computed
expectation is only better than the implementation when the hand computation is right**, and
the way to keep that honest is to show the working.

**Two smaller things decided.** Parameters come back on the *polyline*, not on its segments, so
the result can be fed straight to a split. And a crossing in plan that does not meet in space
is not a crossing — there is a test with a segment passing five units above another.

**O(n²), and the remarks say so rather than apologising for it.** A sweep line is the right
answer above a few thousand segments; this is a member people call on outlines with tens, and a
